In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discourse on the Tafsir of Surat al-Baqarah

Know that Surat al-Baqarah is Madaniyyah (revealed in Madinah) by the consensus of the scholars (a'immah). It is reported from some scholars that he said: it is disliked to name it "Surat al-Baqarah." The better course is to say: "the surah in which the cow is mentioned," and likewise for the other surahs of this kind. The more correct view, however, is that it is permissible, because of what is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he threw the pebble at Jamrat al-Aqabah from the bottom of the valley, then said: "By Allah, this is the place where Surat al-Baqarah was revealed."

And 'Abd Allah ibn Buraydah related from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Learn Surat al-Baqarah, for taking it up is a blessing, leaving it is a regret, and the Batalah cannot master it." That is, the sorcerers (al-Saharah). In this there is evidence for the virtue of this surah and for the permissibility of calling it Surat al-Baqarah. Some earlier scholars called this surah "Fustat al-Quran" (the tent-pole of the Quran), because of its nobility and excellence.

Concerning the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾. Al-Sha'bi and a group of earlier scholars said, regarding this and all the disjointed letters (huruf al-tahajji) at the openings of the surahs: the benefit of the openings of the surahs is that their meaning is not known; they are the secret of the Quran, and every book has a secret, and the secret of the Quran is the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs. The benefit of mentioning them is to seek faith in them, and to know that they are from Allah the Exalted.

Others said: their meanings are known. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: the meaning of His words ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ is: "Ana Allah a'lam" (I am Allah, the Knower). Each letter indicates a meaning: the alif is an indication of His saying "ana" (I), the lam is an indication of His saying "Allah," and the mim is an indication of His saying "a'lam" (the Knower).

He said the same concerning similar openings. Concerning ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ he said: its meaning is: "Ana Allah a'lam wa afsil" (I am Allah, the Knower, and the Distinguisher). Concerning ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra﴾: "Ana Allah a'lam wa ara" (I am Allah, the Knower, and the Seer). Concerning ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾: "Ana Allah ara" (I am Allah, the Seer).

Al-Zajjaj said: this is good, and the Arabs speak in this manner. The Arabs may use a letter in their speech and mean by it a meaning, as the poet said:

(I said to her, "Stop (qifi)," and she said "qaf," do not think that we have forgotten the galloping (al-ijaf).)

The meaning of her saying "qaf" is: "I have stopped (waqaftu)." So the letter indicates a meaning; likewise here.

Qatadah said concerning the disjointed letters that they are a name for the Quran.

Mujahid said that they are names of the surahs.

Others said that it is an oath: Allah the Exalted swore by these letters, because of their nobility and excellence, since they are the building blocks of His revealed books.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 2:

The saying of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿This is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾. As for His saying ﴿This is the Book﴾, it means: this Book, as the poet said: "I say to him while the spear bends its shaft: 'Be patient, lightly, for I am that one [dhalika]'" 

[That is]: "I am indeed this one." It has also been said: "This" is implicit in it, and its meaning is: "This is that Book which I promised you, O Muhammad, that I would send down to you through the tongue of those before you." "Hadha" (this) is used for what is near, and "dhalika" (that) for what is far.

As for "al-Kitab" (the Book), it is the Qur'an, and "al-Kitab" here carries the meaning of "al-maktub" (the written), as one says: "the amir struck" meaning "his struck one" (i.e., the one struck by him).

﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ means: there is no doubt in it. If someone says: how does He inform, saying "there is no doubt in it," when many people have doubted it, and the report of God the Exalted does not contradict what it reports? It is said: its meaning is that it is the truth and the sincere, in which there is no doubt.

It has also been said: it is a report with the meaning of a prohibition, that is: do not doubt in it.

The Exalted's saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾. "Al-huda" (guidance) carries the meaning of right direction (rushd) and clarification (bayan).

As for "al-muttaqun" (the God-fearing), it is derived from "al-ittiqa'" and "taqwa", and its origin is a barrier between two things. From it one says: "ittaqa bi-tarsihi" (he protected himself with his shield), meaning he made it a barrier between himself and what was intended for him of harm. In the report: "When the fighting grew fierce, we would take shelter (ittaqayna) with the Messenger of God (ﷺ)," meaning: when the war intensified, we made him a barrier between us and the enemy.

So the one who is God-fearing makes compliance with God's command and avoidance of His prohibition a barrier between himself and the punishment, and thus he guards himself by obedience to God against the punishment of God.

If someone says: why did He single out the God-fearing for mention, when it is guidance for all believers? It is said: He singled them out for mention to honour them, or because they are the ones who benefit from the guidance, since they have taken the station of taqwa, to the exclusion of others; therefore He singled them out with it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 3:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen and establish the prayer﴾

His saying: ﴿Those who﴾ is a qualifying description (na't) of the muttaqun (the God-conscious). ﴿Believe﴾ is from îmân (faith), which is taṣdîq (affirmation or acceptance as true). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you would not be a believer to us﴾, meaning: one who affirms us as true.

In the Sharia, îmân comprises belief in the heart (i'tiqad), verbal affirmation with the tongue (iqrar), and action by the limbs (amal bil-arkan). It is also said that îmân is derived from amân (security), so the believer (mu'min) is called mu'min because he secures himself from the punishment of Allah. And Allah is Mu'min because He secures His servants from His punishment.

﴿In the unseen﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: the unseen is everything you have been commanded to believe in that is hidden from your sight, such as the angels, Paradise, the Fire, the Sirat (bridge), the Mizan (scale), and the like.

Another said: the unseen here is Allah the Exalted Himself.

Ibn Kaysan said: he meant by it the qadar (divine decree). ﴿They believe in the unseen﴾, i.e., in the qadar.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾, i.e., persist in the prayer. The true meaning of establishing the prayer is guarding its performance with its pillars (arkan), its sunan, and its proper forms (hay'at).

Linguistically, ṣalât (prayer) means du'a' (supplication). It has been reported in a khabar (report): "Whoever is invited to a meal, let him accept; if he is fasting, let him pray (fa-l-yuṣalli)," meaning: let him supplicate. And the poet said:

(My daughter says, when I had set out to depart: "O Lord, keep away from my father the afflictions and pain,")
(Upon you is like what I have prayed (ṣallaytu), so close your eyes, for a person has a place to lie down beside him.)

The meaning of his saying "ṣallaytu" is: like what I supplicated.

It is also said: ṣalât from Allah is mercy (raḥma), from the angels is seeking forgiveness (istighfar), and from people is supplication (du'a'). In the Sharia it comprises specific actions together with praise and supplication.

His saying: ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾. As for rizq (provision), it is a name for everything from which creatures benefit, so it includes children and slaves.

﴿They spend﴾ is from infaq (spending), whose root meaning is bringing out (ikhraj). From it comes nafaq al-suq (the market's bustle), because goods are brought out in it. It is said: "nafaqat al-dabba" when its soul has come out. This verse refers to the believers among the polytheist Arabs.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 4:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾

This verse refers to the believers among the People of the Book, because they are the ones who believed in the Qur'an and in the earlier scriptures before it. It has been narrated in a sound hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever believes in the earlier books and believes in the Qur'an, he will be given his reward twice." The explicit text of the Qur'an also indicates this: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾.

As for His words: ﴿and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾, al-Akhirah is the abode of the Hereafter. The world was called al-dunya (the near) because it is near to the creation, and the Hereafter was called al-akhirah (the last) because it comes after the creation.

﴿They are certain﴾ comes from al-iqan (certainty), which is knowledge. It was also said: iqan and yaqin (certainty) are knowledge derived from inference (istidlal), and for this reason Allah the Most High is not called muqin (one who is certain), since His knowledge is not derived from inference.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 5:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.﴾

As for His saying ﴿Those﴾, it means the people He described, [who are] ﴿upon guidance﴾, i.e., upon right direction and clear proof from their Lord. If it is asked: why did He mention "guidance" a second time when He had already described them as having guidance once? It is answered: He repeated it for the purpose of emphasis (ta'kid). Or it may be said: the first "guidance" is from the Qur'an, and the second "guidance" is from Allah, and in this there is a clarification that guidance comes from Allah the Most High and from His speech, as is the position of the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah).

As for ﴿al-mufliḥūn﴾ (the successful), it derives from al-falah (success), and falah can carry the meaning of remaining (al-baqa'). It is said: "aflaḥa bi-ma shi'ta" (remain with whatever you wish), i.e., remain with whatever you wish. It may also mean triumph and deliverance (al-fawz wa-al-najah). The root meaning of falah is cutting and splitting, and from this the farmer (al-zari') is called a falih, because he splits the earth. In the proverb: "The iron is made successful by iron" (al-hadid bi-al-hadid yuflih), i.e., it splits. The poet said:

(Indeed you know, O son of Umm Sahsah, that iron is made successful by iron.)

i.e., it splits. So the meaning of "al-mufliḥūn" is that they are those who remain in the bliss of eternity, and those who attain it, and those for whom goodness is decreed in this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 6:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾. Kufr (disbelief) is derived from kufr, which means concealing and covering. From this, the night is called kafir (كافر), because it conceals things with its darkness. The farmer is called kafir because he covers the seed with soil. The disbeliever is also called kafir because by his disbelief he conceals the blessings of God, the Exalted, and remains under a covering over the evidences and proofs of Islam.

It has been said: disbelief (kufr) is of four kinds: disbelief of denial (kufr inkar), disbelief of repudiation (kufr jahd), disbelief of obstinacy (kufr 'inad), and disbelief of hypocrisy (kufr nifaq).

As for the disbelief of denial, it is that one does not know God at all, or does not acknowledge Him.

As for the disbelief of repudiation, it is that one knows God, the Exalted, but rejects Him, like the disbelief of Iblis.

As for the disbelief of obstinacy, it is that one knows God, the Exalted, in his heart and acknowledges Him with his tongue, but does not adopt His religion or take it as his faith, like the disbelief of Abu Talib. For he knew God and His Messenger in his heart and affirmed it with his tongue, until he said:

(And indeed I have known that the religion of Muhammad / is the best of the religions of mankind in faith)

(Were it not for reproach, or fear of abuse, / you would find me gracious in declaring it clearly)

As for the disbelief of hypocrisy, it is that one acknowledges with the tongue but does not believe in the heart. These are the kinds of disbelief; whoever meets God, the Exalted, with any one of them will not be pardoned.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾.

﴿It is the same for them﴾ means: it is equal for them. ﴿Whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ means: whether you frighten them or do not frighten them. Warning (indhar) is frightening together with informing.

It has been said: it is the strongest form of frightening. That is: whether you frighten them or do not frighten them, they will not believe. This verse was revealed concerning specific people whom God, the Exalted, knew would not believe.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 7:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing﴾

He mentioned in the first verse that they do not believe, and in this verse He mentioned its cause, saying: ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts﴾. The khatm (seal) is the ṭabʿ (sealing, stamping), and its reality is making something secure, so that nothing from outside enters it and nothing from inside it leaves, and from this comes the khatm upon the door.

As for His words ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts﴾, Ibn Kaysan (Ibn Kaysān) related several opinions about its meaning. The first: that is, He recompensed them for their disbelief by sealing their hearts.

The second, which is the view of the People of the Sunnah: that is, He sealed their hearts with disbelief, because of His eternal knowledge concerning them that preceded.

A third opinion is related: that its meaning is that He placed upon their hearts a sign by which the angels would recognize them. This is the interpretation of the Muʿtazila, from which we disavow ourselves before Allah.

Abū ʿUmar Ghulām Thaʿlab related from Thaʿlab, from Ibrāhīm al-ʿArabī, that the khatm is the prevention of the heart from faith; he mentioned this in the Book of the Yāʾ (Kitāb al-Yāʾ).

As for His words ﴿and upon their hearing﴾, that is, their ears (asmāʿ), where the plural is expressed by the singular form (al-wāḥid), and the like of this is common in the Qur'an. Its meaning is: upon the place of their hearing. So He sealed their hearts, so that they would not accept the truth, and upon their hearing, so that they would not hear the truth.

His words, the Most High: ﴿And upon their eyes is a covering﴾. This begins a new statement, and its meaning is: upon their eyes is a cover.

﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾, that is, a grievous one. He described the punishment of the Hereafter as great, and there is no doubt that it is great.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 8:

Allah the Exalted's words: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: This was revealed concerning the Jews. Most of the exegetes, however, hold that it concerns the hypocrites (munafiqun). Its meaning: among the people there are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," meaning: the Resurrection. ﴿But they are not believers﴾ negates faith from them, since they displayed Islam with the tongue while not believing in their hearts (janan). This is evidence for those who exclude belief of the heart from the totality of faith (iman).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 9:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe﴾ [to the end of the verse]. Al-mukhada'a (deception) and al-khad' (deceit) have one meaning. The reality of deception (al-mukhada'a) is that a person shows one thing and conceals its opposite.

﴿In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased their disease﴾. Ibn al-A'rabi, in his Kitab al-Ya' (Book of the Letter Ya'), said: "His statement, al-mukhada'a is the restraining of the heart from the truth." He said this regarding the hypocrites, since they displayed Islam with their tongues while concealing its opposite.

If someone says: What is the meaning of His statement ﴿They seek to deceive Allah﴾? This suggests partnership in deception, yet Allah is far too exalted to share in deception. The answer: al-Hasan al-Basri said: its meaning is "they deceive the Prophet of Allah."

Others among the exegetes said its meaning is: they deal with Allah in the manner of deceivers.

As for His statement ﴿but they deceive only themselves﴾, it is read in two recitations: "yukhadi'una" and "yakhda'una". Whoever reads "yukhadi'una" (with alif), it is on the principle of mushakalah (agreement of form), because He mentioned the first with the word al-mukhada'a, and this is its form, so He mentioned it with its wording.

Whoever reads "yakhda'una" (without alif), it is on the original basis, and because the word al-mukhada'a does not necessarily imply participation between two parties. Similar to it: "taraqtu al-na'l" and "tara'qtu al-na'l" (I struck the sandal / I struck the sandal in turn), and many such examples occur among the forms of al-mufa'ala.

So the meaning of His statement ﴿but they deceive only themselves﴾ is: the harm of their deception returns to them. ﴿And they do not perceive﴾, i.e., they do not know that. It is said: "shaʿartu" means "I knew," and from it comes their saying: "layta shi'ri," i.e., "would that I knew."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾, the verse, by "disease" He meant doubt and hypocrisy, by the consensus of the exegetes. The heart and the religion are described as being diseased or healthy, just as the body is described with these.

﴿So Allah increased them in disease﴾, that is: in doubt and hypocrisy. For when the verses were revealed, verse after verse, whenever they disbelieved in a verse, they increased in disbelief and hypocrisy. This is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: {As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds to their filth, to their filth} [9:125].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, that is: painful. Here "alim" (painful) is in the sense of "mu'lim" (causing pain), as the poet said:

(Is it the remembrance of Rayhana, the summoner, the hearer, that keeps me awake, while my companions sleep secretly?)

And by "the hearer" he meant "the one who makes to hear."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿because they used to lie﴾. It has been recited in two readings. The lightened form: its meaning is that they lied about what they showed of Islam while concealing the opposite of it. This is like His saying: ﴿And Allah testifies that the hypocrites are surely liars﴾ [63:1].

It has also been recited as "yukadhdhibun" with the doubled letter, and its meaning is: they lie against the Messenger.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth,"﴾ its meaning: "Do not disbelieve," and disbelief is a greater corruption on the earth.

﴿They say, "We are only reformers."﴾ That is, what we have shown of Islam, and what we have gained through it of honor and security, is a benefit for us, and we are reformers through it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 12:

﴿Verily, it is they who are the corrupters.﴾ This is a fresh statement from God. His words "alā" (indeed, a particle of alerting) are used for emphasis. The poet says:

(Indeed, this age is but a day and a night,
and nothing of ancient things remains permanent.)

God the Exalted says: ﴿Verily, it is they who are the corrupters﴾, meaning: by what they displayed of Islam while concealing its opposite, which is corruption, even though they thought it to be righteousness; and they displayed the opposite of what they concealed.

﴿But they do not perceive﴾, that is: they do not know.

If it is asked: How can the proof be binding upon them when they do not know?

It is answered: The proof is binding upon them through what was made clear of the path and what was set up of the indications, and their ignorance does not serve as an excuse for them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed"﴾, to the end of the verse. "As the people have believed" means: the Muhajirun (Emigrants) and the Ansar (Helpers).

﴿They said, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?"﴾ They called them "foolish," so God, may He be exalted, answered them with His saying: ﴿Surely it is they who are the foolish, but they do not know.﴾

Al-safih (the foolish one) is one whose intellect is light and whose forbearance is thin, from their saying: "a safih garment," meaning a thin, worn-out garment.

He says: they are the ones whose intellects are light and whose forbearances are thin. ﴿But they do not know.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 14:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾, and so on. Its meaning: when they meet the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar), they say, "We believe." They manifested Islam with the tongue.

﴿And when they go apart to their shayatin﴾. That is, to their devils (shayatin). "Ila" (to) is mentioned here with the meaning of "ba'" (with), because prepositions may stand in for one another. The shaytan (shaytan, devil) is every rebellious, obstinate one among the jinn and mankind. Its root meaning is distance and extension. It is said: a well shatun, meaning deep in its depth and bottom. And a rope is called shatan, because of its length. The Shaytan was named shaytan because of his extension in evil and his distance from good.

Here, by the shayatin he means their obstinate ones and their leaders in disbelief. He says: when they go apart with their chiefs, they say, "We are truly with you in your religion; we are only mocking" ﴿Indeed, we are only mockers﴾ by what we displayed of Islam together with the Emigrants and the Helpers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 15:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾, the verse. If someone says: What is the meaning of mockery (istihza') from God, the Exalted? We say: There are several views on this. Some of them said: Its meaning is that He repays them for their conduct, except that Allah called it mockery because it is the recompense for mockery, just as He said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾, even though the recompense is not truly an evil deed.

Another group said: "He mocks them" means He disparages them (ya'ibuhum), and from this is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿...by which they are disbelieved in and mocked﴾, meaning: they are disparaged. Likewise, this (verse) is so.

The people of narration (ahl al-riwaya) said: Its meaning is: Allah mocks them in the Hereafter. The mockery of them in the Hereafter may have two aspects. The first: a light is set up for the believers on the Sirat (the bridge over Hell) by which they walk; when the hypocrites reach it, it comes between them and the believers, and that is the mockery of them, just as He said: ﴿So a wall with a gate will be set up between them﴾.

The second: He brings them close to Paradise, so that when they see its blossoms, its beauty and its splendor, and smell its fragrance, He turns them away from it into the Fire, and that is the mockery of them. The Prophet (ﷺ) has spoken of its meaning in a hadith in the Sahih collections.

His saying: ﴿And He extends them﴾, meaning: He gives them respite until He draws them on step by step (yastadrijuhum). ﴿In their transgression﴾, meaning: their misguidance. ﴿They wander blindly﴾, meaning: they are bewildered. The poet said:

(A desert whose edges are in a desert... blind to guidance, with the ignorant in their blindness)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 16:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾, because its meaning is: they chose disbelief over faith. For when they preferred one thing over another, it is as if they had exchanged this for that. ﴿So their commerce has not profited them﴾, that is: they did not profit in their commerce. ﴿And they were not [rightly] guided﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 17:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾, and so on. The mathal (parable, a saying current among people by which the nature of one thing is known through another). This is one of the categories of the Qur'an, for the Qur'an has seven categories.

It was also said: mathaluhum means their ṣifah (description, attribute). ﴿Like the one who kindled a fire﴾: awqada al-nar and istawqada have one meaning, as one says ajāba and istajāba.

It was also said: awqada is when one does it himself, and istawqada is when one asks another to kindle it. ﴿So when it lit up what was around him﴾: meaning the kindled fire lit up what was around the one who kindled it. This was struck as a parable for the hypocrites, and the meaning of this parable is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Like the one who kindled a fire﴾, struck as a parable for what they displayed with their tongues of Islam.

﴿When it lit up what was around him﴾: meaning, what they gained by that outward Islam of adornment, honour and security in this world.

﴿Allah took away their light﴾. It was said that there are several meanings to this. One: Allah took away what they displayed of Islam, by making their belief manifest through the tongue of the Prophet. Another said: its meaning is that Allah took away their light, meaning in the grave. And another said: on the Day of Resurrection, meaning that what they gained by it in this world does not benefit them in the Hereafter, since their destination is the Fire.

If someone says: how can He say ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ when they have no light, and He says elsewhere ﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾ when they have no light? It is answered: He meant by it the light of what they displayed of Islam, and that is a kind of light.

It was also said: a similar expression may be used to mean deprivation, as one says: "You expelled me from your connection," even though he was not inside that connection, meaning: "You deprived me of your connection." Likewise the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Allah took away their light﴾, meaning: He deprived them of that light. (And left them in darknesses), meaning: hardships, ﴿they do not see﴾ the truth.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 18:

His saying: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return﴾. As for "ṣumm" (deaf): it is the plural of "aṣamm" (deaf), who is the one who does not hear. And "bukm" (dumb): the plural of "abkam" (mute), who is the one who does not speak, and who was born unable to speak (ʿalā al-khars).

And "ʿumy" (blind): the plural of "aʿmā" (blind), who is the one who does not see. So its meaning is that they are deaf, not perceiving the truth and not recognising it, as if they had not heard. This is like the saying of the poet:

(Deaf to what displeases him, though he is a hearer...)

That is: he does not hear what displeases him, despite being a hearer.

﴿Dumb﴾ means: since they concealed the opposite of what they displayed, it is as if they had not spoken the truth.

﴿Blind﴾ means: they have no insight, and whoever has no insight is like one who has no sight.

﴿So they will not return﴾ from the misguidance they are upon.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 19:

The Exalted One's saying ﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky, in which are darknesses, thunder, and lightning﴾ — the verse. Al-sayyib (ṣayyib): rain, and whatever descends from above to below is ṣayyib, from their saying ṣāba yaṣūbu, when it descends.

It has been said: there is an omitted word within it, meaning "like the people of the ṣayyib," as in His saying ﴿and ask the town﴾, meaning the people of the town.

﴿from the sky﴾: everything that is high is a sky. So the ceiling is a sky, the cloud is a sky, and what is above it is a sky; and here He means by it the cloud.

﴿in it are darknesses﴾: meaning, in the cloud, because it is never free of darkness. Do you not see that it veils the face of the sun? ﴿and thunder and lightning﴾. ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās and most of the exegetes said: thunder is the voice of an angel driving the clouds, and lightning is the gleam of a whip in the hand of an angel with which he strikes the clouds, driving them to where God the Exalted has decreed.

In a report, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you hear the sound of thunder, remember God, for it does not strike one who remembers." And when he heard the sound of thunder he would say: "O God, do not kill us by Your anger, do not destroy us by Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that."

It has been said: thunder is the name of the angel. It has been said: it is the sound of the wind being suffocated [or: compressed] into the cloud. The first view is more sound.

﴿they put their fingers in their ears because of the thunderbolts﴾: meaning, because of the sound of the punishment, fearing death. It has been said: the thunderbolt is a piece of punishment which God the Exalted sends down upon whom He wills, and this is indicated by His saying ﴿He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾. ﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾, that is, gathers them. Mujāhid said: He gathers them and then punishes them. To encompass a thing is to gather it so that nothing of it escapes, and God's encompassing is by subjugation, power and knowledge.

The meaning of the parable in this: as for His saying, ﴿or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾, meaning: if you wish, liken them to the one who kindles a fire, and if you wish, liken them to the rain-cloud, that is, to the people of the rain-cloud. The rain-cloud was made a parable for what they displayed with the tongue of Islam.

﴿in it are darknesses﴾: a parable for the trials, afflictions and hardships that are in Islam. ﴿and thunder﴾: a parable for the terrors in the Hereafter that are in it.

(And lightning): for the promise and threat that are in it.

It has been said: the rain-cloud was made a parable for the Qur'an, which they recited with the tongue, because in the Qur'an is the life of the inner self, just as in water is the life of the outer. ﴿in it are darknesses﴾: a parable for what we have mentioned in the Qur'an of kinds of disbelief and hypocrisy; ﴿and thunder﴾: a parable for what we have mentioned in it of threat; ﴿and lightning﴾: a parable for what is in it of clarification.

﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾: meaning, that the hypocrites, when they see trial and hardship in Islam, flee and draw back, out of fear of destruction.

﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾: meaning, their caution does not benefit them, because God the Exalted is behind them, gathering them and punishing them.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾, the verse. ﴿Nearly﴾ is a word of proximity: "yakad yafʿal" means "qarib yafʿal," that is, it is about to do so. ﴿Snatches away their sight﴾: al-khatf is to seize something quickly. This is part of the parable, and its meaning according to the first view is: the proofs of Islam nearly unsettle them to look, were it not for the wretchedness that had already been decreed for them.

Its meaning according to the other view: the Qur'an nearly dazzles their hearts.

﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾: its meaning is that whenever they gain booty and ease, they remain steadfast in Islam. ﴿And when it darkens over them, they stand still﴾: meaning that whenever they see hardship and affliction, they draw back. "Qamu" means they stopped and stood still. ﴿And if God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾: this allows two meanings. The first: if God willed, He would have taken away what they gained of honour and security, which is for them in the position of hearing and sight.

The second meaning: if God willed, He would have taken away their outward hearing and sight, just as He took away their inward hearing and sight. ﴿Surely God is capable of everything﴾: meaning, He is able.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾, the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: everything in the Qur'an that contains the phrase ﴿O people﴾ was revealed in Makkah, and everything that contains the phrase ﴿O you who believe﴾ was revealed in Madinah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 21:

And His saying: ﴿O mankind﴾ means: O you people (ya ha'ula'i al-nas). Although this address is general in its wording (wa in 'ammat sigatuhu), it is specific in application (wa lakin dakhalahu al-khusus), for it does not include children or the insane. ﴿Worship﴾ means: affirm the oneness of (wahhidu) [God].

Ibn 'Abbas said: Everything in the Qur'an that mentions 'ibadah (worship) means tawhid (affirming God's oneness), and everything in the Qur'an that mentions tasbih and subha (glorification) means salah (prayer).

And His saying: ﴿worship your Lord, who created you﴾ means: affirm the oneness of God, who created you. He addressed them with this because the disbelievers acknowledge that God is their Creator. Khalq (creation) is the bringing of a thing into being without a prior pattern (ikhtira' al-shay' 'ala ghayr mithal sabaq). ﴿And those before you﴾ means: and He created those before you. If it is asked: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿and those before you﴾, since whoever knows that God is his Creator has thereby known that He created others before him? It is answered: its benefit is emphasis in explanation (al-mubalaghah fi al-bayan). Or it is said: its benefit is emphasis in the call (al-mubalaghah fi al-da'wah), meaning: since God created you and created those before you, do not worship anyone but Him. In it there is also an allusion: He created the earlier ones, caused them to die, and tested them in this world and the Hereafter; by this He indicates, "I will do to you what I did to them."

﴿So that you may be righteous (la'allakum tattaqun)﴾. It has been said its meaning is: in order that you may fear (God) (li-kay tattaqu), as Abu 'Ubaydah said. It has also been said its meaning is: be in hope of attaining taqwa. If someone says: taqwa is worship, so what is the meaning of His saying "worship so that you may worship"? We reply: its meaning is: worship Him and be wary of Him, and this is the practice of the worshipper, that he worships God and is wary of Him. It has also been said its meaning is: worship Him and be in hope of attaining taqwa, by coming to be in a shelter and protection from the punishment of God the Exalted, while the judgment of God is behind you, and He does with you what He wills. This is like His saying the Exalted: ﴿Speak to him gently, perhaps he will be mindful or fearful﴾, meaning: call him to the truth and be in hope of his remembrance and fear. And the judgment of God lies beyond that, and He does with him what He wills.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who made the earth for you a bed﴾, the verse. This refers back to what preceded it, meaning: worship the One who made the earth for you a bed. The "making" (al-ja'l) here carries the meaning of "creating." ﴿A bed﴾ means a spread-out expanse (basat); it was also said: a resting place (wita'). It was also said: a dwelling place (maqam), meaning He made the earth a fixed abode for you, so that you may live upon it. ﴿And the sky a structure﴾, meaning a ceiling (saqf). ﴿And sent down from the sky water﴾. He attributed it to the sky, although it descends from the clouds, because it descends from the direction of the sky.

﴿And brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾. It was said: provision (rizq) is everything that is eaten. It was also said: everything from which one benefits. ﴿So do not set up rivals (andad) to God﴾. Qatadah said: the nid is the like (mithl). Abu 'Ubaydah said: the nid is the opposite (did). This is among the words with two opposite meanings (al-adda', an'-antonyms within one root), and God, exalted is He, is free of any like or opposite. Hassan ibn Thabit said in praise of the Messenger of God:

(Do you satirize him, when you are not his equal (nid)? So may your evil be a ransom for his good.)

meaning: you are not his like. Labid said:

(I praise God; there is no rival (nid) to Him; in His hands is goodness, whatever He wills He does.)

meaning: there is no like to Him. The meaning of His saying ﴿So do not set up rivals to God﴾ is: do not take, besides Him, lords whom you worship as you worship God and obey as you obey God, not that He has a like, or that God has no like.

﴿And you know﴾, meaning: so do not worship other than Him while you know that He is your Creator and the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾, meaning: in suspicion (shakk). If it is asked: how did He mention it in the form of uncertainty (al-tashkik) when they were in doubt in actuality? It is said: the like of this is permissible in the speech of the Arabs; as a man says to another: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such," even though it is known that he is a man in actuality. It is said: He intended by it "and since you are" (wa-idh kuntum), so it is in actuality. ﴿of what We have sent down﴾ of the Qur'an ﴿upon Our servant﴾, meaning: upon the Messenger.

﴿Then produce a surah﴾. Al-sūrah (chapter, lit. "a rank"): a name for an elevated station; and from it comes sūrat al-bināʾ (the level/rank of a building), because of its height. The poet said:

(Have you not seen that God has given you a sūrah... every thing is shaking beneath it)

meaning: He has given you a sūrah, i.e., an elevated rank. And the chapter of the Qur'an was called a sūrah because the reciter attains a rank by the recitation of each sūrah, until he completes all the ranks by completing the Qur'an. It is also said: sūrah is the name of a portion of the Qur'an whose beginning and end are known; and from it comes su'r (leftover) of food, meaning what remains of it. In a report: "When you eat, then leave some remainder" (fa-usʾirū), meaning: leave a remainder. The Qur'an was sent down surah by surah so that the reciter, whenever he recites a surah and begins another, grows more energetic, and so is more vigorous in recitation; or because he may not be able to memorize the whole Qur'an, so he memorizes some of the surahs.

﴿Then produce a surah like it﴾. And His saying ﴿like it﴾ has two meanings. One of them, said by Ibn ʿAbbas and a group: He intended by it "like the Qur'an." If it is asked: how did He say "like the Qur'an" when there is no like of it? It is said: He intended "like it according to their claim."

There is another view: that He intended "like Muhammad," because they used to say: he is a fabricator (muftari), so He said: then produce a surah of a fabricated thing like him.

﴿And call your witnesses besides God﴾, meaning: seek help from your helpers and your lords besides God, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in what you claim. Its benefit: that when they gather and bring their lords and then are unable, it is more emphatic in establishing the proof against them.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾ — the verse. It means: if you do not do that, and you will never do it, — stated as a report. "Lan" (never) is for the future, and "lam" (not) for the past. He said this to demonstrate the miracle (i'jaz), because the Qur'an was a miracle for the Prophet, since all of them were unable to produce anything like it.

﴿So fear the Fire﴾ — that is: so believe, in order that you may guard yourselves against the Fire through faith — ﴿whose fuel is people﴾. Waqud (fuel) means ignition (al-iqad), and waqud with a fatha on the waw means the firewood. ﴿And stones﴾ — the people of Hell. ﴿And stones﴾: ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud said: these are sulphur stones, because they are more intense in kindling and blazing; and the rest said: it is all kinds of stones. This is evidence of the greatness of that Fire. ﴿Prepared for the disbelievers﴾ — that is, made ready for the disbelievers. This is evidence that the Fire is created, not as the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'a) said. It is also evidence that it is created for the disbelievers, even though some believers enter it for discipline and purification (ta'dib wa-ta'rik).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And give good news to those who believe﴾ and so on. Al-bushra (good news): a name for every true report by which the complexion of the face changes and shows upon it, though it may also be used for bad news, as He said: ﴿So give them news of a painful punishment﴾. However, it is mostly used for good news. ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. ﴿And give good news to those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow. Whenever they are provided with a fruit therefrom as provision, they say, "This is what we were provided with before," and they are given it in likeness.﴾

That is, the believers who are among the people of obedience. ﴿That for them are gardens﴾. Al-jannat (the gardens): plural of jannah, which is a name for an orchard in which there are fruit-bearing trees. If the trees are not fruit-bearing, it is not a jannah. It is said: al-jannah is that in which there are palm trees. Al-firdaws is that in which there are vineyards. It was named jannah from al-ijtinan (concealment), because it covers the earth with its intertwining and its branches. It is said: the jinan are seven, and it is said: eight, and all of them are in the Qur'an.

﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾. That is: beneath their trees water flows in rivers. In a hadith: "Indeed the rivers of Paradise flow without a trench," meaning: without a cut (in the ground).

﴿Whenever they are provided with a fruit therefrom as provision﴾. That is: whenever they are provided with something of the fruits of Paradise, they say, "This is what we were provided with before." On this there are two opinions. The first: its meaning is, "We were provided with it before, in the world." The second: the fruits in Paradise are similar in color but different in taste. So when they are given one fruit and then given another, they think it is the first, because the two are alike in color. Thus ﴿they say, "This is what we were provided with before," and they are given it in likeness﴾ (mutashabihan). Mujahid said: that is, similar in color, as we have mentioned. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: its meaning is that all of them are choice, with none of them inferior. Ibn 'Abbas said: there is nothing in this world of the fruits of Paradise except the names.

﴿And for them therein are spouses﴾. It is said: from the dark-eyed houris. It may also mean spouses of this world: ﴿purified﴾ from impurities; they do not blow their noses, do not defecate, and do not menstruate. It is also said: purified in character, so they are purified in form and in disposition. ﴿And they therein are abiding﴾. That is: remaining, not departing.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 26:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a gnat or what is above it﴾. The occasion of revelation of the verse: when Allah, exalted is He, cited the example of the fly and the spider, the polytheists said: "We do not worship a god who mentions the fly and the spider." So the Most High revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed﴾, meaning: He does not refrain and does not abstain, ﴿from presenting an example﴾, meaning: mentioning an example, ﴿[even] of a gnat﴾. (Mā) here is superfluous (lil-silah), meaning: an example with the gnat. The poet said:

(She said: "Would that this dove were ours... to our dove, or half of it, [would be enough]")

Its meaning: would that this dove were ours. The baʿūḍ (gnats) are the small bedbugs; it was named baʿūḍah because it is a part (baʿḍ) of the bedbug. ﴿Or what is above it﴾ means: or what is below it, as one says: "So-and-so is ignorant," and then one says: "and above that," meaning: more ignorant than that. Likewise the Most High's words ﴿or what is above it﴾ mean: in smallness, and smaller than that. It was also said: ﴿or what is above it﴾ is meant literally, because He cited the example of the fly and the spider. Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: The likeness of the gnat is the likeness of the worldly person, for the way of the gnat is that when it is satiated it perishes, and when it is hungry it lives; likewise the worldly person, when he accumulates much of the world he perishes, and when he takes only a little of it he succeeds and is saved. It was also said: the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, in His smallest creatures is greater than His wisdom in His largest creatures. The words of the Most High: ﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾, meaning: that it is the truth from their Lord.

﴿And as for those who disbelieve, they say: "What did Allah intend by this example?"﴾ That is: what did Allah intend by this example? Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿He misleads many thereby and guides many thereby﴾, meaning: He intended this. Idlāl (misguidance) is the turning away from the truth toward falsehood. It was also said: idlāl is destruction (ihlāk); it is said: "the milk was lost (ḍalla) in the water," meaning: it was destroyed.

﴿And He guides many thereby﴾, meaning: He directs many thereby. ﴿And He misleads thereby only the deviators (fāsiqīn)﴾, meaning: the disbelievers. Fisq (deviance) is going out of obedience to the Lord; it is said: "the date-palm fasaqat" when it came out of its skin (fasaqat al-ruṭbah). The meaning of their being misled by the example is that when the example was presented and they disbelieved in it, they increased in misguidance.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 27:

And the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its solidification﴾ means: they oppose the command of Allah. The mithaq (covenant) is a form from "tawthiqah" (making firm), and it is the emphasized pledge. Regarding its meaning there are two opinions. The first: he intended the breaking of the first covenant which He took from Adam and his offspring with His words, ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes﴾.

It was also said: he intended by it the breaking of the covenant which He took from the prophets and the rest of the nations, that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), by His words: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets﴾, to the end of the verse.

﴿And cut off what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ has three opinions. The first: they cut off what they were commanded to join, namely belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in all the messengers. It was also said: he intended by it the severing of kinship ties (qat' al-rahim). The first opinion is preferable, because it is more general. It was also said: he intended by it the severing of action from acceptance, for they did not act upon what they had accepted.

﴿And cause corruption in the earth﴾ through acts of disobedience. ﴿Those are the losers﴾, the defrauded.

"How can you disbelieve in Allah? You were dead and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life again; then to Him you will be returned." Al-Sam'ani's commentary:

Allah's words, ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah?﴾ are spoken in wonder: How can you disbelieve in Allah after the proofs have been set forth and the evidences made clear? Then He mentions the proof, saying: ﴿And you were dead﴾, which is the proof, meaning: you were sperm-drops in the loins of your fathers.

(Then He gave you life) meaning: He created you. ﴿Then He will cause you to die﴾ when your term ends. ﴿Then He will bring you to life again﴾ for the resurrection. ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾: to Allah is your final destination.

It has also been said that by the first death He meant the known death: ﴿And you were dead﴾ means: you will become dead. (Then He gave you life) means: He will give you life in the grave for questioning. Then He will cause you to die after that in the grave, then He will bring you to life for the resurrection. Then to Him you will be returned.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ so that you may take heed and reflect, and it is said: so that you may benefit.

﴿Then He rose over the heaven﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas and most of the early exegetes (al-mufassirun min al-salaf) said: that is, He ascended and rose high to the heaven.

Al-Farraʾ, Ibn Kaysan (Ibn Kaysan) and a group of grammarians (al-nahwiyyun) said its meaning is: He turned toward the creation of the heaven; for He created the earth first, then turned toward creating the heaven, as mentioned in Ḥā Mīm al-Sajda. ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾ meaning: He created them level, without any fissure (fitr) in them, nor any rift (ṣadʿ), nor any crack (shaqq).

﴿And He is Knowing of all things﴾ meaning: He is Knowing of His creatures, the small of them and the great.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 30:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a khalifah (successor/vicegerent)"﴾. Its meaning is: "And your Lord said." The "idh" (when) here is extra (zā'idah).

It was also said: its meaning is: "Remember when your Lord said." The "mala'ikah" (angels) is the plural of "malak" (angel/messenger). The original root of "malak" is "mala'ak," so the hamzah was dropped, and it became "malak." Its derivation is from "al-ulukah," which means the message, and similar to it are "al-ma'lukah" and "al-ma'lukah." The poet said:

(Alkini ilayha wa khayru al-rasul... a'lamuhum bi-nawahi al-khabar)

meaning: "Send me to her."

﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a khalifah﴾. The scholars agree that what is meant by this khalifah is Adam, peace be upon him. "Khalifah" and "khalif" have one meaning; the plural of "khalif" is "khulafa'," and the plural of "khalifah" is "khala'if."

They differed as to why he was named khalifah. Some said: because he is the successor of the jinn, for when God Most High created the earth, He settled the jinn in it, and when He created the heaven, He settled the angels in it. Then, when He created Adam, He drove the jinn out to the far parts of the earth; so he is the khalifah of the jinn on the earth.

It was also said: he was named khalifah only because another will succeed him, so khalifah here means one who succeeds another, and khalifah means that another succeeds him.

It was also said: he was named khalifah because he is God's khalifah on the earth, to establish His rulings and carry out His decrees, and this is the most sound view.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "Will You place upon it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?"﴾ The verse. The angels said: "Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?" If it is asked: From where did they know that? It is said: God Most High informed them of it. It was also said: they became aware of it in the Preserved Tablet.

﴿And we exalt You with Your praise﴾: this is glorifying Him above every evil. Its meaning: "And we declare You free of rivals and partners."

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of His saying ﴿And we exalt You with Your praise﴾ is their saying: "Glory be to God and praise be to Him." ﴿And we sanctify You﴾ means: we extol You with holiness and purity.

It was also said: its meaning is that we purify ourselves through Your obedience and through praising You.

If it is asked: their saying ﴿Will You place in it﴾ resembles an objection to Him, and their saying "we exalt You with Your praise" resembles boasting of works; and both are impermissible for the angels. So what is the meaning of this speech?

We answer: as for their saying ﴿Will You place in it﴾, its meaning is: "You are placing in it" by way of supposition, and similar to it is the poet's saying:

(Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts, and the most generous of all peoples in hospitality?)

meaning that they possess this quality.

It was also said that they said it by way of wonder, seeking to know the wisdom behind it.

As for His saying ﴿we exalt You with Your praise﴾, it is not by way of boasting; rather its meaning is: if they cause corruption and shed blood, will we remain in the state of glorifying and sanctifying, or not? He said: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾. It has two meanings:

One: "Indeed, I know that among them are those who will worship Me and obey Me, from among the prophets, the saints and the righteous."

The second meaning: "Indeed, I know that among you, O angels, is one who will disobey Me," meaning Iblis.

The Exalted's words: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾. As for Adam, he was named Adam because he was created from the surface of the earth (adim al-ardh). When God Almighty created him, He taught him the names of all things.

Ibn 'Abbas said: He taught him the names of things, even the qasi'a (bowl) and the qasi'a (small bowl), and the fasw and the fasiyya.

He taught him this as an honour and a distinction for him. This is evidence that the prophets are superior to the angels, even though they are messengers, as Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) have held.

﴿Then He presented them﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "Then He presented it" [wa-hiya] (this is a shadhdh reading, shadhdh (irregular reading) in the readings). The pronoun [al-kinaya] (the pronominal reference) returns to the named things, which are non-rational. The well-known reading is: "Then He presented them," since the named things included both rational and non-rational beings, so He used the pronoun for the rational beings by way of taghlib (predominance of the rational gender).

He presented them to the angels to show his superiority over them, for they had said: "God will not create a creature more honoured by Him than us." So He said: ﴿Tell Me﴾, inform Me ﴿of the names of these, if you are truthful﴾ in what you claimed.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 32:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They said: Glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾. We have already mentioned the meaning of tasbih (glorification, declaring God free of any imperfection). The meaning of the verse is: You are too exalted than that we should encompass anything of Your knowledge, except that which You have taught us of it.

﴿Indeed, You, You are the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: the Knower, ﴿the All-Wise﴾. Hakim has two meanings. The first: the Judge (al-hakim), who passes judgment with justice.

The second: the meaning of hakim is the one who makes a matter firm (al-muhkim lil-amr), so that corruption cannot reach it. From this comes the expression: "ahkamtu al-dabbah" (I fitted/bridled the beast), because it (the bridle) prevents it from corruption.

"The words of His Exalted Majesty: ﴿He said, "O Adam, inform them of their names."﴾ When He had presented them to the angels and they were unable (to name them), Allah Exalted said to Adam: "Inform them of their names." ﴿So when he had informed them of their names﴾, Adam informed them of the names of those named things and the wisdom for which they were created. When he informed them of it, ﴿Allah said﴾ Exalted to the angels: ﴿"Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth?"﴾ For He had said to them: ﴿"Indeed, I know what you do not know."﴾ The unseen of the heavens and the earth is everything that is hidden and concealed from the sight.

(And I know what you reveal) that is, your saying: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?"

﴿And what you have been concealing﴾ has two interpretations. The first: what they concealed of their saying: "Allah will never create a creation more honored by Him than us."

The second: its meaning is what Iblis concealed among them when Adam was created, for he had said: "If I am given power over him, I will destroy him, and if he is given power over me, I will not obey him."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 34:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾. The scholars differed as to which angels this address was directed. Some of them said: it is an address specifically to the angels of the earth.

It was said: it is an address to all the angels. This is the more sound view, because of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾.

Sujud (prostration) is worship together with humility, submissiveness and lowliness. From it comes the expression "a sajida tree", meaning one that has died from the abundance of its fruit.

Regarding His saying, ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾, there are two views. The first: its meaning is "prostrate towards Adam", so Adam would be like a qibla, and the prostration is to God, may He be exalted.

The more sound view: the prostration was truly to Adam, and it implied obedience to God, may He be exalted, by carrying out His command regarding it. On this basis, the prostration to Adam is in the manner of greeting him. It is like the prostration of Joseph's brothers to Joseph, in the sense of greeting him. Then this was transferred to the greeting (salam) among Muslims.

﴿But they prostrated, except Iblis﴾. Some said: Iblis is derived from iblas (iblas), which is despair of good, as the poet said:

(O friend, do you know a (trace) worn away? He said: Yes, I know it, and it has become desolate.)

It was also said: he is a non-Arabic proper name, arabicized, with no derivation, and for this reason it is not declined.

The scholars differed about Iblis. What Ibn 'Abbas and most of the exegetes said is that he was of the angels.

Al-Hasan said: he was of the jinn, based on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾; and because he was created from fire, whereas the angels were created from light; and because he has offspring, and the angels have no offspring.

The more sound view is that he was of the angels, because the address of prostration was directed to the angels.

As for His saying, ﴿he was of the jinn﴾: it was said that a group of the angels were called jinn, whom God created from fire. This is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾, where they said that the angels are the daughters of God; so He named them "jinn". They were called jinn because they are hidden from eyes.

Iblis was of that category. He had offspring because He expelled him from the angels and then gave him offspring.

It was also said: when God created Iblis, He gave him the kingship of the earth and the kingship of the lowest heaven, and made him the keeper of Paradise.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He refused (abā)﴾, meaning he declined; ﴿and was arrogant (istakbara)﴾, meaning he was proud, since he thought he was better than Adam; ﴿and he was among the disbelievers﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: its meaning is "and he became among the disbelievers in the knowledge of God, may He be exalted."

Mujahid said: God knew in His eternity that disobedience would come from him, so He created him for disobedience.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise"﴾. He meant by "his wife" Hawwa' (Eve). If it is said: Why did He command them to enter Paradise, when He had promised that whoever enters it will abide in it forever? How then did He expel them from Paradise?

We say: That promise applies only to one who enters it for reward and recompense, whereas Adam entered Paradise by honour, not by reward.

﴿And eat from it plentifully, wherever you wish﴾. Raghad (plentiful) means wide-ranging sustenance: that he eats whatever he wishes, when he wishes, however he wishes. ﴿But do not approach this tree﴾, meaning: to eat from it.

Shajara (tree) is the name for what stands upon a trunk, while najm (herb/star-plant) is the name for what does not stand upon a trunk.

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾. Regarding that tree there are three opinions. Ibn Mas'ud said: it was the grapevine. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was the spike-grain tree (sunbulah). Ibn Juraij said: it was the fig tree. It is also said: it was the tree of al-'Alim.

﴿And you will be among the wrongdoers﴾. Zulm (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place. It is said in this regard: "Whoever resembles his father has not wronged," meaning: he has not placed the resemblance in other than its proper place.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Satan caused them to slip from it﴾. Hamza recited: "fa-azalahuma" (fa-azālahumā), and its meaning is: he removed them and distanced them from the Garden.

And His saying "fa-azallahumā" (fa-azalla-humā) is from the slip (zalla), ﴿and he brought them out of that in which they were﴾, meaning from the bounty of the Garden. The attribution of the expulsion to him is because he was the cause of it.

(And We said, "Go down.") Al-hubūt (descent) is the coming down from a higher place to a lower place. The address is directed to Adam, Iblis, Hawwa' (Eve), and the serpent. The serpent was one of the guardians of the Garden, and Iblis deceived it until it let him enter the Garden.

﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾. Al-'aduww (enemy) is a term used for the singular and the plural; its meaning is "enemies."

﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾, that is, a settled abode, ﴿and provision﴾, a provision by which you are sustained, ﴿for a time﴾, until the end of the appointed terms.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 37:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾. Talaqqi (receiving): it is acceptance with insight and understanding, with evidence. So "fa-talaqqa" here means [i.e., learned]: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾, and so on to the end.

Ubayd ibn Umayr said: They are words Adam said when Allah tested him with disobedience.

﴿From his Lord, words﴾. Ibn Abbas and most of the scholars said: The words are his saying: "Our Lord," i.e., he learned while in disobedience: "O Lord, is this a thing You decreed for me, or did I invent it of my own accord?" He said: "Rather, it is a thing I decreed for you." Adam said: "Since You decreed it for me, then forgive it."

﴿Then He turned to him﴾: He accepted his repentance. ﴿Indeed, He is the Accepter of repentance, the Merciful﴾: He is the One who accepts repentance from the servants, and Merciful toward them.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿We said: Go down from it, all of you.﴾ The first descent was from the Garden to the lowest heaven, and the second descent was from the lowest heaven to the earth.

(If there comes to you from Me guidance) meaning: right guidance and the explanation of the Law (sharia).

﴿So whoever follows My guidance﴾ meaning: that right guidance and the Law.

﴿There shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve﴾ in the Hereafter.

"His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾, meaning: they disbelieved in Allah and in the messengers, and denied His signs. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿They will abide therein eternally﴾."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 40:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Children of Israel﴾. Israel is the name of Ya'qub. He has two names in the Qur'an: Ya'qub and Israel. The meaning of Israel is "servant of God": "Isr" is like our saying "servant" ('abd), and "il" is like our saying "Allah." ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾. Remembrance (dhikr) may be with the heart and may be with the tongue, and it is the opposite of forgetfulness. His saying ﴿My favour﴾ means "My favours," the plural being expressed with the singular form, and the like of this is common in the Qur'an.

The scholars differed concerning those favours. Qatadah said: they are the favours specific to the Children of Israel, namely their deliverance from Pharaoh by his drowning, the sending of Musa to them, the sending down of the Torah upon them, and the like of that.

Another said: they are all the favours which God has bestowed upon His servants.

If someone says: Why were they commanded to remember, when they were already mindful of those favours?

We say: "Remembrance" here means gratitude (shukr), and its meaning is: "Be grateful for My favour." It was expressed with the word "remembrance" only because in gratitude there is remembrance, and in ingratitude there is forgetfulness. ﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾: awfa yufi and wafa yafi have the same meaning. The poet combined them in a single verse, saying:

(As for Ibn 'Awf, he has fulfilled his pledge... as the one who drives the she-camels of the star fulfilled it)

The 'ahd (covenant) is a firmly established command. Its meaning: "Fulfil My covenant" by complying with My command. ﴿I will fulfil your covenant﴾ with acceptance and reward. Mujahid said: by this covenant is meant what is mentioned in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿And God had already taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders﴾, to the end of the verse. ﴿And fear Me alone﴾: so fear Me.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 41:

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾: "in what I have sent down" refers to the Qur'an, "confirming what is with you" refers to the Torah. That is, the Qur'an confirms what is in the Torah of monotheism (tawhid) and the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾: that is, do not be the first among those who disbelieve in it. It has also been said: "the first group to disbelieve in it." Both meanings are the same. If it is said: the polytheists of the Arabs disbelieved in it before them, so how does He say, "do not be the first to disbelieve in it"? We say: He meant by it, from among the People of the Book, because the address is with the People of the Book.

﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾: "do not exchange." This is because their scholars and rabbis had a source of food from their wealthy and their common folk, so they feared that their livelihood would vanish if they believed in Muhammad. So they altered his description and concealed his name. This is the meaning of selling the signs for a small price.

﴿And fear Me, and Me alone﴾: "so beware (fa-ittaquni)," meaning, "so be wary (fa-hadhirun)."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾. Al-labs (confusion, mixing) is the mixing and obscuring.

It is said: labisa yalbisu labsan, from al-libas (clothing), and labisa yalbisu labsan, from al-talbis (confusing/obscuring). God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We would have confused for them what they confuse﴾, meaning: We would have mixed it up for them just as they mixed it up. And ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said to al-Ḥārith: "Let it not be obscured for you. The truth is not recognised by men; recognise the truth and you will recognise its people."

So the meaning of His saying: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾ is: Islam with Judaism and Christianity. This is what most scholars said. It was also said that it means mixing the Torah with what they altered of the description of Muhammad.

﴿And conceal the truth﴾, meaning the description of Muhammad. ﴿while you know﴾ that it is true. Muhammad ibn Sīrīn said: this address is with a group of Jews who were in al-Shām. They saw in their books the name of Muhammad and his description, and that he would be raised up from the Arab settlements. So they set out seeking him and descended upon al-Madīnah. When Muhammad was sent, they envied him, and they altered his name and his description, out of fear of the loss of their livelihood.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾. As for prayer (ṣalāh), we have already discussed it. As for zakat (zakāh): it is derived from zakā al-zar‘ (zakā al-zarʿ), meaning the crops grew abundant and increased.

It was also said: it is derived from tazakkā, meaning: purified itself. Both meanings exist in the obligatory zakat, because in it there is an increase of wealth and a purification of it.

﴿And bow with those who bow﴾, i.e., pray with those who pray. The original meaning of rukūʿ (bowing) is worship accompanied by bending. It is said: "The palm tree bowed (rakaʿat al-nakhlah)" when it bent, and from this is the saying of the poet:

(I tell the accounts of the generations that have passed away... a man of refinement, as if I am bowing whenever I stand.)

He mentioned it with the wording of rukūʿ because the prayer of the Jews did not include rukūʿ; so it is as if He said: pray a prayer that has rukūʿ in it.

If it is said: He had already commanded them at the beginning of the verse to establish prayer, so what is the meaning of this second command? We say: the first is general in regard to everyone, and this second is an address to a specific people, Him saying to them: pray with those who [preceded you] in faith and prayer.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people⁠—﴾ meaning: obedience to God; ﴿and forget yourselves⁠—﴾ meaning: you abandon yourselves; ﴿while you recite the Scripture?⁠﴾ meaning: the Torah.

﴿Will you not then reason?⁠﴾ Reason (al-'aql) is derived from 'iqal al-ba'ir (the tether of the camel), which is what is tied around the camel's knee. It is so named because it prevents the camel from straying; likewise, reason prevents its possessor from rebellion and from departing from His obedience. There are two opinions regarding the meaning of the verse. The first: it is an address to their rabbis, since they commanded their followers to hold fast to the Torah, then they opposed it and altered the description of Muhammad.

The second opinion: the people of Medina used to consult their scholars about following Muhammad, and they advised them to follow him, then they opposed him and disbelieved in him.

In the hadith: it is related from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "On the night of my Night Journey I saw in the heaven groups of people whose lips were being cut with scissors of fire. I asked, 'Who are these?' They said, 'These are the preachers from your community who used to enjoin righteousness upon the people and forget themselves.'"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 45:

God's saying ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾. Al-isti'anah (seeking help) is seeking assistance. As for al-sabr (patience), most scholars hold that it is restraining the self from acts of disobedience.

From this comes al-dabbah al-musbarah (the tethered animal), which is one that is held still in order to be shot at, like a target.

In a hadith: "He forbade the tethered animal." And concerning the one who holds another person so that he is killed, he said: "Restrain the one who holds him and kill the killer." That is, restrain the one who holds, and kill the one who actually does the killing.

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: it is fasting. For this reason the month of Ramadan is called the month of patience. If it is asked: what is the meaning of seeking help through fasting and prayer? It is answered: because fasting makes one ascetic regarding this world. (Likewise) in prayer one recites what urges one to asceticism regarding this world. So it is as if He said: seek help through these two in your religion, so that you may be strong enough to turn towards the Hereafter and turn away from this world.

﴿And indeed it is heavy﴾, that is, burdensome. Regarding His saying ﴿and indeed it﴾ there are two opinions. The first: the pronoun (in "innaha," "indeed it") refers to both fasting and prayer together, but one of the two mentioned has been suffice with and the pronoun refers to it. This is like the words of the poet:

(Whoever among us has his dwelling in Medina... then I and Qayyar are indeed strangers there.)

That is: "are indeed two strangers," but he suffices with one of the two. Al-Azhari, in his book al-Taqrib, cited a fine view, saying: its estimated form is: "And seek help through patience, for it is indeed heavy, and through prayer, for it is indeed heavy," but one of them was omitted and the meaning was abbreviated.

﴿except for the humble﴾. Al-khashi' is the one who obeys and is humble.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 46:

﴿Those who think﴾ means those who are certain (yastayqinun). The verb ẓann (thinking, supposing) can carry the meaning of shakk (doubt), and it can carry the meaning of yaqin (certainty). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, I thought that I would meet my account﴾, meaning: I was certain. And the poet said:

(So I said to them: "Think [it certain] with two thousand men who are armored, their chiefs in the Persian mail, well-woven.")

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that they will meet their Lord﴾, meaning they will return to their Lord (ṣā'irūn ilā Rabbihim). Everything in the Qur'an that mentions liqa' (meeting) carries the meaning of arriving at Him, as the exegetes (al-mufassirūn) have said.

It has also been said: it is the promised meeting, which is the seeing of Allah the Exalted.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and that to Him they will return﴾, meaning: they will arrive (at Him).

O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds. (Qur'an 2:47)

The phrase "and that I preferred you" — He says: "O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you" — its meaning is as previously stated. "And that I preferred you over the worlds" — tafdil (preference, favouring) is the opposite of taswiya (equalising). He intended by it preference through those blessings which have already been mentioned. This preference, although it pertains to the forefathers, yet nobility is attained thereby by the descendants, so the address to them is valid.

"Over the worlds" — over the worlds of their own time.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 48:

The words of God Most High, ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in the least﴾, mean: beware of the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. ﴿No soul will avail another soul in the least﴾. Al-Akhfash said: its meaning is that no soul will stand in the place of another soul. Others said: its meaning is that no soul will discharge on behalf of another soul a right that was binding upon it.

﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾. It is read with two readings, with the ta' (feminine) and with the ya' (masculine), and both are permissible, because shafa'a (intercession) and shafa'ah are of one meaning, like wa'z and mawdi'ah (admonition) and sawt and sayhah (voice, cry), which have one meaning. Sometimes it is mentioned with the masculine form according to the meaning, and sometimes with the feminine form according to the wording. God Most High said: ﴿There has certainly come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾, and said in another place: ﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾. He said: ﴿And the Cry seized those who did wrong﴾, and said in another place: ﴿And the Cry seized those who did wrong﴾. Thus is this.

﴿Nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾. ʿAdl and ʿadl (compensation, equivalent) mean the same thing, namely the like. God Most High said: ﴿or an equivalent of that in fasting﴾, meaning its like.

By ʿadl here is meant ransom (fidyah), and it was called ʿadl because it is like that which is ransomed. As for their saying, "No ṣarf or ʿadl will be accepted from him," it was said: ṣarf is the voluntary act (nafilah), and ʿadl is the obligatory act (fari·dah). And it was said: ṣarf is a stratagem (ḥilah), and ʿadl is ransom (fidyah).

(Nor will they be helped) — they will not be protected from the punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 49:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾. Al-injā' (deliverance) and al-tanjiyah (rescue) are one and the same. It means rescue from what is hateful. The "people" (āl) of Pharaoh are his followers, those who followed him and his deeds. Likewise, the "people" (āl) of the Prophet are his followers.

It is related from Anas that the Prophet said: "The āl of every pious believer..." As for the āl of kinship, they are a specific group to whom ṣadaqah (charity) does not apply. This has been mentioned in fiqh.

﴿They afflicted you with the terrible torment﴾. That is, they subjected you to it and put you in charge of it. It was said: they turned you about in torment, now one way and now another, like camels grazing in the wilderness.

﴿Terrible torment﴾: the most severe torment. ﴿They slaughtered your sons and spared your women﴾ is mentioned as a substitution (badal) for His words ﴿they afflicted you﴾. A similar example is the poet's saying:

(Whenever you come to us, you will visit us in our homes, and you will find firewood, plentiful, and a fire blazing.)

His words "you will visit us in our homes" are a substitution for "whenever you come to us."

The meaning of His words ﴿they slaughtered your sons﴾ is: they killed them. Al-dhabḥ (slaughter) and al-dhabīḥ (the slaughtered) have one meaning.

The reason for this is that Pharaoh saw in a dream a fire coming from the direction of Jerusalem, enveloping Egypt and burning every Copt there, but it did not touch the Children of Israel. From this he knew that a prophet would emerge from the Children of Israel, and that their destruction would come at his hands. So he ordered the sons to be killed and the daughters to be spared, until it was said that he killed twelve thousand infants in the search for Moses.

﴿And they spared your women﴾: that is, they left them alive and kept them. It is a form of istif'āl from life (ḥayā), and from it is the Prophet's saying: "Kill the elders of the polytheists and spare their young (shurkh)," meaning their youth. He intended by it the offspring and the women.

﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord﴾. Al-balā' (trial) may mean a blessing and may mean hardship, because it derives from ibtilā' (testing).
