God, exalted, may test through blessing by gratitude, and He may test through hardship by patience. God, exalted, said: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾. The poet said:

(May God reward with goodness what the two have done to him, and what the trial that tests has tried upon them, the best of trials.)

His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And in that was a trial﴾ may bear these two meanings. The first: in what befell you from Pharaoh of harm and hardship, there was a great trial. The second: that He intended by what you attained of deliverance through the drowning of Pharaoh, a great trial, that is, a great blessing.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 50:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And when We parted the sea for you﴾. It was said: "We parted the sea for you." And it was said: "The bā' (in bikum) is in its place, and its meaning is: We parted the sea by your entering it, splitting by splitting, above the head and below the foot, or splitting from that side and splitting from that side." The sea was named "baḥr" (sea) because of its vastness. From this it is said of a horse: "baḥr" when it extends its stride in running, and of a generous man: "baḥr" when his palm extends in giving.

And His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Then We saved you and drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾. It was said regarding the narratives (al-qaṣaṣ): the number of those saved from them was six hundred thousand and twenty thousand, not counting anyone under twenty for his youth, nor anyone over sixty for his old age. As for the number of those drowned, God knows them best.

It was said: At its front was Hāmān with one million and seven hundred thousand men when they drowned, and God knows best who was at the rear.

﴿And you were looking on﴾ at their drowning and their destruction. It was said: "knowing."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 51:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We appointed⦆ (wa-idha wa'adna). He also read: "wa-idh wa'adna" (with the verb in a different form). Their meaning is one and the same. If someone says: "The verbal form mu'ada (to make a mutual promise) is on the pattern of mufa'ala, which requires two parties making promises to each other. How, then, can there be a mutual appointment between God and Moses?"

We reply: The appointing from God, may He be exalted, is by command, and from Moses, peace be upon him, is by acceptance. Likewise is the promise (wa'd).

As for Musa (Moses), it is a Hebrew name. "Mu" in the Hebrew language means water, and "sha" means tree. He was named "Mushe" because he was taken (drawn) from the water and the tree. Then the shin was changed to sin in Arabic, and it became Musa.

His words, ﴿forty nights⦆ mean: the completion of forty nights. God, may He be exalted, commanded him to fast forty days in preparation for receiving the Torah. He had originally been promised thirty; however, God had forbidden him to take anything during these thirty. When he completed the thirty, he passed by a tree and took from its leaves. Because of this, God, may He be exalted, commanded him to fast ten additional days. This is indicated by the words of God, may He be exalted, in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿And We appointed Moses for thirty nights and completed them with ten⦆, and so on.

His words, may He be exalted, ﴿Then you took the calf after him⦆ mean: as a god. It has a well-known story, which will come in Surat Ta-Ha.

﴿And you were wrongdoers⦆ by taking the calf as a god.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 52:

God's words: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾. Al-'Afw (pardon): the effacing of traces. It is said: "The winds effaced (ʿafat al-riyah) such-and-such," when they wiped out the traces. He says: We pardoned you after your taking the calf as a god. ﴿So that perhaps you would be grateful﴾: the meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book﴾ meaning: the Torah. ﴿And the Criterion﴾ concerning this there are three opinions:

The first: he meant by it the Torah as well, except that He mentioned it by two names. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

(Ah, how excellent is Hind, and the land in which Hind dwells... and Hind, distance and remoteness have come between her and us)

Here "al-na'y" (distance) and "al-bu'd" (remoteness) are two names with one meaning.

The second opinion: he meant by it the criterion between truth and falsehood. And God indeed gave Moses that. From this, the day of Badr was named the Day of the Criterion (yawm al-furqan), because on it God distinguished between truth and falsehood.

The third opinion: he meant by it the splitting of the sea, as has already been mentioned. ﴿So that you may be guided﴾ by the Torah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 2, verse 54:

The Most High's words: ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾ means: Remember when Moses said to his people, ﴿"O my people, you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf"﴾ as a god. ﴿"So repent to your Creator (bari')"﴾ your Creator, ﴿"and kill yourselves"﴾ so that some of you kill others. It has also been said that it means: surrender yourselves to being killed.

﴿That is better for you with your Creator﴾ your Creator, ﴿and He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾ by accepting [your repentance], ﴿for He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾, the one who accepts repentance.

It is narrated from ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: The number of those killed among them was [seventy] thousand. When they reached that point, Allah the Most High revealed to Moses: "I have lifted the killing from them, I have had mercy on those who passed away from among them, I have pardoned those who remained, and I have turned to them in forgiveness."

It is related that Yusha' ibn Nun went out to them when they had prepared themselves for the killing and had sat down on their haunches (ihtibaa) for it, and he said: "Indeed Allah has had mercy on whoever loosened his sitting posture." Then those who had not worshipped the calf drew their swords and turned to killing those who had worshipped the calf, until a son would kill his father and a father would kill his son, until they reached seventy thousand. Then the revelation descended as we have described.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 55:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly"﴾ is an address to the seventy whom Moses took to Mount Sinai (al-Tur) so that they might hear the speech of Allah. When they heard the speech of Allah, they said to Moses: "We will never believe you until we see Allah openly." That is: face to face (ʿayānan).

It has also been said that there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, meaning: you said: "O Moses, openly, we will never (believe) (you) until we see Allah (openly)."

﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾. ʿAmr read: "fa-akhadhatkumu al-ṣaʿqatu" (al-ṣaʿqah), which is among the shādh (irregular) readings. The meaning of al-ṣāʿiqah has already been explained. The intended meaning here is death, that is: it seized you ﴿while you were looking on﴾.

If it is asked: when they died, how could they look? It is answered: the meaning is that some of you looked at others at the moment death seized you. It has also been said: the meaning is "you knew," and seeing here carries the sense of knowing.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 56:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We revived you after your death﴾, meaning: We brought you back to life after that death, at the mountain (al-Tur).

Qatada said: He revived them so that they might fulfil their appointed terms. ﴿So that you may give thanks﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 57:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾. Al-ghamam (the clouds): from al-ghamm (covering, concealing). Its root meaning is covering and veiling, and from it is said of a sorrowful heart: maghmum (distressed), because sorrow has covered his heart. And the cloud is called ghamam because it covers the face of the sun. From it is the Almighty's saying: ﴿Then let not your affair be to you ghummah (in confusion)﴾, meaning: obscured for you.

The meaning of the verse: Mujahid said: by the shading of the clouds over them He meant what is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds?﴾, and its explanation will come.

Qatadah said: A people from the Children of Israel remained in the wilderness (al-tih) and became thirsty, and were harmed by the heat of the sun, so Allah shaded them with a cloud so that they would not be harmed.

﴿And We sent down upon you al-manna and al-salwa﴾. Most scholars say: al-manna is the tarangabin (a sweet exudation, manna). Qatadah said: it is a gum that falls upon trees. Wahb said: it is thin bread (khubz raqaq).

As for al-salwa: it is said to be a bird resembling the quail (al-sammani) exactly. And there is a strange opinion: that it is honey.

In the stories (al-qasas) it is related that Allah, the Exalted, would send down to them that every morning from the break of dawn until sunrise, an amount sufficient for their day; except on Friday, for it would descend on the morning of Friday and Saturday together, and nothing would descend upon them on Saturday.

As for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The mushroom is of the manna, and its water is a cure for the eye," that is not from this manna; rather its meaning is that it is from Allah's bounty without toil or hardship.

﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾, meaning: of the lawful things with which We have provided you.

﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾, meaning: they did not diminish Our right, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾.

So zulm (wronging): in the sense of diminishing and decreasing, and its root meaning is as we have explained.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We said: Enter this town﴾. The town (qaryah) was so called because it gathers its people (tajma' ahlaha). From the same root comes al-miqra'ah for a basin, because it is a gathering place for water, and qaryat al-naml (the ant's colony), because it gathers the ants. The intended meaning of "the town" here is the Holy House (al-Bayt al-Muqaddas). It has also been said: it is Jericho (Ariha), a place there.

﴿So eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance (raghadan)﴾. The meaning of raghad has already been given. It has also been said: it is wide provision that does not constrict its seeker (wa la ya'ni talibahu).

﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾. By "the gate" he means the gate of the town. It has also been said: it is the Gate of Hittah, which is the gate of Iliya (Aelia).

﴿Prostrating (sujjadan)﴾: that is, bowing (rukka'an) and humbly submitting (khudda'an). The original meaning of sujud is submission, and in bowing there is submission. The poet said:

(With a host whose horses' hooves stray among its enclosures, you see the hills prostrate before the hooves.)

That is, bowing and humbly submitting.

﴿And say: Hittah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: its meaning is, "Say: remove our sins." Al-Zajjaj said: its implied sense is, "Say: our request is hittah (removal of sins)." 'Ikrimah said: it is the saying, "There is no god but Allah."

﴿We will forgive you﴾. It is read in two recitations: "Naghfir lakum" with the nun, and "Yaghfir lakum" with the ya', and both are the same in meaning. It comes from ghafr, which is covering. From it comes al-maghfirah (forgiveness, or the helmet), because it covers the head. Likewise, forgiveness covers sins.

﴿Your wrongs (khatayakum)﴾: the plural of khati'ah, and it is also plural as khati'at, and it means sins. It is said: khati'a yakhta'u khat'an and khati'ah, when one sins deliberately. And akhta'a yukhti'u ikhta'an when one sins unintentionally.

﴿And We will increase the good-doers﴾: from Our bounty.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 59:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾. They unanimously agreed that they substituted the word "ḥiṭṭah" (a request for forgiveness) with "ḥinṭah" (wheat), and they said in their language: "ḥiṭā samqāthā," meaning: red wheat.

It was also said: they entered the gate dragging themselves on their buttocks, though the gate had been lowered for them. They could not enter standing, and they refused to enter prostrating, so they entered dragging themselves on their buttocks, a disobedience in action just as they had substituted the word.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they used to defy [Our command]﴾.

Al-rijz (الرجز): the punishment. And al-rijs (الرجس): filth. And al-rijz (with a ḍammah on the rā'), an idol, according to the one who recited ﴿And the idol, flee from it﴾ [Q. 74:5]. It was also said: when they did that, God sent down upon them a plague (ṭā'ūn) which killed twenty-four thousand of them in a single hour.

﴿Because they used to defy [Our command]﴾: through disobedience, in deed and in word.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 60:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people﴾. Istisqa' (seeking water) is the request for watering. The reason for this: the Children of Israel remained in the wilderness (al-tih) and became thirsty, so they asked Moses to seek water for them, and he did.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿So We said: Strike the rock with your staff﴾. They differed concerning that rock. Some of them said: it was a specific stone, the size of a man's head.

It was also said: it was a cubit by a cubit. It was also said: it was a stone of the stones, not specified; whichever stone it was.

﴿And there gushed forth from it﴾, meaning: he struck, and there gushed forth (wa-tafajjarat). Its implied construction is: from it ﴿twelve springs﴾, according to the number of the tribes (asbat). ﴿Each group knew its drinking place﴾: each tribe among them knew its drinking place.

It was also said: twelve holes would appear in it by Moses' striking, and each tribe among them knew its own hole.

It was also said: he would carry the stone with himself in a container; whenever they needed water, Moses would strike the stone. ﴿Eat﴾ of what We have sent down to you, of the manna and the quail, ﴿and drink﴾ from these watering places. [﴿from the provision of God﴾].

﴿And do not commit abuse on the earth, causing corruption﴾. Al-'ayth: the most severe corruption. It was also said: its meaning is: and do not strive on the earth causing corruption.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 61:

The words of God Most High: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not be patient with one food"﴾ — it is as if they had agreed together and grown weary of eating the manna and quails, so they asked Moses to request for them other food besides it.

If it is said: They had the manna and the quails, so why did they call them "one"? It is said: they would eat one of them together with the other, so it was like one food.

﴿one food. So call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic (fūm), its lentils, and its onions. He said: "Would you exchange what is lower for what is better? Go down to a city (miṣr), and indeed you will have what you ask."﴾

It is also said: it was always of one kind, and because of its uniformity it was like one food.

﴿So call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows, its herbs and its cucumbers﴾ — they asked for these foods.

As for God Most High's words ﴿and its fūm﴾, the scholars differed concerning it. Ibn ʿAbbās and most of the scholars said: it is wheat. It is also said: bread. And it is related that some of the Bedouin said to his wife: "Fūmī lanā" (fūmī for us), meaning: knead the dough for us (ajziʾ lanā).

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim said: he meant by it garlic, having replaced the ṯāʾ with the fāʾ. And from this is the saying of the poet:

(Their dwellings were then exposed, in them were the paradises, the fūmān and the onion.)

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn Masʿūd read it as "nawmihā" with the ṯāʾ (ﷺ not applicable here), and ﴿and its lentils and its onions﴾.

The words of God Most High: ﴿He said: "Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?"﴾ — meaning: would you choose the lower over what is better? If it is said: Did they not ask for wheat and bread, which are better than the manna and quails, so why did He call it "lower"? It is said: He meant lower in value, or He meant easier to obtain according to custom.

﴿Go down to a city﴾ — that is, descend and go to Egypt (Miṣr). The scholars differed concerning this. Most hold that it is the well-known Egypt. Ibn Masʿūd read "ihbiṭū miṣran" without tanwīn (diacritical nunation). Whoever reads it with tanwīn does so because of the small number of letters.

Al-Aʿmash said: he meant by it the Miṣr upon which Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī was, which is the well-known Miṣr. It is also said: it was a city among the cities, not specified, meaning: "Descend to a city." ﴿And you will have what you asked for, and humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them.﴾ It is said: he meant by it the jizya (poll tax). ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib said: it is the kustīj and the zunnār.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: the holders of land-tax contracts are among those upon whom humiliation was stamped.

﴿And poverty (al-maskana)﴾ — and destitution. It is said: "tamaskana al-rajul," meaning the man became poor, and the poor man was named miskīn because poverty made him still (asknahu) and kept him from movement.

﴿And they returned with anger from God﴾ — meaning: they went back and bore the anger of God.

﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God﴾. The word āya means sign, and āya also means a group; it is said: "the people went out with their āya," meaning with their group. An āya of the Qur'an is a collection of words with a known beginning and end.

The words of God Most High: ﴿and they killed the prophets﴾. Nāfiʿ read it with hamza and madd (ā-). The rest read it with talyīn (without hamza). Its origin is anbāʾ (information), so whoever reads it with hamza is following the original form, and whoever softens it does so because of its frequent use.

It is also said that it is derived from nubuwwa, which is a high place; on this view, the softened reading is the original form.

In a hadith: "A man said, 'O Prophet of God' with hamza and madd, and he said: 'You are not the Prophet of God; I am only the Prophet of God.'"

The words of God Most High: ﴿and they killed the prophets without right﴾. If someone says: Why did He say "without right," since the killing of prophets can only be without right? We say: He mentioned it as a descriptor of the killing, and killing is described sometimes as rightful and sometimes as without right. This is like God Most High's words ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth"﴾. He mentioned "truth" as a descriptor of the judgment, not that His judgment is divided into injustice and truth.

﴿That is because they disobeyed﴾ with sins, ﴿and they used to transgress﴾ — exceeding the limit.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 62:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who were Jews﴾. By "those who were Jews" he means the Jews. They were called Yahud (Jews) because they said ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾, meaning: we have inclined toward You.

It was also said: they were called so because they were descendants of Yahuda son of Ya'qub (Jacob). As for the Christians (al-Nasara), they are a known people. They were called Nasara because they settled in a town called Nasira (Nazareth). It was also said: it is due to the saying of Jesus: "Who are my helpers (ansari) for the sake of God?" They said: "We are the helpers (ansar) of God."

﴿And the Sabians﴾: Nafi' recited it with a soft hamza (al-layn), and the rest recited it with a hamza. Its root is ṣabw, which means inclination and departure.

It is said: "Sabi'a nabu al-ba'ir" when the camel's tooth came out. "Sabā qalbuhu ila fulan" means: his heart inclined toward so-and-so. The poet said:

(My heart inclined to Hind... and Hind, like her, inclines the heart)

That is, my heart inclined toward her, and one like her inclines the heart.

They differed about its meaning. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are a people among the Jews and Christians.

Qatada said: they are a people who recite the Zabur, worship the angels, and pray toward the Ka'ba. (Those who believe in God.) If it is said: He has already mentioned ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ in general, how then does His saying ﴿those who believe in God﴾ fit?

It is said: this refers to Salman and his followers who believed in Muhammad before the Prophethood (al-ba'th), and then affirmed it after the Prophethood.

It was also said: he meant by it those who remained steadfast in faith. And it was said: by "those who believe" he meant the hypocrites who believed with their tongues.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿whoever believes in God﴾, meaning with the heart along with the tongue, ﴿in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, they will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾ in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 63:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [when] We took your covenant﴾, meaning: your pledge, ﴿and raised above you the Mount﴾. It was said: he meant by it Mount Sinai (Tur Sina').

It was also said: every mountain is a tur. In the stories it is related that God, exalted is He, uprooted the mountain of Tur, raised it above their heads, and said to them: "If you do not accept the Torah, I will send this mountain down upon you." So they accepted the Torah. This is what the saying of God, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them﴾, to the end of the verse.

﴿Take what We have given you﴾ from the Torah ﴿with strength﴾, meaning with earnestness and diligence, ﴿and remember what is in it﴾, meaning study what is in it, ﴿that you may become righteous﴾, meaning that you may guard yourselves against the Fire in the Hereafter.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾, meaning: you turned away after you had accepted the Torah. ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾, meaning: by granting respite and postponement. ﴿You would have been among the losers﴾, meaning: among those punished immediately. It is as if He showed them mercy by granting them respite.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 65:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you certainly knew those who transgressed among you in the Sabbath﴾. That is: they went beyond the limit. It is said: "He exceeded his bounds," meaning he went beyond his limit.

﴿among you in the Sabbath﴾. The root of sabt (Sabbath) is "cutting off," and the day of Saturday was named thereby, because the Jews were commanded to cease their works on it. He meant by it the people of Ayla, which is a town on the shore of the sea, and they were to abstain from fishing on Saturday; but they opposed (the command) and went fishing. Their story will come explained in detail in Surat al-A'raf.

﴿So We said to them: "Be apes, despised."﴾ This is a command of bringing into being (takwin), in which the servant has no action or choice.

﴿despised﴾: removed, distanced. From it is said: [akhsa], meaning: he was distanced. If it is asked: why did He say "apes despised," when the apes are described only as "despised" (feminine plural)? It is said: there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in it, and its original form is: "despised apes."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 66:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We made it a deterrent punishment for what was before it⁠﻿⁠ and what was after it﴾. That is: We made their punishment, by transformation, a deterrent (nakal). Nakal is a term for any punishment that deters the observer from doing what the punishment was made a requital for. From it comes nukul (refusal) regarding an oath, which is the refusal to swear.

﴿For what was before it﴾. If it is asked: how can it be a deterrent for what was before it, when they have already passed away? It is said: by it He meant those who were present at that time.

﴿And what was after it﴾: those who would come after. Here "ma" (what) carries the meaning of "man" (those who). There is another view: by "what was before it" He meant the sins that had preceded, and by "what was after it" the sins that were present, for which they were seized.

There is a third view: by "what was before it" He meant the towns that were then built, and by "what was after it" the towns that would come after, through what happened to them.

﴿And an admonition for the God-fearing﴾: from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 67:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾ (wa-idh-kur idh qala Musa li-qawmihi): remember when Moses said to his people: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾. Al-baqarah (the cow): the female of the cattle (al-baqar). It is derived from al-baqr, which means splitting. It was named so because it splits the earth with ploughing.

In a report: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade tabaqqur (excessive expansion) in family and wealth," meaning: expansion. The story concerning this is: among the Children of Israel there was a wealthy man who had a poor cousin. The cousin grew impatient for his life, so he killed him, carried him to another tribe, and dumped him at their courtyard, then in the morning began demanding his blood. They asked Moses to ask his Lord who the killer was. He asked, and Allah the Exalted revealed to him [to him] that he should command them to slaughter the cow.

So he said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow.﴾ ﴿They said: Do you take us in mockery?﴾ Because when they asked him to ask his Lord who the killer was, he said: Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow. Due to the distance between the question and the answer, they said: "Do you take us in mockery?" This was from the extremity of their ignorance and their presumptuousness in speech; they attributed mockery to their Prophet.

﴿He said: I seek refuge in Allah﴾ (a'udhu billah): I hold fast to and refrain by Allah. ﴿Lest I be among the ignorant﴾ (an akuna min al-jahilin): by giving an answer not in accordance with the question. For everyone who is asked about something and answers not in accordance with the question is ignorant.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 68:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what she is."﴾ This is a request for description (istiwsaf) of the cow's age.

﴿He said: "Indeed, He says: 'She is a cow neither old (fariḍ) nor virgin (bikr), but between that (ʿawān).'"﴾ That is, he asked, and he said: "Indeed, He says: '...'" It is said: al-fāriḍ is the old, aged one, al-bikr is the young one, and al-ʿawān is what lies between them.

From this it is said: ʿānat al-mar'ah ("the woman became ʿawān") when she exceeded thirty years of age. And it is said in the proverb: "The ʿawān does not learn the ikhtimār" (i.e., the adornment/ripening, ikhtimār).

It is also said: al-fāriḍ is the one that has given birth to many offspring (buṭūn), al-bikr is the one that has never given birth at all, and al-ʿawān is the one that has given birth to one or two offspring. ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾, namely the slaughter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 69:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾, meaning: ask your Lord on our behalf. ﴿That He may show us what its color is﴾. This is a request for a description of the color. ﴿He said: Indeed He says it is a cow, yellow [in color]﴾. Al-Hasan said: "Safra' (yellow) means black."

From this is the saying of the poet:

(Those are my horses from it, and those are the mounts... they are yellow in color like raisins)

He means black. The correct view is that He intended by it the well-known yellow, on the evidence of His saying: ﴿bright in its color (fāqi' lawnuhā)﴾. It is said: "aṣfar fāqi'" (intensely yellow), "aswad ḥālik" (intensely black), "aḥmar qān" (intensely red), and "abyaḍ yaqiq" (intensely white). This is said for emphasis.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Its horns and hooves were yellow." The correct view is that it was yellow in all of its parts.

﴿Pleasing to the beholders﴾, meaning: it pleases them and brings joy into their hearts because of its beauty, and this is the custom of everything beautiful that is seen. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wears yellow sandals will remain in joy until he takes them off."

The Exalted's statement: ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us"﴾ means "Ask your Lord for us." ﴿"To make clear to us what it is"﴾. This is a request to describe the action: is it from the working animals (al-'awamil) or not? ﴿"Indeed, the cows look alike to us"﴾, meaning they have become confused (ashtabaha). ﴿"And indeed, if Allah wills, we will be guided"﴾.

In a report (khabar), it says: "If they had not said, 'If Allah wills,' they would never have been guided."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 71:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow not trained to plow the earth"﴾. Dhalul (trained, tame) means between tameness (dhilla), and dhalil means between humiliation (dhull). The cow dhalul is the one whom work has tamed by plowing the earth.

﴿And not irrigating the tilth﴾: it is not one that draws water. ﴿Sound, with no blemish in it﴾ (musallama): free of defects. ﴿No mark upon it﴾ (la shiyya fiha): al-Zajjaj said, "There is no color in it that differs from the majority of its color."

﴿They said, "Now you have come with the truth"﴾. If it is said: "He had already come with the truth every time. So what is the meaning of His words ﴿Now you have come with the truth﴾?" It is said: its meaning is, "Now you have brought the complete, healing clarification, with which no ambiguity or confusion remains."

﴿So they slaughtered it, though they nearly did not do so﴾. That is, because of its high price, for it is related that they bought it for its hide filled with gold.

And it is related from Ikrimah that he said: "They did not buy it for that; they bought it for three dinars."

It was also said: the meaning is, "though they nearly did not do so," because of the severity of their confusion and their disagreement about it. The first view is more sound. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They made it hard upon themselves, so Allah made it hard upon them. Had they merely slaughtered any cow, that would have fulfilled their requirement."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 72:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ — this is placed later in recitation but earlier in meaning, because it is the beginning of the story. ﴿And you disputed about it﴾ — meaning: you were at odds, and from this is the poet's saying:

(So he turned away from them the repelling of enemies... and they treated madness with madness)

Meaning: their crookedness.

It was also said: its meaning is: you pushed against one another, when each of them would shift the blame onto another; and the root of *al-darʾ* (repelling) is pushing away.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And God will bring forth what you were concealing﴾ — meaning: He will make manifest what you were concealing, for the killer used to conceal the killing.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We said: Strike him with part of it.﴾ God, exalted is He, commanded that the slain man be struck with part of the cow. The scholars differed concerning that part. Ibn ʿAbbas and most of the exegetes said: it was from the cartilage to the shoulder. Mujahid said: it was the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanab, the "tailbone" of the tail). Others said: it was the thigh. Some of them said: it was the tongue.

It has also been said: "part of it" is unspecified; that is, any part of it would do.

﴿Thus God brings the dead to life⦆ because He showed them the revival of the slain man when he was struck with part of the cow. In the account: when he was struck with part of it, he rose up alive and said: "My killer is so-and-so," and then he fell down dead; so his killer was deprived of the inheritance.

And in a report: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No killer inherits after the companion of the cow."

﴿And He shows you His signs, so that you may understand⦆ — that is, that you may restrain yourselves from acts of disobedience.

It has also been said: the cow was singled out for that slaughter because they had worshipped the calf, so He wished to show them its lowliness and that it is powerless to ward off death from itself.

Or He tested them with the command to slaughter it, so that He might see whether they would kill or not.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that﴾, meaning they dried up and became parched, and the drying of the heart is through the departure of mercy and tenderness from it. ﴿After that﴾ means after what had become apparent to you of those signs. ﴿Then they were like stones﴾, meaning in hardness, ﴿or even harder in hardness﴾.

If it is said: Why did He say "or even harder" when "or" is a word of uncertainty? And why was it compared to stones, when iron is harder than stones?

We say: As for the first, its meaning is "and harder in hardness." It has also been said: it means "rather, harder in hardness," like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to a hundred thousand or more﴾, meaning "or rather more."

A group of the grammarians (al-nahwiyyin) said: the meaning is that if you wish, liken them to stones; and if you wish, liken them to what is harder than stones, and you are correct in all of it. This is a good view.

As for why they were not compared to iron: because iron is receptive to softening, for it softens by fire, and it softened for Dawud, peace be upon him, whereas stones never soften at all.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among stones there are those from which rivers gush forth﴾. It has been said: He meant by it all stones. It has also been said: He meant the stone upon which Musa struck for the tribes (al-asbat).

﴿And among them are those that split open so that water comes out of them﴾: He meant by it springs rather than rivers, and these are found in some rocks. ﴿And among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah﴾, that is, descend out of fear of Allah.

If it is said: A stone is inanimate and does not understand; so how can it fear? We say: The People of the Sunna have said: Allah, may He be exalted, has a knowledge in the inanimate that no one other than Him knows.

It has also been said: Allah, may He be exalted, gives them understanding and inspires them with that, so they fear by His inspiration, and reports have come in the like of this.

For it has been narrated that the Prophet was on Thabir while the disbelievers were seeking him, and the mountain said: "Get down from me, for I fear that you will be seized upon me and Allah will punish me for that." Then Mount Hira said to him: "Come to me, O Messenger of Allah."

It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "A stone used to greet me in Makkah before I was sent, and I recognise it now." The report is sound.

On this subject there are the hadiths of Anas and Sahl ibn Sa'd: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to deliver the khutbah standing against a trunk (jidh) in the mosque; when a pulpit (minbar) was made for him, he moved to it, and when he ascended it, the trunk cried out.

It is related: that it lowed like a bull lows, until the mosque shook; so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came down from the pulpit, and the trunk kept lowing until he embraced it, and it became still. The Prophet (ﷺ) then gave it a choice between being a tree in this world or a tree in Paradise, and it chose Paradise, so he ordered that it be buried.

Mujahid has said: No stone descends from [the high] to the low except out of fear of Allah.

All that we have said is witnessed by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of Allah﴾.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾, that is: He observes what you do.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 75:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you then hope﴾, i.e., do you expect ﴿that they will believe you﴾, i.e., that they will confirm you in what you tell them. ﴿And there was a group of them who used to hear the words of Allah, then they would distort it after they had understood it﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: they heard the Torah, then they distorted the rulings in it and the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second opinion: he meant by this the seventy whom Musa (Moses) took with him to the Mount (Tur) when they said: "If you see Allah, then we should see Allah, and if you hear the words of Allah, then we should hear the words of Allah." Musa said: "As for me, I do not see Allah, but I hear His words." Then Musa asked his Lord, exalted is He, that He let them hear His words. Allah, exalted is He, said: "Command them that they fast for such-and-such, and that they wash or put on new, clean garments, then let them come." So they did that, and they heard the words of Allah.

In the exegesis (tafsir) it is related that He said to them: "I am Allah, there is no god but Me. I brought you out of Egypt with a mighty hand. So worship Me and do not associate anything with Me, and do such-and-such and such-and-such." When they heard His words, their souls departed and they died, then Allah, exalted is He, brought them back to life. They said to Musa: "We cannot bear to hear His words, so you listen, and convey it to us." Then they returned to their people and said: "We have heard the words of Allah, and He has commanded us to do such-and-such and such-and-such, but He said: 'Do it if you wish, or if you are able.'"

In another narration he said: "Do not commit such-and-such unless you have no alternative," so they committed it. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿they heard the words of Allah, then they distorted it after they had understood it﴾, i.e., they understood it, (while they knew) that it was the truth.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 76:

God the Exalted said: ﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾. It was revealed concerning a group of Jews who believed and then became hypocrites. ﴿But when they are alone with one another, they say, "Do you tell them what God has opened up to you?"﴾ The word *al-fath* (opening) means judgment (*al-qada'*). God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾, meaning: We have decided for you a clear judgment.

Al-Asma'i said: I heard a Bedouin say: "Come to al-Fattah" (meaning: come to the judge).

There are three opinions regarding the meaning of the verse:

The first: They said to the people of Medina, when they consulted them about following Muhammad: "Believe in him, for he is true." Then some of them said to others: "Do you tell them what God has opened up to you, so that they will have the proof against you before your Lord," meaning: they will seize you.

The second opinion: They informed them of what God had punished them for because of their crimes. So some of them said to others: "Do you tell them what God has opened up to you of the punishment," ﴿so that they may argue with you before your Lord﴾, so that they would gain for themselves a superiority over you before God.

The third opinion: When the Prophet conquered Khaybar and besieged the Banu Qurayzah, he said to them: "O brothers of the apes and the swine!" Then some of them said to others: "This word did not come out except from you," meaning: "You told him about that." ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 77:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾ He means: He is Knowing of what they keep secret and (what they) make public.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among them are unlettered folk﴾. The ummi (unlettered) is the one who neither reads nor writes. Concerning its derivation there are two opinions:

One of them: it is from umm (mother), so the ummi remains as he was when separated from his mother (i.e., in the state of having just been born, unable to read or write).

The second: it is from ummah, which means creation, and from it is the saying of the poet:

(And indeed Mu'awiyah, the most noble, ... fair of face, tall of ummam)

He means the sons of Mu'awiyah, and "tall of ummam" means tall of creation. So the ummi remains as he was in his original created nature.

﴿They know not the Book, except wishful fancies﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: Mujahid said: al-amani (wishful fancies) are falsehoods.

From this is the saying of Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him): "Since I embraced Islam, I have neither wished (tamannaytu) nor sung (taghannaytu)," meaning: I have not lied. Ibn Da'b said to a man who had mentioned something: "Is this something you narrated (ruwwaytahu) or something you wished (tamannaytahu)?" meaning: did you fabricate it and invent it from your own mind?

The second opinion: that it means recitation, i.e., they know not the Book except recitation. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Except when he recites (tamanna), Satan casts [something] into his recitation (umniyyatihi)﴾, meaning: his recitation. It was also said concerning Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him):

(He recited (tamanna) the Book of Allah at the start of his night ... [would that] he had not met the doom of the fates)

meaning: he recited the Book of Allah.

The third opinion: al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: it is from tamanni (wishing), and these are their false wishes, from their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾, and from their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾, and from their saying: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾. According to this view, "illa" (except) carries the meaning of "lakin" (but), i.e.: they do not know the Book, but they wish for things that will not come to them.

﴿And they are only conjecturing﴾. Mujahid said: they are lying. The people of Basra did not recognize zann (conjecture) in the sense of lying, so they said: its meaning is: they are only guessing (yakhrusun).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 79:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah"﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: they used to write things of their own accord, then they would say to the Bedouins, "This is from Allah," seeking gain from them. It was also said: He meant by it what they altered with their own hands of the description of Muhammad in the Torah, for it stated in it that he was kohl-eyed, of medium build, with straight hair; so they wrote in it that he was fair-skinned, blue-eyed, tall of stature, with curly hair.

﴿That they may purchase with it a little price. Woe to them for what their hands have written; and woe to them for what they earn.﴾ Scholars differed regarding the word "woe" (wayl). Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said, and it is also narrated with a marfu' chain from the Prophet (ﷺ) as well: "Indeed, Wayl is a valley in Hell into which the disbeliever will plunge for seventy autumns."

'Uthman said: it is a mountain of fire. The original meaning of wayl is destruction and an invocation of punishment. If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿for what their hands have written﴾, since writing can only be done by hand? It is answered: He mentioned it for emphasis in affirming the matter. It was also said: its meaning is that they wrote with their own selves, by fabrication.

﴿And woe to them for what they earn﴾ — from the sins.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 80:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days.﴾ Scholars have differed concerning this. Some of them said: they meant by it forty days, corresponding to the number of days during which we worshipped the calf.

Others said: seven days, because the measure of the lifespan of the world is seven thousand years, so they said: we will be punished one day for every thousand years.

It was also said: they said, "We have heard from our prophets that they said: the distance between the two edges of Hell is a journey of forty years. So we will cover a journey of one year each day, and the journey across Hell will remain forty days, and we will be saved from it."

﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant with Allah, so that Allah will not break His covenant?﴾ Its meaning: "How do you know this? Is it a statement from Allah, so that it cannot be contradicted?" His saying: ﴿Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾

"The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾. "Balā" (بلى) is mentioned in response to a negation, and "naʿam" (نعم) is mentioned in response to an affirmation. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said, "Balā" (Yes).

And He said: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?﴾ They said, "Balā" (Yes). And He said: ﴿So have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ They said, "Naʿam" (Yes). ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾: the evil deed is shirk. ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, meaning: he dies in shirk.

It has been said: He intended by "the evil deed" the major sin. ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, meaning: he persists in it and dies without repenting. Ibn al-Sarraj the grammarian said: its meaning is that the paths of salvation are closed off to him. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾"

Almost-complete translation:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds—those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever﴾ up to the end of the verse. Its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: You shall not worship except Allah﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud read: "Do not worship except Allah" in the imperative form. The well-known recitation is "You shall not worship" (la ta'budūna).

It is also read with the yā' and with the tā', and its meaning is one: the Arabs sometimes use the second person (mukhāṭaba) in place of the third person (mughāyaba), and the third person in place of the second person. In this covenant there is a pledge and an oath, and its implied sense is: "By Allah, you shall not worship except Allah."

﴿And to parents, kindness﴾, meaning: and show kindness to parents. Kindness to them is righteousness, tenderness and compassion, and submitting to their command in what does not contradict the command of Allah, may He be exalted. ﴿And to the near of kin﴾, meaning: the people of kinship ties. ﴿And the orphans﴾: "yatīm" is the name for one who has no father among humans, and for one who has no mother among animals; and it is also the name for a poor person among them.

ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I have memorized for you six things from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): there is no divorce before marriage, no manumission where there is no ownership, no vow in disobedience to Allah, there is no orphanhood after reaching puberty, there is no silence from morning until night, and no continuous fasting (ṣawm wiṣāl)." ﴿And the needy﴾ are the poor, as has already been explained.

﴿And speak to people good words﴾ is read in two ways: ḥusnan and ḥusnā.

Its implied sense: "And speak to people a good speech," or "speak to people a speech that is good." Regarding its meaning there are three opinions. The first: Sufyān al-Thawrī said, "Good speech is enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong." The second opinion: it is gentleness in speech and good conduct in companionship. The third opinion: it is addressed to the People of the Torah, meaning: "And speak to people the truth concerning the description of Muḥammad in the Torah."

﴿And establish prayer and give zakāt﴾ has already been explained.

﴿Then you turned away﴾, meaning you withdrew, ﴿except a few of you﴾. That is because a group of them had believed, ﴿and you are averse﴾, like the aversion of your forefathers.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 84:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when We took your covenant: Do not shed your blood﴾ means: let not some of you shed the blood of others.

It is also said: Do not shed the blood of others, lest your own blood be shed; for it is as though you had shed your own blood.

﴿And do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾ means: let not some of you expel others.

It is also said: its meaning is: do not mistreat those who are your neighbours, so that you compel them to leave by means of bad neighbourliness.

﴿Then you acknowledged﴾ means: you accepted, ﴿while you were witnessing﴾ meaning: you confessed to accepting it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 85:

The words of God Most High: ﴿Then you are these (people)﴾ mean: O you (these people), ﴿you kill your own selves﴾ (by killing) some of you others.

﴿And you expel a group of you from their homes, supporting (tazhaharun) against them﴾. It is read with tashdid (doubling) and with takhfif (lightening). Its origin is tatazaharun (tataẓāharūn), so the taʾ (tāʾ) was assimilated into the ẓāʾ (ẓāʾ), and it became doubled (mushaddad). Its meaning is: you assist one another (tuʿāwinūn).

﴿against them with sin and aggression﴾. Al-ithm (sin) and al-ʿudwān (aggression) means excessiveness in wrongdoing. It has been narrated that al-Nawwas ibn Samʿan asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "What is righteousness (al-birr)?" He said: "What your soul is at peace with." He said: "What is sin (al-ithm)?" He said: "What wavers in your breast."

The words of God Most High ﴿And if they come to you as captives (usara)﴾ are read in two readings: "usra" and "usara". Abu ʿAmr distinguished between them in meaning, saying: al-ʾUsara are those who are in hand together with bonds (wathaq), and al-Usra are those who are in hand without bonds. They did not accept this distinction from him, and the correct view is that they are one and the same.

﴿You ransom them (tufduhum)﴾ and ﴿you ransom them (tufadūhum)﴾ are two readings. It is said: they have the same meaning. It is also said: (tufadūhum) is used of the exchange of captives for captives, while (tufdūhum) is used of ransom with property.

﴿And it is forbidden to you to expel them﴾. There is here a transposition (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr). Its sense is: "And you expel a group of you from their homes; and it is forbidden to you to expel them; you support against them with sin and aggression."

﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ Because they opposed (God) in some matters and complied in others.

﴿...and aggression. And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while it is forbidden to you to expel them. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part? So what is the recompense of whoever does that among you except disgrace in the life of this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment. And God is not unaware of what you do.﴾

Al-Suddi said, in clarifying the meaning of the verse: They were commanded with four things: that some of them should not kill others; that some of them should not expel others; that they should not cooperate in sin and aggression; and that they should ransom the captives. They opposed in the three and complied in the ransoming.

The story concerning it is: the Banu Qurayza were allies of the Aws, and the Banu al-Nadir were allies of the Khazraj, and there was fighting between the two tribes. Fighting broke out between the allies of the two tribes. Then, when a captive from the allies of one of the two tribes fell into the hand of the other tribe, the allies of the other tribe would ransom him, even though the captive was from their enemy. When they were asked, "Why do you ransom them?" they said, "We were commanded to ransom." And when they were asked, "Why do you fight them?" they said, "We are their allies, so we must fight alongside them." This is the meaning of the verse.

As for the words of God Most High ﴿So what is the recompense of whoever does that among you except disgrace in the life of this world﴾: it is said: "khizy yakhza khizyan" (to be disgraced), meaning from humiliation and abasement; and "khazia yakhza khazayah" (to be ashamed), meaning from embarrassment, shyness and exposure. From this is the saying of the poet:

(And death is ashamed, looking ashamed...)

That is: shy.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment. And God is not unaware of what you do.﴾

﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life at the price of the Hereafter﴾: they chose the worldly life over the Hereafter.

﴿So their punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped﴾: they will not be protected from the punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 87:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾ — gave (aʿtaynā) — the Torah (al-Tawrāh). ﴿And We followed up after him with messengers﴾ — We sent successively (atbaʿnā). That is: one messenger follows another messenger.

﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear proofs (al-bayyināt)﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions. The first: they are the miracles that Jesus was given, such as raising the dead, healing the blind (al-akmah) and the leper (al-abraṣ), and the like.

The second opinion: they are the Gospel (al-Injīl). ﴿And We strengthened him﴾ — We made him strong — from al-ayd, which is strength (al-quwwah).

﴿with the Holy Spirit (rūh al-qudus)﴾ — the scholars differed concerning the Spirit. Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said, and this is one of the two reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he meant by it Gabriel (Jibrīl). It was said: he was commanded to walk with him wherever he went, until he ascended with him to heaven. It was also said: the Spirit is the Greatest Name (al-ism al-aʿẓam) by which he used to revive the dead. It was also said: it is the Gospel.

He was named a spirit because he was a cause of the life of hearts; and for this reason the Qur'an is also called a spirit.

Jesus was named a spirit because he came into being by the creation of God without the generation of a father.

As for Gabriel: he was named a spirit for his subtlety, or for his position with respect to the revelation, which is the cause of the life of hearts.

As for the qudus: it was said that it is an attribute (naʿt) of Gabriel. The root of qudus is purity (al-ṭahārah). From it comes al-quddūs, and it is purity. And "the sacred land" (al-arḍ al-muqaddasah) is the purified one. Gabriel was described as holy (qudus) only because he never committed a sin at all; he was pure from sins.

It was also said: al-Qudus is God, Exalted.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire﴾ — what your hearts did not want — ﴿did you become arrogant?﴾ — you became proud and magnified yourselves — ﴿and a group of them you denied, and a group of them you kill.﴾

So the deniers are such as Jesus and Muhammad (ﷺ). And the killed are such as Zechariah and John (Yaḥyā), peace and blessings of God be upon them all.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 88:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are uncovered."﴾ Ibn 'Abbas read "ghulf" with a damma on the lam, and this is the reading of al-A'raj and Ibn Muhays; and it is among the irregular readings (shawadh).

The well-known reading is with a sukun on the lam, and they are the plural of "aghlaf" (uncircumcised, or closed-off), and its meaning: our hearts are in containers (awiya) from what you say, so we do not understand anything of that. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are in coverings."﴾

As for "ghulf" with a damma on the lam, it is the plural of "ghilaf" (sheath, covering). Its meaning: our hearts are containers of knowledge, and there is nothing in them of what you say. That is, what you say is nothing.

﴿But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief.﴾ Allah has expelled them from understanding and mercy. The original meaning of la'n (curse) is expulsion and distancing. And the poet said:

(He frightened the sandgrouse with it, and drove away from it the station of the wolf, like the accursed man)

That is: the station of the accursed wolf, meaning: the expelled one.

﴿So little is it that they believe.﴾ It was said: He meant by this the polytheists, and its meaning: their faith is little, and what is meant [by it] is their belief that Allah is their Creator and the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

It was said: He meant by this the People of the Book, because those among them who believed are fewer than those among the polytheists who believed.

It was said: its meaning: they do not believe at all.

Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "Little grows in this land except the leek and the onion." That is: nothing grows except the leek and the onion.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 89:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah﴾, meaning the Qur'an. ﴿Confirming what was with them﴾, from the Torah and the Gospel.

﴿And previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved﴾, meaning they were seeking victory (yastaftihuna, "seeking victory" or "seeking help"). From this is the saying of the poet: (Ala ubligh Banu 'Isma rasulan ... fa-inni 'an qabaihikum ghaniyy) [Unquestioned: "Ah, convey to the Banu 'Isam a messenger... for I am independent of your ugliness"].

That is: independent of your help.

And in a report: "The Prophet used to seek victory (yastaftih) through the poor among the Emigrants" (ﷺ is not part of the report here). That is, he sought help through them in supplication for the military campaigns.

The meaning of the verse is: the polytheists used to harass the Jews, and perhaps they would gain the upper hand over the Jews in battle. So the Jews said: "O Allah, grant us victory through the unlettered Prophet whom You will send at the end of time." So they would be victorious through him. But when he was sent, they disbelieved in him. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved. So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it. So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 90:

God's words: ﴿Wretched is that for which they have sold themselves﴾. Bi'sa (wretched): a noun that encompasses every kind of blame. Ni'ma (excellent): a noun that encompasses every kind of praise. ﴿They have sold themselves﴾: they chose for themselves ﴿that they disbelieve in what God has sent down﴾ of the Qur'an, ﴿out of spite (baghyan)﴾, meaning envy. Al-baghy (transgression) is oppression, and its origin is seeking; so the one who transgresses (al-baghi) is one who seeks oppression. The envier is a wrongdoer, because he wants the blessing to cease from the one envied without any offence committed by him. ﴿That God should send down of His bounty﴾, which is prophethood, ﴿upon whom He wills of His servants﴾, meaning the prophets.

﴿So they incurred﴾, that is, they returned ﴿wrath upon wrath﴾. In this there are three opinions:

The first: the first wrath was for worshipping the calf, and the second wrath was for disbelieving in Muhammad.

The second opinion: the first wrath was for denying Jesus, and the second wrath was for denying Muhammad.

The third opinion: the first wrath was for disbelieving in the Gospel, and the second wrath was for disbelieving in the Qur'an.

﴿And for the disbelievers there is a humiliating punishment﴾, that is, one that disgraces.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 91:

The words of God, the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what God has sent down,"﴾ meaning the Qur'an. ﴿They say, "We believe in what was sent down to us,"﴾ meaning: what was sent down to us, the Torah, suffices us.

﴿And they reject what is beyond it,﴾ Abu 'Ubayda said: "what comes after it." Al-Farra' said: "what is other than it of the scriptures," and this is the more correct view. ﴿while it is the truth,﴾ meaning the Qur'an, ﴿confirming what is with them,﴾ from the Torah. ﴿Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of God before, if you were believers?"﴾ If someone says: the killing was done by their forefathers, so how did He address the sons with it?

The answer: We say, the killing of the prophets, although it was done by the fathers, the sons approved of it and sided with them in it; therefore He addressed the sons with it. Also, He said: ﴿Why do you kill the prophets of God before?﴾ in the present-future form (taqtulūna), whereas what suits the situation is to say "Why did you say?"

As for His words ﴿Why do you kill﴾, its meaning is "Why did you kill," but the Arabs sometimes place the past tense in the position of the future and the future in the position of the past. The evidence for this is His words ﴿before, if you were believers﴾, meaning "in your claim."

It has also been said: its meaning is "you were not believers," in negation, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first to worship"﴾, meaning: the Most Merciful had no son. There is another view on this which will come later.

"The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs﴾ — that is, with the miracles. ﴿Then you took the calf [as deity] after him﴾ — regarding the pronoun in "after him" (min ba'dihi) there are two opinions: the first is that it refers back to Moses, and the second is that it refers back to the coming (al-majī'). ﴿And you were wrongdoers﴾ — by that."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you, [saying], "Take what We have given you with determination"﴾. This has already been explained. ﴿And listen﴾, meaning hear and accept. ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey."﴾ That is: we hear with our ears and disobey with our hearts.

It has also been said: when they heard and opposed it through their actions, it was as if they had said, "We hear and we disobey," even though they did not say it. A similar usage is the saying of the poet:

(The basin filled and said, "Enough, enough!" ... "Gently, gently, I have already filled my belly.")

Here the saying is attributed to the basin, though it said nothing.

﴿And they were made to drink﴾, meaning they were made to mix (ushribū, from ishtibāh, "to be mixed"). From this comes the expression "so-and-so is mushrab in color," when his whiteness is mixed with redness. ﴿In their hearts [was the calf]﴾, meaning the love of the calf. The word "love" is omitted, and the second term is left standing in its place, and a similar usage is the saying of the poet:

(And how can one who has become like the essence of ... be joined, like Abu Marhab?)

That is, like the essence (khalāla) of Abu Marhab.

In the stories it is related that Moses, upon whom be peace, commanded that the calf be ground down with a file, then commanded that it be scattered into the river, and ordered them to drink from it. Whoever still had some love of the calf left in his heart, the traces of gold dust appeared on his lips. ﴿Say: "Evil is that which your faith commands you, if you are believers."﴾ That is: an evil faith that commands this.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 94:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is yours exclusively, to the exclusion of the people,﴾ because they said: "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians." So He rebuked them for that.

﴿Then wish for death, if you are truthful.﴾ Because whoever knows that he will enter Paradise when he dies wishes for death, and it does not weigh heavily upon him to die.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 95:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forward﴾. He informs that they will never wish for that, as if God had turned them away from wishing for death, in confirmation of the Messenger and in verification of his miracle, since it was possible that some of them might wish for it in order to deny the Messenger.

In the report it is said: "Had they wished for that, death would have seized them on the spot."

﴿And God is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ among them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 96:

His saying: ﴿And you will find them the most eager of people for life﴾ means the Jews. ﴿And of those who associated partners with God﴾ means: and more eager than those who associated partners with God. This is like their saying: "So-and-so is the most generous of people, and of Hurm," meaning: and more generous than Hurm.

They mean by it Hurm ibn Sinan. He was a man well known for generosity, and he had a poet called Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma.

And what is meant by "those who associated partners" here is the Magians (al-Majus), because some of them say to one another: "Live a thousand years," in their language, "bazh hazha rasal." So God, exalted is He, informed that the Jews are the most eager of people for love of life, and [more eager] than the Magians who say that.

﴿Each one of them wishes he could be granted a life of a thousand years﴾ as we have described, ﴿but it will not remove him from the punishment that he should be granted life.﴾ That is, long life will not remove them from the punishment.

﴿And God is Seeing of what they do﴾: the meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel...﴾ Regarding the occasion of the revelation of this verse there are two accounts.

The first: Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the Jews: "I adjure you by the Merciful, who sent down the Torah to Moses, do you find Muhammad in your book?" They remained silent. Then he questioned them a second time, and they said: "Yes." Umar said: "Then why do you not believe in him?" They said: "Because Gabriel is the one who descends to him, and he is our enemy; he is the one who brings punishment. Had Michael descended to him, we would have believed in him." Umar said: "I bear witness that whoever is an enemy to Gabriel is an enemy to Michael, and whoever is an enemy to them both, then Allah is an enemy to him." So the verse was revealed in accordance with Umar's statement.

It has also been related from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "My Lord agreed with me in three matters." It is also narrated: "My Lord agreed with me in three." One of them is this, the second is the verse of hijab: ﴿And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a screen﴾; and the third is praying behind the Station of Abraham: ﴿And take the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer﴾.

The second account concerning the occasion of revelation: Ibn Suriya al-A'war, who was the most learned of the Jews, came to the Prophet and said: "I am going to ask you questions that none but a prophet knows. If you answer me, I will know you to be truthful." He said: "Ask." Ibn Suriya said: "What is the sign of a prophet?" He said: "That his eyes sleep but his heart does not sleep." He said: "You have spoken truly." Then he said: "How is the child created from the two waters?" He said: "When the man's water overcomes the woman's water, it becomes male, by Allah's permission; and when the woman's water overcomes the man's water, it becomes female, by Allah's permission."

He said: "And which of the angels descends to you?" He said: "Gabriel." He said: "If Michael had descended to you, we would have believed in you, for he is our enemy." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel...﴾

(In it there are four readings: "Jibrīl" with a kasra and softened pronunciation; "Jabrīl" with a fatha and softened pronunciation; "Jabrīl" with a fatha, a hamza, and elongation; and "Jabrīᵓīl" with a fatha and hamza without elongation.

"Jabr" means "servant," and "ʾīl" is a name of Allah; likewise Mīkāʾīl, and its meaning is "servant of Allah" or "servant of the Merciful." Thus said Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī.

Jibrīl is on the pattern of qindīl, barṭīl and zanbīl; Jabrīʾīl is on the pattern of ʿandalīb; and Jibrīl has no equivalent pattern.)

﴿For he has brought it down upon your heart﴾, meaning the heart of Muhammad, ﴿by Allah's permission, confirming what came before it﴾ of the Torah and the Gospel, ﴿and as guidance and good news for the believers.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 98:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and [Mikal], then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾. This was revealed in accordance with the statement of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, and his saying: ﴿Jibril and (Mikal)﴾. Although they (Jibril and Mikal) are included in the category of angels and messengers, He singled them out for mention to honour them.

The Lord's words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs﴾, meaning the Qur'an and its verses. ﴿And none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾, that is: the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 100:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is it not that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them casts it aside?﴾ It was said: He meant by this the covenant that God took from the Jews, that they would believe in Muhammad; so they opposed it and cast it aside.

It was also said: It is the covenant that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took from the Banu Qurayza and the Nadir, that they would not assist the polytheists against his fighting. So they opposed it and cast it aside. Al-nabdh (casting aside) means to throw away, and from it is the saying of the poet:

(I looked at its title, then cast it aside... as you cast aside a sandal worn out from your sandals)

﴿Rather, most of them do not believe﴾, though a few of them did believe.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 101:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah﴾, meaning: Muhammad.

﴿Confirming what they already had﴾ of the scriptures. ﴿A party of those who were given the Book threw the Book of Allah behind their backs﴾, meaning by it the Torah.

Al-Sha'bi said: They would recite the Torah but not act upon it. So their casting it away was like this.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: They wrapped it in silk and brocade and adorned it with gold and silver, and then they did not act upon it, so they are the ones who cast it aside.

It was also said: By "the Book" is meant the Qur'an. ﴿As if they did not know﴾, meaning: when they opposed what they knew, it was as if they did not know.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 102:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾, meaning: the Jews, ﴿what the devils recited﴾, i.e., what they recited. The verb is in the present tense with the meaning of the past. al-Ḥuṭay'a said:

(Al-Ḥuṭay'a bears witness when he meets his Lord ... that al-Walīd is more deserving of treachery.)

Meaning: he bears witness.

The meaning of His words ﴿recited﴾ is: they related and narrated ﴿over the kingdom of Sulaymān﴾, during the reign of Sulaymān's kingdom. It was also said: concerning the kingdom of Sulaymān. The story in this regard is what is related: that in the time of Sulaymān, peace be upon him, there were sorcerers who had books on this matter. Sulaymān seized the books of magic from their hands and buried them in a chest beneath his throne. When he died, the devils said to mankind: "Shall we direct you to a treasure with which Sulaymān used to do what he did?" They then extracted those books. Some of the ignorant among them said: "It was by this that Sulaymān did what he did."

It was also said: when God did not take the kingdom away from Sulaymān, the devils wrote books of magic and buried them beneath the throne. When God restored the kingdom to him, that magic remained buried as it was. When Sulaymān died, they extracted those books and said that Sulaymān used to do by it what he did. It was also said: the devil appeared in the form of the Prophet and said that to them. It was also said: he whispered that to him, and this is what the devils recited over the kingdom of Sulaymān. ﴿And Sulaymān did not disbelieve﴾, i.e., Sulaymān did not practise magic. It was also said: by it is meant the well-known disbelief.

﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾ is read with a light and a heavy (shaddah) pronunciation. When it is read with the shaddah, it governs the accusative for "the devils." When it is read lightly, it remains in the nominative: ﴿disbelieved﴾, i.e., practised magic. It may also be the well-known disbelief, ﴿teaching mankind magic﴾. Magic in the language is an expression for deceptions, illusions and tricks. Imru' al-Qays said:

﴿We see ourselves as those who are deceived (by the... unseen)﴾ ... and we are bewitched with food and drink.

Meaning: we are deceived.

al-Farrā' said: magic is a speech that a person utters by which he causes a man to be estranged from his wife.

﴿And what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Hārūt and Mārūt. And they taught no one until they said: "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve."﴾

It is related from al-Shāfi'ī that he said: magic causes a change, causes illness, and may kill. Magic's existence is established according to the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and it has effect. But practising it is disbelief. Its effect is what we have mentioned. It was also said: it affects the essence of things, so that a human is made into the form of a donkey and a donkey into the form of a dog. The more correct view is that it creates an illusion of that, as we have explained.

The Messenger of God was himself bewitched and was affected by it. It is related: "Labīd ibn A'ṣam, the Jew, bewitched the Prophet so that it seemed to him that he did a thing when he had not done it. God informed him of this, so he ordered that it be extracted, and it was taken out from a well of Dhī [Arwān]. On it were eleven knots. God then sent down the two protective chapters, eleven verses. Whenever he recited a verse, a knot was undone, until the knots were all undone, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And what was sent down to the two angels﴾ is read in the negative form, and this is related from ʿAṭiyya ibn ʿAwf. According to this reading, there is inversion and reordering in the verse. Its sense is: "And Sulaymān did not disbelieve, and what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Hārūt and Mārūt, but the devils disbelieved, teaching mankind magic, and they taught no one," and this is a strange opinion.

The correct view is that "mā" means "alladhī" ("that which"), i.e., "and that which was sent down to the two angels."

Ibn ʿAbbās read "al-malakayn" with a kasra on the lām, and this is an irregular reading (shādh). al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: they were two non-Arab men (ʿilj) from the non-Arab people of Babylon, and they were not two angels.

The correct view is that they were two angels, and this is the familiar recitation.

The story concerning this is what Ibn ʿUmar related from Kaʿb al-Aḥbār; this is also the statement of ʿAṭā' ibn Abī Rabāḥ and a group of the exegetes. They said: the angels marvelled at the abundance of the sins of the children of Adam, so they said: "Our Lord, these are the ones You made vicegerents on earth, and they do such things." God said to them: "If I sent you down to the earth and placed in you what I placed in them, you would do as they did." So they chose two of their best, Hārūt and Mārūt, and God sent them down to the earth, and took a covenant from them that they would not associate partners with Him, nor kill, nor commit fornication. Kaʿb said: "Not long had passed for them until they committed all of it."

In the story: the woman with whom they committed fornication was Zuhra; she was transformed into a star and raised up to heaven, and Ibn ʿUmar, whenever he saw it, would curse it.

In the story: when they committed that, God gave them the choice between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, and they chose the punishment of this world, so they were hung by their feet.

ʿAṭā' ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: their heads were folded beneath their wings.

As for Bābil (Babylon): Ibn Masʿūd said it is the land of Kūfa. It was also said: it is the mountain of Damāwand. It was also said: it is from Naṣībīn to Rās al-ʿAyn. It was named Bābil because the tongues were confused (tabalbalat) in it, i.e., they scattered and spread throughout the lands.

﴿And they taught no one until they said: "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve."﴾ Fitna (trial): testing. From this it is said: "I tested the gold in the fire," i.e., I examined it, so that the good might be distinguished from the bad.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of the sending down of magic upon the two angels, and what is the meaning of their teaching magic, when both are far-fetched?

It is answered: as for the sending down of magic, it means teaching and inspiration, that is, they were given knowledge of magic and inspired with it.

It was also said: it is the literal sending down, namely the sending down of the form and manner of magic, so that people might refrain from it. As for the teaching of magic by the two angels, it means informing. A similar usage is the poet's saying:

(Know that after error [guidance] ... and that for this dust there is clearing.)

Meaning: know.

It was also said: it is the literal sense of teaching. Then there are two opinions in this: first, that they taught the manner of magic so that people would refrain from it; a man would come to them and say: "What has God forbidden?" They would say: "Associating partners." He would say: "And what is associating partners?" They would say: "Such and such." Another would come and say: "What has God forbidden?" They would say: "Magic." He would say: "And what is magic?" Then they would teach him the manner of magic so that he might refrain from it, and likewise for all sins.

The second opinion: it is teaching as a trial.
