God empowered them to teach magic as a trial for mankind, so that whoever learned it, believed in it, and practised it would be a disbeliever, and whoever did not learn it nor practise it would not be a disbeliever. The evidence for this is His words, exalted is He: ﴿We are only a trial﴾, i.e., a tribulation, ﴿so do not disbelieve﴾, i.e., do not learn magic and practise it, for then you would disbelieve.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿so they learn from them what they use to separate a man from his wife﴾ mean the magic by which a man is estranged from his wife, as we have described.

﴿And they could not harm anyone with it except by God's permission﴾: its meaning is, except by God's creation. The sorcerer practises magic, and God brings it about.

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: its meaning is, except by God's decree and predestination.

﴿And they learn what harms them and does not benefit them﴾, meaning: magic harms them and does not benefit them.

(And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it, chose it) ﴿for him there is no portion in the Hereafter﴾, i.e., no share.

﴿And wretched is what they sold their souls for, if only they had known﴾: wretched is the choice they chose for themselves.

If it is asked: did He not say: ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it, for him there is no portion in the Hereafter﴾? So what is the meaning of His words: ﴿if only they had known﴾, when He has informed that they did know?

It is answered: by His words "and they certainly knew" He means the devils, and by His words "if only they had known" He means the Jews.

It was also said: both refer to the Jews; but since they did not act upon what they knew, it is as if they did not know.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if only they had believed and been mindful of Allah﴾ — they had believed in you, O Muhammad, ﴿and been mindful﴾ of disbelief and sorcery. ﴿A reward from Allah would have been better, if only they knew﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina"﴾. Its meaning: "Give us your attention (arina sam'aka) and listen to us." Its literal sense (haqiqatuhu) is "empty out (farigh) your hearing for our speech."

﴿But say, "Unzurna"﴾, i.e., "wait for us" (intazirna). It was also said: "Look at us" (unzur ilayna).

Al-A'mash read "Anzirna," meaning "give us respite" (amhilna). The poet said:

﴿Abā Hind, do not hasten against us ... and give us respite, we will inform you with certainty﴾

i.e., give us respite.

﴿And listen﴾, i.e., obey. ﴿And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾, i.e., a punishment that is painful. Concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse there are two accounts:

The first: the Companions used to say to the Prophet, "Ra'ina," intending by it what we have mentioned, and the Jews heard it. For them it was an insult (sabb), and it has the meaning of "O fool" (ya ahmaq).

Al-A'mash read "Ra'ina" with tanwin, and al-Hasan read "Ra'una." Both are dialects derived from ra'ana (ru'una, foolishness). When the Jews heard it they rejoiced, since they saw them insulting him without knowing it. They used to say that to the Prophet in agreement with the Muslims outwardly, and they would laugh among themselves, "We insult him while they do not know." So God, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿Do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna"﴾.

The second opinion: their saying "Ra'ina" contained coarseness and harshness, because its literal sense is "empty out your hearing for our speech so that you may understand," and in this there is a kind of rudeness. So He revealed: ﴿Do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna"﴾, so that they would say what they say in a manner of reverence and request, and choose the finest of words and the most sound of meanings.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 105:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieve, among the People of the Book and among the polytheists, do not wish﴾. "Yawaddu" means "yuhibbu" (loves, desires), and "al-wadd" means "al-hubb" (love).

The meaning of the verse is that the prophets before him were sent from the descendants of Isaac (Ishaq). When the Prophet was sent from the descendants of Ishmael (Isma'il), this did not happen by the approval and love of the Jews. As for the polytheists, his prophethood did not come about by their approval because he came to deny their misguidance and to disparage their gods. This is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, wish that there should be sent down upon you﴾, meaning upon you, O Muhammad. [The Qur'an] mentions the singular by addressing the plural, as is the habit of the Arabs. ﴿Any good from your Lord﴾, meaning prophethood. ﴿But Allah selects for His mercy whom He wills﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and most of the exegetes said: "Mercy" here means prophethood. It was also said: it means Islam and guidance to it. ﴿And Allah is the Owner of great bounty﴾. Bounty (al-fadl) is a beginning of benevolence without cause ('illah).

The Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 106:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate﴾. Ibn 'Amir read "mā nunsikh" with a dammah on the nūn and a kasrah on the sīn, and its meaning is "whatever you find to be abrogated," and it is like their saying: "aḥmadtu fulānan," meaning: I found him praiseworthy; and "abkhaltu fulānan," meaning: I found him stingy.

The well-known reading is ﴿mā nansakh﴾ with a fatḥah.

Naskh (abrogation) linguistically means: lifting a thing and establishing something else in its place. It is said: "nasakha ash-shams aẓ-ẓill," meaning: the sun abrogated the shadow, i.e., it removed it and the light took its place.

It may also mean lifting a thing without establishing anything else in its place. It is said: "nasakhat ar-riyāḥ al-āthār" when it removes the traces from their root with nothing to take their place.

Naskh is permissible in general by the consensus of the Muslim community. And the abrogation of the Qur'an occurs in several ways:

Among them is abrogation that entails the removal of both the recitation and the ruling together. This is like what is narrated from Abu Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf: that some of the Companions stood one night to recite a surah, but they did not recall from it except His saying: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾. So they went in the morning to the Prophet and informed him of that, and he (ﷺ) said: "That was a surah whose recitation and rulings were lifted."

It was also said that Surat al-Aḥzab was like Surat al-Baqarah; then most of it was lifted, in recitation and ruling.

Among abrogation is that which entails the removal of the recitation but not the ruling, like the verse of "stoning" (al-rajm): its recitation was lifted while its ruling remained.

And among it is that which entails the removal of the ruling but not the recitation, like the verse of "bequest to parents and relatives" (al-waṣiyyah lil-wālidayn wal-aqrabīn), and the verse of "the waiting period of widowhood being a year" (ʿiddat al-wafāh bil-ḥawl), and like it the verse of "lightening in fighting" (al-takhfīf fi'l-qitāl), and the verse of "al-Mumtaḥanah," and the like.

And among the aspects of abrogation is that which entails the removal of the ruling and the establishment of something else in its place, like the qiblah being abrogated to the Ka'bah, the bequest being abrogated to inheritance, the waiting period of widowhood being abrogated from a year to four months and ten days, and the resisting of one man against ten in fighting being abrogated to resisting of one man against two. And the like.

﴿Do you not know that to God belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, and that you have not, besides God, any protector or helper﴾.

And among it: the removal of a ruling without establishing anything in its place; like the testing of women, abrogated without a replacement. Likewise similar cases.

Returning to the interpretation of the verse: His saying ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate﴾ means: whatever sign We lift. As for His saying ﴿or cause it to be forgotten﴾, the scholars differed about its meaning. Ibn 'Abbas said its meaning is: or We leave it, so We do not abrogate it. It is like His saying: ﴿They forgot God, so He forgot them﴾, meaning they abandoned God, so He abandoned them. From this is the saying of the poet:

(Indeed, a difficulty lies before me that I will settle; I am neither forgetting it nor letting it be forgotten.)

meaning: I am neither forgetting it nor abandoning it. On this view, His saying ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾ refers back to His saying ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate﴾.

It was also said: the meaning of His saying ﴿or cause it to be forgotten﴾ is: We cause you to forget it, O Muhammad. This is like what we narrated in the hadith of Abu Umamah.

And 'Aishah narrated that the Messenger of God heard a man reciting a surah and said: "This man reminded me of a verse I had forgotten." This is the counterpart of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We will make you recite, and you will not forget, except what God wills﴾. Ibn Mas'ud read: "mā nunsika min āyatin aw nunsikhhā" (Whatever sign We cause you to forget or abrogate it), and this supports this view; on this view, causing to forget upon the heart has the sense of abrogation.

There is a third view: the meaning of His saying "or cause it to be forgotten" is: We command its abandonment and permit its abandonment, like the abrogation of the verse of al-Mumtaḥanah and the like.

If someone says: if causing to forget means permitting abandonment, what is the difference between it and abrogation?

We say: they are two aspects of abrogation, except that by the first abrogation he meant the removal of a ruling and the establishment of something else in its place, and by the second he meant the abrogation of the ruling without establishing anything else in its place, as we have mentioned.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read ﴿aw nunsa'hā﴾ with a fatḥah and a hamzah. Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam related from Abu Nu'aym the reciter that he said: "I saw the Messenger of God in a dream, and I recited to him with the reading of Abu 'Amr, and he corrected me on two words: his saying 'wa-arinā' (and show us), and he said: 'Say wa-argina' with a kasrah on the rā'." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "I think he said the second word was: aw nunsa'hā, and he said: say: aw nunsihā." Al-nasa' and al-ins'ā' mean postponement; the Arabs say: "ansa'a Allāhu ajalak" and "nasa'a Allāhu fī ajalik" (God postpone your term). Regarding its meaning there are two views:

One: the meaning of His saying "aw nunsa'hā" is: We lift its recitation and postpone its ruling, as was done with the verse of stoning. The first abrogation would then mean the removal of both recitation and ruling together.

The second view: the meaning of His saying "aw nunsa'hā" is: We postpone its sending down and leave it in the Preserved Tablet, so it is not sent down.

His saying "mā nansakh min āyah" means: whatever is sent down, or "nunsa'hā" so it is not sent down, We bring a better one than it or its like.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying "We bring a better [than it]", when the verses of the Qur'an are equal, with no excellence of some over others? And if by "better" is meant ease, then the easier has been abrogated by the more difficult, like fasting, which was optional between it and ransom (fidyah), then abrogated by fasting Ramadan as an obligation. So what is the meaning of "betterness"?

We say: it has been said, its estimate is: We bring from it something better, i.e., We lift a verse and bring a verse.

The correct view is that by "better" He meant "more excellent," in benefit and ease. Its meaning is: We bring one better than it, i.e., more beneficial and easier.

"Or its like" in benefit and ease. And if the easier is abrogated by the more difficult, then the meaning of "better" in it is in reward, for the reward of the more difficult is greater. If it is asked: both are equal in complying with the command, so how do they differ in reward? The answer: God, the Exalted, may reward the more difficult more than the easier, and He has promised reward for fasting Ramadan what He did not promise for the optional fast earlier.

There is another view: that by His saying "We bring a better one than it" He meant specifically in the abrogation of the qiblah, and by "or its like" He meant generally; for facing the Ka'bah was better for the Arabs and more inviting to them to Islam, since there was aversion in their hearts toward facing the Bayt al-Maqdis, because the Jews had made it their qiblah.

There is a third view: that the meaning of His saying "We bring a better one than it" is: in the state of the abrogation of the first, for the second, which was newly revealed and acted upon, is better than the first abrogated one which is not acted upon. This view is far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 107:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you not know that Allah has power over all things?﴾ Although "Do you not know" (alam ta'lam) is in the form of a question, what is meant by it is confirmation (al-taqrir). Its meaning is: you know that Allah has power over all things. Likewise His statement: ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ As for al-mulk (dominion), it is complete power, and from it comes the word al-malik (the king), which is the sovereign authority of complete power.

﴿And you have not, besides Allah,﴾ Abu 'Ubayda said: "besides Allah" means "after Allah." Others said: "other than Allah." ﴿any protector (wali)﴾ meaning a governor (wal), and He is the one who manages affairs ﴿nor any helper (nasir)﴾ nor any preventer of the punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 108:

His saying: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger⦆ — "Am" (or) occurs in the language in several senses.

﴿Would that they could turn you back, after your belief, into disbelievers, out of envy from their own selves, after the truth has become clear to them⦆

So it takes the meaning of confirmation (taqrir), and this is what is intended here. Its meaning is: "You wish."

It may also occur in the sense of doubt (tashkik). It is said: "I saw Zayd, or ('am) 'Amr?"

"Am" may also occur in the sense of "bal" (rather). The poet said:

(It appeared like the horn of the sun in the brilliance of the forenoon... and its image, or (am) you are in the eye more beautiful.)

That is: "Rather, you are in the eye more beautiful."

﴿that you question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before⦆. Regarding its meaning there are two opinions. One: they asked the Messenger, saying: "We will not believe you until you bring God and the angels before us as a tribe (qabilan)," just as the people of Moses said to Moses: ﴿We will not believe you until we see God openly⦆.

The second: they asked the Messenger to turn the Safa into gold, just as the people of Jesus asked Jesus for the table (al-Ma'idah). The first is more apparent. The intent of the verse is to prevent them from open-ended questions after the proofs have become manifest.

﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for belief⦆ — that is, he substitutes disbelief for belief. For such a question after the proof has become manifest is disbelief.

﴿has indeed strayed from the right way⦆ — that is, the middle of the way (sawa' al-sabil).

It is also said: "the intended way (qasd al-sabil)." Both are sawa'. It is related from 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Nahwi that he said: "I kept writing until my sawa' (middle) was cut off," meaning my middle.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 109:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish⦆ meaning: many of the People of the Book loved and desired (ود, wadd) ﴿that they could turn you back, after your faith, into disbelievers﴾. It was said: this was revealed concerning ʿAmmar and Ḥudhayfah. The Jews invited them to their religion, and ʿAmmar said: "How is the covenant broken among you?" They said: "Severely." ʿAmmar said: "I have covenanted with God that I will not disbelieve in Muhammad." Then they said to Ḥudhayfah: "What do you say?" He said: "God is my Lord, Muhammad is my Prophet, and the Qur'an is my imam." Then God the Exalted revealed this verse.

It was also said: it refers in general to the disbelievers and the Muslims, because they have never ceased to wish for the return of the Muslims to disbelief.

﴿out of envy﴾: that is because they knew that Muhammad is a true prophet, and that by following him the Muslims attained from Islam what they had not attained; so they envied them for their religion.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿out of envy from themselves﴾, since envy does not come from others? It is answered: its meaning is: of their own accord, nothing has been sent down concerning it in a Book, nor has any command come regarding it.

It was also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, and its construction is: "Many of the People of the Book wish, from themselves, that they could turn you back, after your faith, into disbelievers, out of envy."

﴿after the truth has become clear to them﴾: after it has become evident that it is the truth.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿So pardon and overlook⦆ al-ʿafw (pardon) is erasure, and al-ṣafḥ (overlooking) is turning away. This was revealed before the verse of fighting, and then it was abrogated (naskh, abrogation) by the verse of fighting.

﴿until God brings His command⦆ meaning: by the legislation of fighting. Ibn ʿAbbas said its meaning is: "until God brings His command," namely: the conquest of Constantinople, Rome, and Amorium.

It was also said: "until God brings His command" means: the conquest of the villages of the Jews, such as Khaybar, Fadak, the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, and such as the Banu Qurayza.

﴿Indeed, God is over all things competent⦆: that is, Capable.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 110:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾ is well known.

﴿And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ — that is, of obedience — ﴿as a store that will not be lost.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 111:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say: None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians.﴾ Its implied sense: The Jews said: "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew." And the Christians said: "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Christian." So it is abridged with a brief omission.

The verse was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran, who were Christians. They gathered in the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) together with the Jews, and they disputed, and some of them disbelieved in others, and some of them denied others. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed these verses.

﴿Those are their wishful fancies.⦆ That is, their false desires. ﴿Say: Produce your proof, if you are truthful.﴾ Bring the argument for what you claim. ﴿Yes, whoever submits himself⦆ That is: the matter is not as they wish; rather, the judgment belongs to Islam.

﴿Whoever submits his face﴾ means he sincerely devotes his worship to God, ﴿while being a doer of good﴾ means a believer, ﴿for him is his reward with his Lord, and no fear shall befall them, nor shall they grieve﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 113:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Jews say, "The Christians have nothing [to stand] upon," and the Christians say, "The Jews have nothing [to stand] upon,"﴾ — this is what occurred in the gathering of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the dispute of the Jews with the Christians. As for His saying: ﴿while they recite the Book﴾, it means: each of them denies the other and misguides the other, while they recite the Book, and this disagreement is not in their Book. So their recitation of the Book and their opposition to what is in the Book indicate that they are upon falsehood.

﴿So likewise said those who do not know the like of their words﴾. It was said: he meant by this the polytheists. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Mujahid said: he meant by this the common Christians.

﴿So Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾ — He will show them the entry of the Muslims into Paradise and their entry into the Fire.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 114:

God's words: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein and strives for their destruction?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and a group of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the verse refers to the Christians who assisted Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar), the Magian, in destroying the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis).

﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear.﴾ This is because Bayt al-Maqdis is the place of pilgrimage (hajj) and visitation for the Christians, so no Christian enters it except in fear, from that time until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾ meaning: the jizyah for their protected subjects (dhimmi) and killing for their combatants (harbi). ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ meaning: the punishment of the Fire.

It is also said that the verse was revealed concerning the polytheists who prevented the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from entering Makkah in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah.

As for God's words ﴿and strives for their destruction﴾, it is because they prevented the Muslims from entering the Mosque. They did not become Muslims until they entered it; so it is as if they strove for its destruction.

﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear.﴾ This is our law: that a polytheist is not permitted to enter the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and none of them enters it except in fear.

﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾ meaning humiliation. ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 115:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾. Concerning it there are four opinions:

The first: it was revealed concerning the abrogation (naskh) of the qiblah, meaning the Ka'bah. When the qiblah was changed to the Ka'bah, the Jews taunted the Muslims and said: "They have no fixed qiblah; sometimes they face this way and sometimes that way." So the verse was revealed in refutation of their saying.

The second opinion: what 'Umar narrated, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray on his mount, facing wherever his mount turned. So the verse was revealed concerning the permissibility of voluntary prayer (nafl) on a mount, facing wherever the mount turns.

The third opinion: Jabir narrated that he said: "We were on a journey, and the qiblah became unclear to us, so each one of us prayed facing a direction, and drew a line in front of himself. When we woke in the morning, behold, the lines were pointing away from the qiblah. We asked the Messenger of Allah about that, and he did not order us to repeat the prayer, and the verse was revealed with that meaning."

The fourth opinion: it was revealed at the beginning of Islam, when the qiblah was not yet fixed and it was permissible to pray facing any direction they wished. According to this view, the verse is abrogated by the verse of the qiblah, and this opinion is strange (gharib).

As for His saying: ﴿then there is the Face of Allah﴾, Mujahid said: "The qiblah of Allah." The "face" here carries the meaning of the qiblah, and likewise the wijhah and the jihah are the qiblah. It was also said: its meaning is the good pleasure (ridwan) of Allah; and it was said: its meaning is the intention (qasd) of Allah. From this is the saying of the poet:

(I seek forgiveness from Allah for a sin I cannot count... Lord of the servants, toward Him is the face and the deed)

meaning: toward Him is the intention and the deed.

Allah, may He be exalted, mentions the "Face" in His Book in eleven places, and it is an attribute of Allah, may He be exalted; its interpretation is to recite it and to believe in it. This will come later.

﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, meaning: Rich, who bestows from His abundance; ﴿All-Knowing﴾, meaning: Knowing of affairs.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 116:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say: "Allah has taken a son."﴾ He means the Christians. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ — a declaration of His transcendence. ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ — by way of ownership and possession. ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ Al-qanit: the obedient one. The original meaning of qunut (devout obedience) is standing. In a report, the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the best prayer and he said: "Its long qunut," meaning: its long standing.

As for His saying, ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, meaning: all are standing in servitude. There are several opinions regarding its meaning:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: it is general in wording but specific in meaning, and what is intended is the Muslims. This is also the view of al-Farra'. The grammarians of Basra did not approve of this from al-Farra', and they said: "all" (kull) requires encompassing the thing so that nothing is left out of it, and its meaning is: all the servants are devoutly obedient. The believer prostrates willingly, while the disbeliever prostrates with his shadow unwillingly, as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows in the mornings and the evenings﴾.

The second opinion: its meaning is: ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ — subjected and made subservient to that for which they were created.

The third opinion: ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ means: on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 117:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: their Creator (mubdi'uha). Ibn 'Abbas said: He is the Creator, not according to any pattern that preceded. From this comes "mubtadi'" (the innovator), because he introduces what has not been done before.

﴿And when He decrees a matter﴾, meaning: He determines it and perfects it. The original sense of qada' (decree, judgment) is "completion," and from it one says of someone who has died, "he has fulfilled his term" (qada nahbahu), because he has finished with the world. From it also comes the qadi (judge), because he has finished with the settlement of disputes. And from it comes the qada' of Allah and His qadar (decree and measure), because He has completed it in measure and arrangement. The poet said:

"And upon them two (coats of mail, masrudatan), David decreed them, and the making of the full-length coats was the work of Tubba'."

That is, "sunna' al-sawabigh" (the makers of the full-length coats). His saying "qadahuma Dawud" means: David perfected them. Likewise His saying ﴿And when He decrees a matter﴾ means: He determines it and perfects it. ﴿Then He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾.

If someone asks: how does He say "He only says to it," when what is non-existent is not addressed? It is said: Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is "He only says to it," that is, for the sake of its bringing into being, and on this view the sense of address is removed.

It was also said: even though it is non-existent, since its existence has been determined, and it will certainly exist, it is as if it were existent, and so the address is valid.

There is a third view: it is expressed in the manner that people understand in custom, for everyone who wants to do something either says a word or does an action. Its meaning is merely bringing into being, but He said ﴿Then He only says to it﴾ because this is how people understand it.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and it is﴾: Ibn 'Amir recited "fa-yakuna" with a fatha on the nun, and this is more evident in grammar, because it is the answer to the imperative introduced by the fa'. So "fa-yakuna" is in the subjunctive (nasb).

The well-known recitation is "fa-yakunu" with a damma (raf'), and its meaning is: "fa-huwa yakunu" (so it comes to be).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 118:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who do not know said﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He meant by it the Jews.

Mujahid said: He meant by it the Christians.

(Why does Allah not speak to us?) That is: why does Allah not speak to us? "Lawla" (why not / if only) throughout the Qur'an carries the meaning of "hal" (why not / would that), except in one place, and that is in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Then had he not been of those who glorify [Allah]﴾. Its meaning is: "Then had he not been of those who glorify [Allah]" (i.e., "if he had not been of those who glorify").

﴿Or there come to us a sign﴾, that is: a sign we propose, just as they proposed signs. ﴿Thus said those before them﴾, namely the disbelievers of the past generations. ﴿Their speech is similar to one another's. Their hearts have become alike﴾, that is: some of them resemble others in hardness and in seeking the impossible. ﴿We have certainly made clear the signs for a people who are certain.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾, means: "with the truth." The prepositions (ṣilāt, particles) alternate with one another. Similar to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Enter among My servants﴾, meaning: "with My servants."

By "the truth" is meant the Qur'an. It is also said: the Sharia (sharī'ah, the divine law) of Islam.

﴿A bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ means: one who gives good tidings and one who warns.

(﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blaze﴾) has been recited in two readings: "wa lā tus'al" and "wa lā tas'al." As for His saying ﴿and you will not be questioned﴾, it means: We sent you as one who will not be held accountable for the state of the disbelievers. This is like His saying: ﴿Your duty is only to convey the message, and upon Us is the reckoning﴾.

Ibn Mas'ud recited "wa mā tas'al" ("and you are not questioned"), and Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "wa lan tas'al" ("and you will never be questioned"). The meaning of all of them is one. As for His saying "wa lā tas'al," it has two meanings. The first: it is in the sense of the people's saying, "Do not ask about the evil of so-and-so, for it is beyond what you imagine."

It is also said: it is in the form of a prohibition. Its occasion is what Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi narrated: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'I wish I knew what my two parents did.' So there was revealed His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not ask about the companions of the Blaze﴾."

Al-Jahim (the Blazing Fire) is the name for the fire that is intensely blazing.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 120:

The words of God Most High: ﴿Never will the Jews be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion.﴾ Their meaning: the Jews will never be pleased with you except through Judaism, and the Christians will never be pleased with you except through Christianity.

﴿Until you follow their religion.﴾ Al-milla (religion, creed) means the path, and from it comes khubz al-milla (the bread of the milla). The ash in which the bread is placed is called milla, because traces and lines appear in it.

﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God is the guidance.﴾ That is: the religion of God is the religion in which you are.

﴿And if you were to follow their desires.﴾ It has been said: this is an address to the Prophet, but what is meant is the community, because he was protected from following desires. A similar example is the words of God Most High: ﴿If you were to associate partners with God, your deeds would surely be nullified﴾ and ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have no protector or helper against God.﴾ This is well known.

It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is this: the Jews asked the Prophet for a truce, saying: "Do not fight us or kill us, and give us time; perhaps we will embrace Islam." So God Most High revealed: ﴿Never will the Jews be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion.﴾ That is: if you make a truce with them, they will never be satisfied with it. They only ask for this as a pretext and fabrication, and they will not be pleased with you unless you follow their religion.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 121:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾. It was said: He meant by this a group of Jews who embraced Islam.

It was also said: He meant by this a group of Christians who came with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib when he returned from Abyssinia (al-Habasha) and embraced Islam.

﴿They recite it with its true recitation﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud said: they treat its lawful as lawful and its unlawful as unlawful, and they do not distort the words from their places.

Al-Hasan said: they act upon its commands, believe in its clear (muhkam) verses, and leave its ambiguous (mutashabih) verses to God the Most High. 'Ikrimah said: they follow it with true following, from the phrase "talā," meaning "followed," and from it is the words of the Most High: ﴿And the moon when it follows it﴾.

﴿Those believe in it﴾, meaning: what we have mentioned. ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾, meaning: the ones who lose their own souls.
His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ He repeated it for emphasis of what preceded.

The Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 123:

The words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all﴾. We have already mentioned its meaning.

﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped﴾. If it is said: Did He not assign intercession to the prophets and others, when He said: ﴿And they cannot intercede except for those whom He approves﴾, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My intercession is for the people of major sins from among my community"? It is said: By His words ﴿nor will intercession benefit it﴾ He meant specific people, namely the Jews and the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 124:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord﴾: meaning, He examined him. The testing (ibtila') of the servants does not mean that He tests them in order to know their states, for He already knows them and what they possess of things; rather, it is so that the servants may know their own states, and so that some of them may come to know others.

﴿With words﴾: as for the words (al-kalimat), it has been said that they are those mentioned in the report in the saying (of the Prophet ﷺ): "Ten things are part of the fitrah (natural disposition): five in the head and five in the body. The five in the head are rinsing the mouth (al-madmadah), snuffing water into the nose (al-istinshaq), trimming the moustache (qass al-sharib), using the siwak (tooth-stick), and parting the hair (farq al-ra's). As for those in the body: paring the nails (qalm al-adhfar), plucking the armpit hair (nataf al-ibt), shaving the pubic hair (halq al-'anah), circumcision (al-khitan), and cleansing with water after defecation (al-istinja') according to one narration, and washing the finger joints (ghasl al-baraji)."

In the report it is related that Allah, may He be exalted, sent Jibril to Ibrahim, saying: "Purify yourself for Me." So he rinsed his mouth. Then He sent to him: "Purify yourself for Me," so he snuffed water into his nose, and so on up to ten. When He commanded him the tenth time, "Purify yourself for Me," he looked at his body and found nothing that needed cleaning, so he was alerted to circumcision and was circumcised.

In the report: "He was circumcised after eighty years, with the adze (bil-qadum)." Al-Qadum is the name of a place. And he lived for eighty years after that.

In the reports: "Ibrahim, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, was the first to trim the moustache, the first to be circumcised, the first to pare the nails, and the first to see grey hair. When he saw it he said, 'O Lord, what is this?' He said, 'Dignity (al-waqar).' He said, 'O Lord, increase me in dignity.'"

﴿Then he fulfilled them﴾: meaning, he discharged them completely. Ibn 'Abbas said: No one has carried out the obligations of Islam as completely as Khalil (the Friend) Ibrahim, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, did.

There are two other opinions concerning this: that the meaning of "the words" is that Allah tested him with the star, and he was content; He tested him with the moon, and he was content; He tested him with the sun, and he was content; He tested him with the fire of Namrud, and he was content; He tested him with the sacrifice of the son, and he was content; He tested him with circumcision, and he was content.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Indeed I will make you a leader (imam) for the people"﴾: meaning in goodness, though an imam may also be in evil, in a figurative sense, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We made them leaders (a'immah) calling to the Fire﴾. The real meaning of imam is one who intends, in his actions, what he intends, and it is derived from umm, which is qasd (intention).

﴿He said, "And from my descendants?"﴾: meaning, make from my descendants leaders.

﴿He said, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers"﴾: meaning, whoever among them is a wrongdoer does not attain it. They differed concerning this covenant: Ibn 'Abbas said it is prophethood. Mujahid said he meant by it leadership (al-imamah), and this is the most fitting to the apparent context. There is another opinion: that it is security from the Fire.

The wrongdoer (al-zalim) is the sinner (al-fasiq). It has also been said that he meant by it here the polytheist (al-mushrik). This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing (zulm)﴾, meaning with shirk, ﴿for them is security﴾. So security was assigned to those who do not associate partners with Him. Likewise His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: My security does not reach those among them who are polytheists.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 125:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return (mathaba) for the people and a place of security﴾. ʿAṭāʾ said: mathaba means a gathering place (majmaʿan).

Another said: mathaba means a place of return (marjiʿan), and it is derived from thāba, meaning "returned"; the House is a mathaba because they return to it time and again.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they never tire of it (lā yaqḍūna minhu waṭaran), meaning they do not grow weary of it. The mathāb and the mathaba have the same meaning. The poet said:

(A place of return for the tribes of every kind, / to which the swift, lean she-camels hasten.)

As for His saying ﴿and a place of security﴾, it means: possessing security. Ibn ʿAbbās said: its security is that whoever commits a crime and enters it is safe, and he is not punished within it until he leaves it. Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, held this view.

Another said: its meaning is that it is a refuge from the hands of the polytheists, for they used not to attack the people of Makkah, saying, "They are the people of Allah and His special ones." Rather, they would attack those around it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ As for Ibn ʿAbbās's statement, it is to be understood as recommendation (istiḥbāb). This is preferable in our view: that one should not be pursued within it until he leaves, but, despite this, carrying out the retaliation (istīfāʾ) is permitted, because the sanctuary does not prevent the exacting of rights.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And take, from the station of Ibrāhīm, a place of prayer﴾. It has been recited in two readings: "wa-ittakhadhū" as a statement (khabar), and "wa-ittakhidhū" as a command (amr). As for al-maqām with a fatḥa, it is the place of standing; al-maqām with a ḍamma is the act of standing. Its meaning according to the correct view: the station of Ibrāhīm is the stone in the mosque, on which the imams pray; it is the stone on which Ibrāhīm stood when building the House, and for this reason it was named the Station of Ibrāhīm.

It was said: the marks of the toes of his foot were clear upon it, but they were effaced from the great amount of hands touching it.

In a report: "The Corner (al-Rukn) and the Station are two rubies from the rubies of Paradise. Had they not been touched by the hands of the polytheists, they would have lit up what lies between the east and the west."

It is also narrated from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "My Lord agreed with me in three matters: I said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), 'If only you would take the Station of Ibrāhīm as a place of prayer,' and then the verse was revealed: ﴿And take, from the station of Ibrāhīm, a place of prayer﴾."

There is another view on this: that by the station of Ibrāhīm he meant all the places of Ḥajj, such as ʿArafa, Muzdalifa, and the rest of the sacred sites.

His saying ﴿muṣallā﴾ means a place of supplication (mad'an); He commanded them to take them as places for du'ā'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We charged Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl﴾ means: We commanded; the word ʿahd here carries the meaning of command.

As for Ismāʿīl: its origin is "Ismaʿ Īl" (hear, O God), because Ibrāhīm, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, used to supplicate Allah to grant him a son, saying, "Ismaʿ Īl." When Allah granted him the child, he named him Ismāʿīl.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that purify My House﴾, meaning from polytheism and idols, ﴿for those who circumambulate﴾, those who go around the Kaʿba, ﴿and those who stay (in devotion)﴾, the residents who remain as neighbors, ﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾, those who pray. Rukʿ is the plural of rākiʿ, and suḥūd is the plural of sājid. al-Kalbī and Muqātil said: the circumambulants are the strangers (ghurabāʾ), and the ʿākifīn are the people of Makkah.

ʿAṭāʾ and Mujāhid said: circumambulation is more excellent for strangers, because it would escape them, while prayer is more excellent for the people of Makkah, because it does not escape them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 126:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And when Ibrahim said: "My Lord, make this a secure land"﴾, that is: make the Haram a place of security. ﴿And provide its people with fruits﴾. He only supplicated for this because he had settled in a valley without cultivation.

In the stories (al-Qasas) it is related that al-Ta'if was a city from the cities of al-Sham in al-Urdunn. When Ibrahim made this supplication, Allah the Most High commanded Jibril until he uprooted it from its base and circled it seven times around the House, then placed it in the position where it is now. Hence it is from that [source] that the people of Makkah have their fruits.

﴿Whoever among them believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾: Ibrahim supplicated that the believers specifically be provided with fruits.

﴿He said: "And whoever disbelieves"﴾: Allah the Most High says: and the disbelievers too. That is because Allah, glorified and exalted is He, promised provision for creation in its entirety, believers and disbelievers alike.

﴿Then I will let him enjoy briefly﴾: it is read with light and with emphatic (shaddah) forms, and both meanings are one, meaning: I will let him remain in blessing for a little while.

He only mentioned "a little" because al-Imta' (enjoyment) originally means length and abundance. It is said: "matu'a al-nahar" (the day lengthened and rose high), and "nakhla mati'a" (a tall palm). He intended by it enjoyment in this world, which is little, because it ends.

﴿Then I will compel him﴾: force him, ﴿to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination﴾: that is, the place of return.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 127:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House﴾. Al-Farra' said: al-qawa'id (the foundations) are the footings (asas) of the House.

Al-Kisa'i said: they are the walls (judur) of the House. It is related that when Ibn al-Zubayr demolished the House in order to rebuild it, large white stones appeared, and he said: "These are the foundations upon which Abraham built the House."

Ibn 'Abbas said: The House was built from five mountains: Tur Sinai (Mount Sinai), Tur Zayta, Lebanon, which is a mountain in al-Sham (Greater Syria), al-Judi, which is a mountain in al-Jazira, and Hira', which is a mountain in Makkah.

It is mentioned in the reports that God, exalted is He, built a House in the heavens, which is the House frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur), and it is called Sirah. He commanded the angels to build the Ka'bah on earth opposite it, according to its measure and likeness.

It has also been said: the first to build the Ka'bah was Adam, peace be upon him. It was then obliterated during the time of the Flood, and then God, exalted is He, revealed it to Abraham until he built it.

He said: ﴿And Ishmael: "Our Lord, accept from us"﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "yaqulani Rabbana taqabbal minna" (they both say, "Our Lord, accept from us"), and this is a shadhdh (irregular) reading, but this is the meaning. ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 128:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and make us submitting to You﴾. He says: surrendering, humbling ourselves, submitting (mustaslimin, khadi'in, muniqadin).

﴿And from our offspring a community﴾. The ummah (community): the followers of the prophets. ﴿Submitting to You﴾: humbling themselves before You. ﴿And show us﴾. Abu 'Amr recited it as "mukhtalasan" (with the vowel rapidly reduced, ikhtilas), and others recited it with a kasra on the ra' (wa-arina). ﴿Our rites (manasikana)﴾, that is: our acts of worship (mutabbadatuna).

Al-nusk (ritual devotion): worship, and from it the worshipper is called nasik; its meaning: the places of our Hajj (pilgrimage). ﴿And turn to us in forgiveness; indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 129:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from among themselves﴾ refer to Muhammad. In a report, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham and the glad tidings of Jesus," and he meant by the prayer of Abraham this (verse), for he prayed that a messenger from among them be sent among the children of Ishmael.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: All the prophets were from the Children of Israel except ten: Noah, Hud, Salih, Shuʿayb, Lot, Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and Muhammad, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all.

It is mentioned in the stories (al-qasas) that every prophet who has passed is mentioned in the Qur'an by one name, except for two: Jacob and Jesus. As for Jacob, he has two names: Jacob and Israel; and as for Jesus, he has two names: Jesus and the Messiah.

﴿He recites to them Your verses﴾, meaning from the Qur'an, ﴿and teaches them the Book﴾, the Qur'an, ﴿and the wisdom﴾. There are several opinions regarding it:

It has been said: wisdom is the understanding of the Qur'an. Abu Bakr ibn Duraid, author of al-Jamharah, said: wisdom is every word that restrains you, admonishes you, forbids you from an ugly deed, and calls you to what is good. It has also been said: wisdom is jurisprudence (al-fiqh). This is a good opinion.

﴿And purifies them﴾, that is: cleanses them and makes them pure and clean. There is another opinion regarding it: that it means purification (al-tazkiyah). It testifies to the messengers' prophethood from all other nations, because the believers of all other nations testified for the messengers to prophethood and the conveyance of the message; so this nation purifies those witnesses.

﴿Indeed, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾. It has been said: al-ʿAziz is the One who cannot be overpowered, and Allah is inaccessible; no hand can reach Him and nothing can attain Him. It has also been said: al-ʿAziz is the Strong, the Dominant. From this is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and [he] overpowered me in speech﴾, meaning: he overcame me.

It is said in a proverb: "Whoever overpowers, plunders," meaning: whoever overcomes, takes spoil. ﴿Al-Hakim﴾ is well known.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 130:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And who turns away from the religion of Abraham﴾, i.e., the way (ṭarīqah) of Abraham, ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. Abū ʿUbayd related from Abū ʿUbayda that its meaning is: he destroyed himself.

Al-Zajjāj said: Its meaning is that he ignored (jahila) his own self, and every foolish person (safīh) is ignorant (jāhil), because whoever is ignorant of himself does not know God.

In the reports: God the Exalted revealed to Dawud: "Know yourself and know Me." He said: "O Lord, how can I know myself, and how can I know You?" God revealed to him: "Know yourself through weakness, incapacity and mortality, and know Me through strength, power and permanence."

It was also said: its meaning is that he made himself foolish (safiha nafsahu) and made it a fool. There is a fourth opinion: its meaning is that he was foolish in himself (safiha fī nafsihi), and the word "fī" (in) was omitted, so it became "safiha nafsahu."

﴿And We certainly chose him⦆ — i.e., We selected him — ﴿in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾ — among the prophets.

When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."

That is, "Submit" means: surrender, and devote your worship sincerely to Allah.

﴿He said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ I have devoted myself sincerely and entrusted myself to Him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: He truly fulfilled the entrusting to Him, and did not seek help from any of the angels when he was cast into the fire.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 132:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And Abraham charged his sons with this, and [so did] Jacob﴾ — it is recited as "wa-awṣā" (wa-awṣā), from al-īṣā' (the act of enjoining). "Wa-waṣṣā," from al-tawṣiyah, is for emphasis and intensification, meaning: Abraham enjoined his sons, and Jacob enjoined his sons. ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion﴾ — He chose for you the religion of Islam — ﴿so do not die except while you are Muslims﴾. If it is said: How could He say "so do not die except while you are Muslims," when it is not in their hands that they not die except as Muslims?

It is said: its meaning is, "Persist in Islam until death does not overtake you while you are [still] Muslims." This is like the saying of the speaker: "I would not see you do such-and-such," meaning: "Do not do such-and-such, so that I do not see you while you are doing it."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 133:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ means: "Were you witnesses?" and what is meant is: "You were not witnesses."

﴿When death approached Ya'qub﴾ means: you were not present when Ya'qub drew near to death.

﴿When he said to his sons﴾, and they were twelve tribes (asbat), as will come later, ﴿"What will you worship after me?"﴾ meaning: "What is it that you will worship after me?" ﴿They said: "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we are submitting."﴾ Al-Hasan al-Basri and Asim al-Jahdari recited: "and the God of your father" (wa-ilaha abika). It is as if, according to this reading, he did not make the paternal uncle or the grandfather a father.

The well-known reading is "and the God of your fathers" (wa-ilaha aba'ika), so the grandfather and the paternal uncle are called fathers.

Ibrahim is the grandfather and Isma'il is the paternal uncle. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ also called his uncle al-Abbas a father when he said: "Indeed he is the remnant of my fathers (min baqiyyat aba'i)." And he said: "Return my father to me, lest Quraysh do to him what Thaqif did to 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud," because they had killed him.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 134:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾, meaning: it has gone by. ﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn, and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾. Its meaning: each will be recompensed according to his own earning, and each will be questioned about his own deeds. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 135:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians, [then] you will be guided.﴾ Hud is the plural of ha'id (one who repents and returns), and it is like ha'il and haul. It was also said: the original form was kunu yahudan (be Jews), and the yā' was dropped, so it became hudan.

It was also said: hud is a verbal noun (masdar) of yahudu hudan, and it is a masdar used with the meaning of the plural, as one says: qawm sawm and qawm fitr (a people fasting, a people breaking the fast).

Its meaning: the Jews said, "Be Jews," and the Christians said, "Be Christians." This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Be Jews or Christians, [then] you will be guided.﴾

﴿Say: Rather, [we follow] the religion of Abraham, a hanif.﴾ Al-A'raj read "bal millatu" with the nominative (raf'). Its meaning is: rather, our religion is the religion of Abraham.

The well-known reading is ﴿bal millata Ibrahim﴾ (with the accusative), meaning: rather, we follow the religion of Abraham.

It was also said: its meaning is: rather, we are upon the religion of Abraham, so "ʿalā" (upon) was deleted and the word became accusative.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is accusative as an incitement (idhgha'), as if he were saying: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif. As for hanif, it means the Muslim (muslim), and its origin is inclination (al-mayl), and from it comes al-Ahnaf, who is the one whose feet incline. The Muslim inclines away from all other religions toward the religion of Islam.

It was also said: its meaning is upright (al-mustaqim), and he was called hanif by way of antonym, as one calls a deadly desert a mafazah (place of escape) and a stung person salim (safe).

It was also said: the hanif is the pilgrim who has been circumcised, because nothing remained among the Arabs of the religion of Abraham except the Hajj and circumcision, and they would recognise anyone who performed the Hajj and was circumcised as being upon the religion of Abraham, and they knew a man by that as a hanif. So He said: rather, the religion of Abraham, a hanif, in accordance with what they recognised. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 136:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Say: We believe in God, and in what has been revealed to us, and in what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what was given to the prophets from their Lord.﴾

Al-Dahhak said: Teach your children the names of the prophets mentioned in the Qur'an so that they may believe in them, and do not suppose that belief in Muhammad suffices in place of belief in all the other prophets.

It is related in a report that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited in the first rak'ah of the two rak'ahs of the dawn prayer this verse, the words of the Most High ﴿We believe in God﴾ to the end of it, and he recited in the second rak'ah ﴿Say: We believe in God, and in what has been revealed to us﴾ to the end of it. Narrated by Muslim in the Sahih.

It is related from the early generations (al-salaf) that when one of them was asked, [Are you a believer?], he would recite ﴿We believe in God, and in what has been revealed to us﴾, the verse.

As for the Asbat (al-asbat): they are twelve tribes (asbat), and they are the sons of Jacob. The asbat among the Children of Israel were like the tribes among the Arabs.

It has also been said: the sibt (sibt) means a tree, and it was so named because of the abundance of its branches.

﴿We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting Muslims.﴾ That is: we believe in all of them, and we do not prefer some over others.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 137:

The words of the Most High: ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you have believed in﴾. Ibn 'Abbas recited "bi-alladhi amantum bihi" (with that which you believed in), and this is the meaning. It has been said that its meaning is: "bi-ma amantum bihi" (with what you believed in).

Al-mithl (the like) is here an equivalent, as in His words: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, meaning: there is nothing like He (kamahu) is anything.

The poet said:

(O my blamer, leave me alone from your blame... one like me does not accept from one like you.) That is: he does not accept from you.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: if they come with a faith like your faith, and an affirmation like your affirmation, and a monotheism like your monotheism. Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi said: its meaning is: if they believe in your Book as you believed in their Book.

﴿Then they are rightly guided; but if they turn away, then they are only in opposition﴾. That is: in dispute; because every disputant is in another side during the dispute.

﴿So Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. His promise that He would suffice him against their evil, and He has sufficed by the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir, the killing of Banu Qurayza, the imposition of the jizya upon the Jews and Christians, and the killing of the polytheists.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 138:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The colouring of Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of al-Kalbi, and Qatadah, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and al-Suddi said: its meaning is: the religion of Allah. He called it "colouring" only because the effect of religion appears upon the one who adheres to it, just as the effect of dye appears upon cloth.

Mujahid said: its meaning is: the fitrah (innate disposition) of Allah. This is close to the first.

It was also said: he intended by it circumcision. And His saying ﴿the colouring of Allah﴾ means: Allah's purification through circumcision. He called it "colouring" only because it took the place of the act of the Christians, for they used to dip the child in yellow water instead of circumcision, in the manner of the Jews, and they considered this a purification of the child. So Allah, exalted is He, placed purification through circumcision, for the Muslims, in the position of what they dipped.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the accusative case as an incitement (al-ighra', a formula urging someone to hold fast to something), and its implied meaning is: "Hold fast to the religion of Allah." And who is better than Allah in religion? Or: "Hold fast to the purification of Allah." ﴿And who is better than Allah in colouring?﴾ That is, in purification. ﴿And we are worshippers of Him.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 139:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Say: Do you argue with us about Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord?﴾ Al-muhajjah (mutual argument, disputation) is contending with proof in order to make the truth manifest.

It was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians of Najran, when they argued with the Messenger of Allah and said: "Our religion is older than your religion, and our Book is older than your book, so we have a better claim to Allah than you do." So Allah revealed His saying: Say, O Muhammad, ﴿Do you argue with us about Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord?﴾ That is: we and you are equal regarding Allah, for He is our Lord and your Lord.

(﴿And for us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾) That is: we will be recompensed for our deeds, and you will be recompensed for your deeds. (﴿And we are sincerely devoted to Him﴾) Meaning: how can you claim that you are closer to Allah, when we are sincerely devoted to Him and you associate partners with Him?

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 140:

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Or do you say﴾: meaning, "Do you say?" The form is that of a question, and its meaning is rebuke, i.e., "Do you say (that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians)?" This is because they claimed that these prophets were Jews or Christians.

﴿Say: Are you more knowing, or is God?﴾ This is because God, the Exalted, has informed the Muslims that they were upon the religion of ḥanīfiyyah (pure monotheism, the upright faith), and that they were neither Jews nor Christians, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim﴾.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God?﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: that it refers to the fact that God, the Exalted, had made them bear witness in their scriptures that Abraham was upon the ḥanīfiyyah and was neither a Jew nor a Christian; but they concealed that testimony.

It was also said that the testimony refers to the description of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾: meaning, nothing of what you do is hidden from Him.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 141:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿That is a community that has passed away.﴾ That is: it has gone by. ﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn. And you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾ That is, you will not be held accountable for their deeds; rather, they are the ones who will be held accountable.

If it is said: this is a repetition, for it has been mentioned once before.

We answer: the first mention concerned the prophets who were mentioned earlier, and this second mention concerns the Jews and Christians who were mentioned earlier in these verses. Or it was repeated for emphasis.

It is related from some of the scholars that they were asked about the strife that occurred between ʿAlī, Muʿāwiyah, Ṭalḥah, al-Zubayr and ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with them all. He recited: ﴿That is a community that has passed away; for them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn﴾, to the end of the verse. This is a good answer to such a question.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 142:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾, meaning: the foolish, ignorant ones will say. The safih (foolish) is one whose forbearance and intellect are light. From this comes the phrase "thawb safih," meaning a thin garment. And it is said: "ramh safih," meaning a spear that penetrates quickly.

﴿What has turned them away﴾ from their qiblah, meaning: what has diverted and deflected them ﴿from their qiblah which they were facing﴾, meaning: Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). ﴿Say: To God belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾, meaning: He directs His servants to whichever of them He wills. ﴿A straight path﴾ means a path that is upright. The straight path is that which leads to the intended goal.

The verse was revealed concerning the Jews, when they reproached the Muslims for changing their qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 143:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you﴾ means: just as We chose the prophets, and chose the Children of Israel from among creation, so too have We chosen you from among the nations. (ummatan wasatan) means: just, excellent. The poet said: (They are a middle course, with whom people are content in judgment, when one of the great calamities descends upon them.)

It is related in a report that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You will complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most just."

It has also come in a report from him that he said: "The best of religion is the middle path" (al-namat al-awsat), meaning that which contains neither excess nor deficiency. That is the religion of Islam, because the Christians went to excess in their religion, and the Jews fell short. As for the Muslims, they took the middle path.

(li-takunu shuhada' 'ala al-nas) This is on the Day of Resurrection, when the nations are asked about the conveyance of the messengers, and they deny that their messengers conveyed the message. Then the messengers are asked, and they say: "We conveyed." It is said to them: "Who will bear witness for you?" They then bring this nation, and they testify for them to the conveyance. The nations say: "They came after us, so how can they testify to that?" Then this nation is asked, and they say: "You sent to us a messenger, and You revealed to us a Book, and You informed us in it of the conveyance of the messengers, and You are truthful in what You have informed. By that we testify for them to the conveyance."

(wa-yakuna al-Rasulu 'alaykum shahidan) over your deeds.

It was also said: its meaning is "one who purifies and confirms your testimony over me."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you used to face﴾ means: We did not turn the qibla from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah ﴿except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾. If someone says: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿except that We might know﴾, when He knows things before they occur? ﴿...the Messenger a witness over you. And We did not make the qibla which you used to face except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels. And indeed, it was difficult except for those whom Allah guided. And Allah would never...﴾

We say: Yes, He knew it with knowledge of the unseen. He intended by this the knowledge upon which reward and punishment depend, which is the knowledge of the existence of the followers; for its being existent is only known after it exists.

It was also said: its meaning is "except that We might see," and this is close to the first.

It was also said: the trial (al-ibtila') is implied in it, and its estimate is: "except that We might test, so that the follower is distinguished from the one who turns back." It is related in a report: "When the qibla was changed to the Ka'bah, some of the Muslims apostatized to Judaism, and they said: 'Muhammad has returned to the religion of his forefathers.'" This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿from who turns back on his heels﴾. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, it was difficult﴾ means: heavy.

It was said: its meaning is: "And indeed, the qibla was difficult." Al-Zajjaj said: "And indeed, the change was difficult."

﴿except for those whom Allah guided﴾ means: whom Allah guided. ﴿And Allah would never let your faith be lost﴾. This was revealed concerning specific people. That is what is related: "When the qibla was changed, a group asked the Messenger of Allah and said: 'Some of our people had prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis and died, so what is their state?' Among them were As'ad ibn Zurarah, Abu Umamah, and al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur. Then the words of Allah, may He be exalted, were revealed: ﴿And Allah would never let your faith be lost﴾, meaning your prayer." So He made prayer faith, and this is evidence against the Murji'ah, since they did not regard prayer as part of faith. They were called Murji'ah because they deferred action (al-'ilm) from faith.

It is related that Abu Yusuf testified before Shurayk ibn 'Abd Allah the judge, and he rejected his testimony. It was said to him: "Do you reject the testimony of Ya'qub?" He said: "How can I accept the testimony of one who says that prayer is not part of faith?!"

It was also said: the meaning of His saying ﴿And Allah would never let your faith be lost﴾ is: [your faith in regard to] the changing of the qibla.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful toward the people﴾. Ra'fah is the most intense mercy.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 2, verse 144:

The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾. This verse, although it comes later in the recitation, is earlier in meaning, for it is the head of the story.

The occasion of revelation of the verse is what Jabir narrated: "After the Prophet arrived in Madinah, he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) for sixteen or seventeen months, and he wished that Allah would turn him toward the Ka'bah. He used to say to Jibril: 'I wish that Allah would turn me toward the Ka'bah, for it is the qiblah of my father Ibrahim.' And he would say to Jibril: 'Ask your Lord.' Jibril said to him: 'Ask yourself, for you have a station with Allah.' Whenever Jibril descended, he would turn his face toward the heaven, hoping that it would descend with the abrogation (naskh)."

Al-Suddi said: Whenever he began a prayer, he would turn his face toward the heaven, hoping that Allah would turn him toward the Ka'bah. So Allah kept him at that for sixteen months, then the saying of Allah the Exalted was revealed: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, so We shall surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾, meaning: that you love and desire. For the first qiblah was also [pleasing] to him.

﴿So turn your face toward the Masjid al-Haram﴾, meaning: toward the House.

﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾, meaning: toward it. In a report, the Prophet said: "This is the qiblah," and he pointed to the House.

﴿And indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾, meaning the turning toward the Ka'bah. ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what they do﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: The first thing abrogated after he arrived in Madinah was the qiblah.

It was said: The first prayer prayed toward the Ka'bah was the 'Asr prayer. It is also narrated that it was turned toward the Ka'bah while they were in prayer. The sound view is that the change occurred outside the prayer, and that this applied specifically to the people of Quba', for they had begun the 'Asr prayer, and the 'Asr prayer was facing Bayt al-Maqdis. A man came to them and said: "I bear witness that I prayed this prayer with the Messenger of Allah toward the Ka'bah," so they turned toward the Ka'bah and built upon their prayer.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 145:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And even if you brought to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾ means: even if I brought them every miracle, they would not follow you in the direction of the Kaaba. ﴿Nor are you one who follows their qibla﴾, meaning: the qibla of the Jews and the Christians. ﴿Nor are they followers of each other's qibla﴾, meaning: the Jews and the Christians. That is because the qibla of the Jews is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which is to the west, and the qibla of the Christians is to the east, while the qibla of the Muslims is the Kaaba.

Ibn 'Umar related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Between the east and the west is a qibla." Ibn 'Umar said: he meant for the people of the east. Its form is that one places the sunrise of winter, on the shortest day of the year, on one's left, and the sunset of summer, on the longest day of the year, on one's right, so that one's face is toward the Kaaba. This is achieved by facing the place where the heart of Scorpio sets when it sets. This is the meaning of his saying: "Between the east and the west is a qibla."

﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾. Although the address is to the Messenger, what is meant is the community, as has already been mentioned.

﴿After the knowledge that has come to you, indeed you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾. Its interpretation is well known.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 146:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their own sons.﴾ It was said: He meant by it the qibla (direction of prayer). And it was said: He meant by it Muhammad (ﷺ).

It is related that ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam said: "My recognition of this Prophet is stronger than my recognition of my son." ʿUmar said to him: "How so?" He said: "Because I do not know what the women have invented, but I know that he is a true Prophet." ʿUmar said: "May God bless you (lillah darruka)."

{And indeed a party of them conceal the truth while they know it.}

The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among those who doubt.

Here the verse is "﴿The truth is from your Lord, so never be among the doubters﴾". That is, "al-mumtarin" means: those who are in doubt.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 148:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And every nation has a direction toward which it turns﴾. Mujahid said: "He" (the one who turns it) is "its direction," meaning: the qiblah. And Abu Hatim, from al-Akhfash, said its meaning is: "God is the one who turns it."

So His saying "He" is a reference to God the Most High, meaning: God turns the nations toward their qiblah. Ibn 'Amir recited: "He is its (the nation's) patron" (huwa mawlaha), meaning: the direction (al-mustaqbal) is turned toward it.

﴿So race to good works﴾, that is: hasten. And what is meant here is: hastening to accept (the truth) from God. ﴿Wherever you are, God will bring you all together. Indeed God is over all things competent﴾.

“And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque”: i.e., toward it.

“And indeed it is the truth from your Lord.” He mentioned it as an emphasis on the first [command]. “And Allah is not unaware of what you do.”

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 150:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it, so that people will have no argument against you﴾. He means: the Jews. That is because they said: "Muhammad has followed our qibla, so he will return to our religion."

﴿Except those who have wronged﴾. They are the polytheists. It was said: "Illa" (except) here means "wa la" (and not), so that ﴿except those who have wronged﴾ means "and not those who have wronged." An example of this is the saying of the poet:

(Every brother will part from his brother... by the life of your father, Amr, except the two Farqads)

He means: "and not the two Farqads."

The correct view is that this is an exception of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), and "illa" here means "but" (lakin). ﴿Those who have wronged﴾ dispute with you and argue against you with false proof. That is because the polytheists said, when the qibla was changed to the Ka'ba: "He has returned to our qibla, so he will return to our religion." False proof may also be called a proof, as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Their argument is refuted﴾. So He invalidated the argument of the Jews by the change to the Ka'ba, then He invalidated the argument of the polytheists by another proof.

﴿Except those of them who have wronged, so do not fear them, but fear Me, that I may complete My favor upon you and that you may be guided﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: His favor upon the Muslim is not completed except by his entering Paradise.

It is also reported in a khabar: "The Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man say: 'Praise be to God for Islam.' He said: 'You have indeed praised God for a great blessing.'"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 151:

The words of His, exalted is He: ﴿As We have sent among you a messenger from among yourselves﴾. If someone says: the kaf is for comparison (tashbih), so where is the object of comparison (al-mushabbah bihi)? We say: ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: its implied sense is: "So remember Me (fa-dhkurhu li), just as We sent among you a messenger." Thus the remembrance (dhikr) in this view means gratitude (shukr).

It is also said: its implied sense is: "And that I may complete My favour upon you, just as We sent among you a messenger from among yourselves." This is because Abraham, peace be upon him, had made two supplications: he asked that a messenger from among them be sent to them, and he asked for the completion of the favour upon his descendants through provision of fruits. So He granted one of the two supplications by sending messengers among them, and then He answered the second supplication, saying: ﴿And that I may complete My favour upon you, just as We sent among you a messenger from among yourselves.﴾

﴿He recites to you Our verses﴾, meaning: the Qur'an. ﴿And purifies you﴾, as we have explained. ﴿And teaches you the Book and the wisdom﴾, which we have mentioned. It is also said: the wisdom (al-hikmah) is the Sunnah, and it is said: it means the admonitions of the Qur'an.

﴿And teaches you what you did not know﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 152:

﴿Remember Me, and I will remember you.﴾ It has been said: the remembrance of God here means praise and extolling of Him.

In a report from the Prophet (ﷺ) it is related that God, may He be exalted, says: "I am as My servant thinks I am, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself; and if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than it. If he draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; if he draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; and if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running." Related by Muslim in the Sahih.

It has also been said: its meaning is, "Remember Me as We have sent [you]," and this is close to the saying of 'Ali.

It has also been said: the remembrance from the servant is obedience, and the remembrance from God is forgiveness and mercy. Its meaning is: remember Me through obedience, and I will remember you with forgiveness and mercy.

﴿And be grateful to Me and do not deny Me.﴾ That is, be grateful to Me through obedience, and do not disbelieve in Me through disobedience. Whoever obeys God has indeed thanked Him, and whoever disobeys Him has indeed denied Him.

It is related that Moses, upon him be peace, asked his Lord, saying: "What is the gratitude that is fitting for You?" He said: "That your tongue never ceases to be moist with My remembrance."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 153:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer﴾. So "istiʿanah" (seeking help) means seeking assistance. Regarding "patience" (al-sabr) there are two opinions: the first is steadfastness upon the religion, and the second is fasting. The reason for seeking help through them is what has already been mentioned.

﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾. ʿAṭāʾ said, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās: "with protection and victory."
