Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 154:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead."﴾ The verse was revealed concerning particular people who were martyred on the day of Badr. The Muslims would say, "So-and-so has died," and Allah, may He be exalted, did not approve of this from them, so He revealed this verse.

(Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive) That is, they are martyrs, because the martyr is alive.

It has also been said: its meaning is what has come in the report: "The souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds, which graze on the fruits of Paradise, that is, they eat and take shelter in lamps suspended beneath the Throne." This is His words: ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord.﴾

It has also been said: its meaning is that they are alive with reward and good praise, and they are not dead through evil mention and the lack of reward.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 156:

Those who, when a calamity afflicts them, say: ﴿Indeed, we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return.﴾

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The phrase of return (al-istirja') was not given to any nation other than this Ummah. Do you not see that Ya'qub (peace be upon him), when he was tested with separation from Yusuf, said: ﴿Oh, my grief over Yusuf!﴾ and did not say: "Indeed, we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return"? Its meaning: indeed, we belong to Allah in ownership and servitude, and indeed to Him we will return on the Day of Resurrection. It was restricted to this because on the Day of Resurrection the matter becomes entirely for Allah, the Exalted.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had his lamp extinguished, and he said: "Indeed, we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return." He was asked about that, and he said: "Everything that harms the believer is a calamity for him."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 157:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those upon them are blessings from their Lord, and mercy; and those are the rightly guided.﴾ The meaning of "blessings" (ṣalawāt) here is mercy upon mercy, because the ṣalāh (prayer, or divine blessing) from God is mercy; from the angels it is seeking forgiveness (istighfār); and from people it is supplication (du'ā'). The poet said: (Send blessings upon Yahya and his followers... a generous Lord and an obeyed intercessor).

That is: have mercy upon him.

His saying: "and mercy" is mentioned as an emphasis of the first. ﴿And those are the rightly guided.﴾ 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Excellent are the two portions, and excellent is the addition": the two portions are the blessings and the mercy, and the addition is the guidance.

Many reports have been transmitted concerning the reward for affliction, among them what is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "No affliction befalls a believing servant but that Allah expiates his sins by it, even for a thorn that pricks him."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 158:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾. Al-Safa is a mountain at one of the two ends of al-Mas'a (the place of sa'y, the ritual running between the two hills). Al-Marwah is a mountain at the second end. Al-Safa is the hard rock, and al-Marwah is the soft rock.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿among the symbols of Allah﴾: al-Sha'a'ir is the plural of sha'ira, which is the markers placed upon the rites of Hajj. Similar to it is al-mash'ar (the sacred sites), so the standing place (at 'Arafat) is a sha'ira, the circumambulation area (al-mataf) is a sha'ira, the place of sacrifice (al-manhar) is a sha'ira, and al-Mash'ar (al-Muzdalifah) is a sha'ira.

﴿So whoever performs Hajj to the House or makes 'Umrah﴾. The origin of Hajj (al-Hajj) is intention (al-qasd). The poet said:

(And I witness, from 'Awf, many groups that intend, cursing al-Zibriqan the saffron-dyed)

That is, they intend. The origin of 'Umrah (al-'Umrah) is visitation (al-ziyarah). The poet said:

(The soul was stirred when there came to them, and a rider came from Thalith, a visitor)

That is, a visitor. In Hajj and 'Umrah there is both intention and visitation.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿there is no sin upon him for going around them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas recited: "there is no sin upon him that he not go around them." This is also the reading of Anas, and it was likewise in the codices of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud. The well-known reading is: ﴿that he go around them﴾.

It is also narrated from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr that he said to 'A'ishah: "I do not see any sin upon one who does not go around between al-Safa and al-Marwah," and he recited this verse.

'A'ishah said: "How wrong your opinion is, nephew! " and she mentioned the story concerning the occasion of the revelation of the verse.

The story regarding that is that in the Jahiliyyah there were two idols upon al-Safa and al-Marwah: Isaf and Na'ilah. Isaf was upon al-Safa and Na'ilah upon al-Marwah, and the people of the Jahiliyyah used to go around between al-Safa and al-Marwah in veneration of the two idols. When the Prophet (ﷺ) conquered Makkah and broke the idols, the Muslims were reluctant to perform the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah because of the place of the two idols that were upon them; so the verse was revealed to lift that hardship.

Then the obligation of sa'y was established by the report: "Indeed Allah, may He be exalted, has prescribed for you the sa'y, so perform sa'y."

As for that reading, "that he not go around them," it is an abandoned reading, so the well-known recitation is not abandoned for its sake.

It is said that the "la" in it is extraneous (ṣilah), and the meaning is "that he go around." The poet said:

(I do not blame the fair ones that they do not mock, when they saw the gray-haired old man)

That is, that they mock.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾. Hamzah recited: "wa man yaṭawwa'" with a shaddah, and its meaning is yataṭawwa'; the well-known reading is ﴿wa man taṭawwa'﴾. Then, whoever said that sa'y is not a pillar (rukn) directed this statement ﴿whoever volunteers﴾ to sa'y.

Whoever said that it is a pillar directed it to the essential Hajj and 'Umrah.

It is possible that he intended voluntary acts in all other deeds.

﴿Indeed Allah is Appreciative and Knowing﴾. Appreciation (al-shukr) from Allah is that He gives beyond what the servant deserves.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 159:

The words of God the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance, after We have made it clear to the people in the Book﴾ — the verse was revealed concerning the Jews.

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah curses, and the cursers curse them.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The cursers (al-lāʿinūn): they are all creatures other than jinn and humankind."

It is related in the traditions: "When the earth becomes barren, every created thing curses the disobedient among the children of Adam, to the point that the beetles say, 'O Allah, curse the disobedient among the children of Adam, for we are deprived of provision because of the evil of their sins.'"

Qatadah said: "The cursers: they are the angels and the believers." It was also said: "They are the jinn and humankind."

It is related from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him: "No two people curse each other while they do not deserve it, except that the curse returns upon the Jews."

Allah's words: ﴿Except those who repent﴾, that is: embrace Islam; ﴿and make amends﴾, that is: persist in repentance; ﴿and make clear﴾ what they had concealed; ﴿then those, I accept their repentance; and I am the Accepting of Repentance, the Most Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 161:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, all together.﴾ If someone says: Has He not said ﴿mankind, all together﴾, and is not the one who is cursed part of mankind? So how can he curse himself? It is said: he will curse himself on the Day of Resurrection. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And some of you will curse others.﴾

"And His saying: ﴿abiding therein﴾ means in the curse, and it may also mean in the Fire, even though it is not mentioned in the verse. ﴿Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be reprieved﴾ — its interpretation is well known."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 163:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your God is one God﴾. The occasion of the revelation of this verse is what is related, that the polytheists said to the Messenger of Allah: "Describe your Lord for us, tell us the lineage of your Lord." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And your God is one God﴾, and Surat al-Ikhlas.

Al-Azhari said: al-Wahid (the One) is the one who has no equal. It is said: "So-and-so is the unique one of the world," meaning he has no equal in the world. The true meaning of al-Wahid is the one who is singular, who has no equal and no partner. ﴿There is no god but He, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾. Shahr ibn Hawshab related from Asma' bint Yazid al-Nahshaliyyah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The Greatest Name of Allah is in two verses of Surat al-Baqarah: the Verse of the Throne, and this verse, ﴿And your God is one God﴾."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 164:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. It is narrated that when His saying was revealed: ﴿And your God is one God﴾, the polytheists said to the Messenger of Allah: "What is the proof that He is one?" So there was revealed His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Creation (khalq) is the originating (ibtida') and measuring (taqdir) of a thing, and from it is the saying of the poet:

(Yet you cut what you measured, while some of the people create and then do not cut.)

That is: he cuts what you have measured.

"Heavens" (al-samawat) is the plural of "sky" (sama'), and they are seven heavens. Likewise the earths are seven, according to the correct view.

The heavens were mentioned in the plural form, while the earth was mentioned in the singular form, because each heaven is of a different kind, whereas all the earths are of one kind, which is soil. The sign in the heavens is their height, their breadth, and their elevation without pillars or supports, and what is seen in them of the sun, the moon, and the stars.

The sign in the earth is its extension, its spreading out, its vastness, and what is seen in it of trees, rivers, mountains, seas, precious stones, and plants.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the alternation of the night and the day﴾, that is, their going and coming. From this is the saying: "So-and-so frequents (yakhtalif) to so-and-so," meaning he goes and comes again and again. Similar to it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day in succession (khilfah)﴾, meaning one of them succeeds the other. The sign in the night and the day is their decrease and increase, and that the light of the day departs so that one does not know where it went, and the darkness of the night departs so that one does not know where it went.

﴿...the people, and what Allah sends down from the sky of water, by which He gives life to the earth after its death, and disperses in it every kind of creature, and the turning of the winds and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth are signs for a people﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the ship that runs in the sea with what benefits the people﴾. Al-fulk is a name for the collective, and it may be singular or plural. When it is intended as a collective it is feminine, and when it is intended as a singular it is masculine. Both forms occur in the Qur'an, and what is meant here is the collective.

The sign in the ship is its subjugation (taskhir) and its running upon the surface of the water. It is laden and heavy yet does not sink beneath the water, but rises above its surface.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾. It was said: Allah creates the water in the clouds, and according to this the "sky" here means the clouds. And it was said: rather, He creates the water in the sky, and from the sky it descends to the clouds, then from the clouds it descends to the earth.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿by which He gives life to the earth after its death﴾, that is, after its drying up and barrenness, for when the earth becomes barren it has died, and when it becomes fertile it has come to life.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and disperses in it every kind of creature﴾, that is, He scatters in it. As for His saying: ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾, it was said: their turning is that the winds are at times northern, at times southern, at times eastern (qabul), at times western (dabur), and at times intermediate (nakba'), and the nakba' is the wind that has no known direction.

It was also said: their turning is that the wind is at times gentle, at times stormy, at times hot, and at times cold.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The greatest of Allah's hosts are the wind and the water. Ibn al-Mubarak said: The wind has two wings, and the cloud is a sack full of water.

In the codex of Hafsah it is read "wa-tasrif al-arwah" (the turning of the spirits), which is close in meaning to "al-riyah" (the winds). The wind was called rih (wind) because it refreshes (yurih) the soul.

Shurayh the judge said: No wind blows except for the healing of a sick person or the sickening of a healthy one.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and the clouds subjected (al-musakhkhar)﴾, that is, made subservient (al-mudhallal), ﴿between the sky and the earth are signs for a people who reason﴾.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: There are three things of which one does not know from where they come: the thunder, the lightning, and the cloud.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 165:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals (andad)﴾. It is as if He is blaming the polytheists for taking equals besides Him after the proofs had been made manifest to them and the evidences of His oneness had been set up. ﴿Andad﴾ means: idols.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They love them as they love Allah﴾. Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad, the grammarian, said: the meaning of His saying ﴿they love them as they love Allah﴾ is: they love their gods as the believers love Allah.

It was also said that its meaning is: they love the idols as they love Allah, because they have associated them with Allah.

﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾, because they do not prefer anything over Allah, whereas the polytheists, when they take an idol and then see one better than it, discard the first and choose the second.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if only those who have done wrong could see when they see the punishment﴾. This is read with two readings: "wa-law yara" with the yā' (ya), and "wa-law tara" with the tā' (ta).

The meaning: know first that the answer (jawab) of "law" (if) here is omitted, and the like of this is frequent in the Qur'an.

Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾, and He said: ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which the mountains were moved, or the earth was split apart, or the dead were made to speak...﴾. Then the answer was omitted for brevity, since it precedes understanding.

Then, whoever reads "wa-law yara" with the yā', its implied sense is: if those who have done wrong could see the severity of Allah's punishment and His retribution when they see the punishment, they would know that what they had taken of idols neither harms them nor benefits them.

As for whoever reads "wa-law tara" with the tā', there are two views on its meaning. The first: if you could see, O Muhammad, those who have done wrong in the severity of the punishment, when they see the punishment, you would see a wondrous matter.

The second: its meaning is: say, O Muhammad, "O wrongdoer, and if you could see those who have done wrong in the severity of the punishment, you would be astonished at it and see a dreadful matter."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That power belongs to Allah entirely, and that Allah is severe in punishment﴾. His saying "anna al-quwwata" is read with a kasra on the alif and with a fatha. Whoever reads with the kasra, it is an inceptive clause after the completion of the first; whoever reads with the fatha, it is a continuation of the first, and its meaning is: because the power belongs to Allah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 166:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾. This is about the Day of Resurrection, when God gathers the leaders and their followers, and some of them disown others.

﴿And they see the punishment, and their bonds are cut off [from them]﴾, i.e., the connections in the world, such as kinship ties and friendships.

Mujahid said: it means the connection (al-wasl), which is close to the first meaning.

It has also been said that the asbab (causes, means of connection) are the deeds. The word may also be used to mean the gates of the heavens and the earth.

This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the asbab, the asbab of the heavens﴾, i.e., its gates. The poet said:

(And whoever shrinks from the asbab of death, [it will reach him], ... even if he seeks the asbab of the sky by a ladder.)

The root meaning of sabab is that which connects. From this, a rope is called a sabab. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were cut off from them﴾ means "from them" (ʿanhum), and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So ask about Him one who is informed﴾, meaning "ask about Him one who is informed."

And as for His saying, ﴿And those who followed will say: "If only we had a return [to the world]"﴾, that is, a return to the worldly life. ﴿Then we would disassociate ourselves from them as they have disassociated themselves from us.﴾ ﴿Thus will Allah show them their deeds as regrets upon them, and they will not emerge from the Fire.﴾

In this there are two opinions:

The first: that He shows them the evil deeds they committed, and those are the regrets.

The second: that He shows them the good deeds and virtues they abandoned, so that they become regrets upon them.

O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 168:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth﴾. Abu Muhammad Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna al-Hilali (ibn 'Uyayna) is reported to have been asked about eating clay, and he said: "Do not eat it, because God, the Exalted, said: ﴿eat of what is on the earth﴾ and did not say: 'eat from the earth'." ﴿Lawful and good﴾: so the lawful (halal) is everything that the Sharia has made lawful.

Regarding the good (tayyib) there are two opinions:

The first: everything that is found agreeable and pleasant is good. The Muslim finds the lawful agreeable and shuns the unlawful.

It is also said: the good (tayyib) is the pure (tahir).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions:

The first, Mujahid said: they are the sins of Satan. Abu Mijlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd al-Sadusi said: they are vows made in disobedience. The third opinion: they are all the works of Satan. Its derivation is from the "khutwa" (step), because steps leave traces that remain. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾: its meaning is apparent.

The Exalted said: ﴿He only commands you to evil and indecency﴾. "Evil" (al-sū') is disobedience.

"Indecency" (al-faḥshā') has two interpretations. The first is that it refers to fornication (al-zinā). It has also been said that it means stinginess (al-bukhl), and from this is the saying of the poet:

(The treasured jewel of the wealth of the immoderate, the excessively stingy...)

That is, the stingy one who is excessively tight-fisted.

﴿And that you say about God what you do not know﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 170:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow that upon which we found our fathers."﴾ That is: "we found" means "we found [them doing it]" (wajadnā).

﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything, nor were they guided?﴾ Its meaning is: how can they follow their fathers when their fathers did not understand anything and were not guided?! And in this there is a prohibition against blindly imitating the fathers (taqlid al-ab) in religion.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 171:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and cry﴾. Al-na'q (ناعق): the voice of the shepherd calling to the sheep. Al-Akhtal said:

(So shout to your sheep, O Jarir, for indeed / your self has deluded you in the wilderness into error)

In the verse there is an omitted element, whose estimated form is: The likeness of the disbelievers, and your likeness, O Muhammad, in calling them, is like the likeness of the shepherd who calls out to the sheep, and they hear nothing but a voice and understand nothing but a call.

﴿And a call and cry; deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not reason﴾. It was also said: its meaning is: the likeness of the disbelievers in calling upon the idols.

With this view there is a difficulty, because the idols do not hear a call or a cry. And how can it be a likeness that one who hears that is like one who shouts to that which does not hear, as we have explained?

Ibn al-Anbari said: He meant by "the one who shouts" the caller in the mountain who calls out and hears a voice, which is the echo. There is no understanding or comprehension there. And the example was given for the disbelievers in respect of their lack of understanding and intellect.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾. There is a report from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers. He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾ [23:51], and He said to the believers: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you, and be grateful to Allah﴾." We have already mentioned the meaning of the good things (ṭayyibāt).

﴿And be grateful to Allah, if it is Him that you worship﴾. Meaning: just as you worship Him as God, give thanks to Him for His beneficence.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 173:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you only the carrion﴾. "Innama" (indeed, only) is for negation and affirmation, because it is composed of two particles, the particle of negation and the particle of affirmation: "inna" is for affirmation and "ma" is for negation.

You say: "Inna fi al-dar Zaydan" (indeed, in the house is Zayd), which conveys the existence of Zayd in the house. But when you say: "Innama Zaydun fi al-dar" (only Zayd is in the house), it conveys that no one is in the house except Zayd.

As for "al-maytah" (carrion): it is a name for what has died without slaughter (dhakah). ﴿And blood﴾, which is well known. Both are restricted (takhsis): the Law permitted from carrion fish and locusts, and from bloods the liver and the spleen.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the flesh of swine﴾, meaning: the swine with its flesh, its fat and all its parts.

﴿And that over which has been invoked the name of other than Allah﴾, meaning: slaughtered in the name of idols. The origin of "al-ihlal" (invoking) is raising the voice, and they used to raise their voices over slaughtered animals. Ibn Ahmar said:

(Its riders raise the cry over al-Farqad, as the pilgrim in ihram raises the cry)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But whoever is compelled﴾ is read in two ways: with a kasra on the nun, and with a damma on it. Whoever reads with the kasra, it is according to the original form; and whoever reads with the damma, the damma of the ta' is then not considered. And the compulsion to eat carrion ﴿without being disobedient or transgressing﴾. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: "Without being disobedient" means: not rebelling against the ruler. ﴿Nor transgressing﴾, meaning: nor exceeding, being sinful in his journey. So this is evidence that one who is sinful in his journey does not take the concession of eating carrion.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: ﴿Without being disobedient﴾ means: not seeking carrion to satisfy hunger, so that he eats it for pleasure. ﴿Nor transgressing﴾ means: not exceeding the limit of necessity in eating it.

﴿Then there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: the meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 174:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book and sell it for a small price﴾ have already been explained.

As for the words of the Most High: ﴿They eat not into their bellies except the Fire﴾, there are two opinions. The first: those who consumed the bribe, the food becomes a fire in their bellies.

It is also said: its meaning is that this eating, since it leads them to the Fire, is as if they were eating fire into their bellies.

A similar usage is the words of the poet:

(And the mother of Sulaym, so do not grieve... for death is what the mother bears)

And another said:

(Beget for death and build for ruin... for all of you will come to perishing)

It is known that a child is not born for death, but since it inevitably ends in death, it is attributed to it.

As for the words of the Most High: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, there are two opinions. The first: He will not speak to them, but He will speak to them with threat and reproach.

It is also said, regarding its meaning: He is angry with them; as one says, "So-and-so does not speak to so-and-so" when the latter is angry with him.

﴿Nor will He purify them﴾, that is, He will not cleanse them of sins. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 175:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance and punishment in exchange for forgiveness. So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is: "What is it that makes them patient for the Fire?" (with a question mark and exclamation).

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: its meaning is: "How bold they are toward the Fire!" Al-Kisa'i related that two Bedouins brought a dispute before a judge, and the one who denied the claim swore an oath. The claimant said to him: "How patient you are for the Fire!", meaning: "How bold you are toward the Fire!"

Some grammarians said: its meaning is: "How long they will remain in the Fire!" It is said: "So-and-so, how patient he is in prison!", meaning: "How long he remains in prison!" Here "mā" is for exclamation (ta'ajjub).

Al-Kisa'i said: "The exclamation (ta'ajjub) attributed to God means the exclamation directed at the creatures."

﴿That is because Allah has sent down the Book with truth﴾, while they deny this.

﴿And indeed, those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme dissension﴾. That is: a long-standing opposition.

The reason khilaf (disagreement) is called shiqaq (dissension) is that the one who opposes is on one side (shiqq), and his companion is on the other side (shiqq).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 177:

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west﴾. Al-birr (righteousness): every act of goodness that leads its doer to Paradise.

Regarding its meaning there are two opinions. The first: the address is to the Muslims, for in the beginning they would perform the two testimonies and the prayers facing any direction they wished.

So He said: Not all righteousness is that you pray toward the east or the west. ﴿But righteousness is in one who believes in Allah﴾, so He commanded them with the rest of the legal obligations mentioned in the verse:

﴿And the Book and the prophets, and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and for freeing captives; and who establishes prayer and gives zakah; and those who fulfill their promise when they promise﴾.

It was also said: it is an address to the Jews and the Christians, since the qiblah of the Jews was the west and the qiblah of the Christians was the east.

So He said: It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east, O Christians, or toward the west, O Jews. ﴿But righteousness is in one who believes in Allah﴾.

Regarding its implied wording there are two opinions: the first is that its implied wording is ﴿but rather, the one of righteousness is one who believes in Allah﴾; the second is that its implied wording is ﴿but rather, righteousness is in one who believes in Allah﴾ and ﴿the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets; and gives wealth in spite of love for it﴾, meaning: love for wealth.

Ibn Mas'ud said: it is that you give charity while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for longevity and fearing poverty. ﴿To relatives﴾: the people of kinship. ﴿Orphans and the needy﴾: we have already mentioned them.

﴿And the traveler﴾: this is the one cut off (from his journey). It was also said: it refers to the guest. ﴿And those who ask﴾: well known. ﴿And for freeing captives﴾: meaning the mukatabun (slaves who are contracted to buy their freedom).

﴿And who establishes prayer and gives zakah, and those who fulfill their promise when they promise﴾. If someone asks: why did He say "wal-muwfuna" (and those who fulfill) in the nominative? It is said: there are two opinions. The more correct is that it is conjoined to the predicate of "lakinna" (but), and its implied wording is: but rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah and those who fulfill.

It was also said its implied wording is: and they are those who fulfill, as if He enumerated categories and then said: they and those who fulfill such-and-such.

There is a third opinion: when speech is long, the Arabs may deviate in case endings (i'rab).

﴿And the patient﴾ is in the accusative by way of praise. It was also said its implied wording is: I mean the patient. The poet said:

(Let not my people be far away, those who are ...
the poison of enemies and the calamity of the blow-ers,)

(Who descend upon every battlefield,
and who are the good ones at the knots of the cords.)

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿In adversity﴾ is hunger; ﴿and hardship﴾ is illness and harm.

﴿And in the time of battle﴾: the time of fighting. ﴿Those are the ones who are true﴾: they fulfilled the covenant. It was also said: their deeds confirmed their words. ﴿And those are the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 178:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retaliation (al-qisas) in the matter of the slain﴾, meaning: obligated upon you. ﴿The free for the free, and the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: This was at the beginning of Islam, and retaliation was between free and free, slave with slave, and female with female. A free person was not killed for a slave, nor a slave for a free person, nor a male for a female, nor a female for a male. Then that was abrogated (nasakha) by His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the soul is for the soul﴾, and retaliation then applied to all.

As for 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, he said concerning a free person who kills a slave: the free person is killed for him. Then the master of the slave pays the heir of the free killer the difference between the blood-money (diyah) and the value of the slave. And if a slave kills a free person, the slave is killed for him. Then the master of the slave who killed pays the heir of the free slain person the difference between the blood-money and the value of the slave.

There is also another view, reported from Ibn 'Abbas: that the verse was revealed concerning two tribes, one of which had superiority over the other. The superior tribe said: a free man among you may be killed for a slave among us, and a male among you for a female among us. So the verse was revealed in rejection of their statement.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But whoever is granted some remission by his brother, then pursuit should be made in a reasonable manner, and payment made to him in a good way﴾. The root of 'afw (remission) is leaving or relinquishing. The most apparent of the views on it is the position of the majority of the Companions and the Successors: that whoever waives retaliation, he is entitled to take the blood-money. So he is pursued "in a reasonable manner," meaning he should not demand more than his due right. And it is paid "in a good way," meaning he should not delay in payment.

Al-Azhari said: In the verse there is an elision (taqdir), and its meaning is: whoever is given, from the property of his brother, meaning the killer, or from the compensation for the blood of his brother, meaning the slain, some remission (afw), i.e., excess, then the claimant should pursue in a reasonable manner, and the one owing should pay in a good way.

Its apparent meaning requires that brotherhood of religion is not severed between the killer and the slain, since He said: "from his brother," and this is what we say. It has also been said: its meaning is brotherhood of lineage (nasab).

It has also been said: He only called him a brother at the time of the verse's revelation, and at the time of its revelation he was a brother to him before the killing occurred, not that he remains a brother to him, for killing severs the allegiance between the killer and the slain and necessitates disavowal from him, because of his wickedness and his killing.

﴿That is a lightening (takhfif) from your Lord and a mercy﴾. Its meaning: that blood-money was obligatory (hatm) in the law of the Christians, and retaliation was obligatory in the law of the Jews, and this community was given the choice between retaliation and blood-money. That is the lightening.

﴿So whoever transgresses after that﴾, meaning: kills after the pardon. ﴿For him is a painful punishment﴾, meaning: retaliation.

Ibn Juraij said: retaliation is obligatory upon him, such that pardon is not accepted.

"His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you, O people of understanding﴾. The meaning of "life" is that when a man reflects that if he kills, he will be killed, he does not kill; so he remains alive, and the one who would have been killed is alive too. ﴿That you may become righteous﴾: that you may refrain from killing."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 180:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is prescribed for you﴾, i.e., it is obligatory upon you, ﴿when death approaches one of you﴾, i.e., when the time of death draws near. ﴿If he leaves behind wealth﴾, i.e., property and abundance, and "good" (khayr) in the whole Qur'an carries the meaning of wealth.

﴿Bequest to parents and relatives in a fair manner is a duty upon the God-conscious﴾. This is because bequest was obligatory at the beginning of Islam for parents and relatives, then it became abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of inheritance (ayat al-mirath).

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Allah, may He be exalted, has given every rightful person his right. Verily, there is no bequest to an heir."

Al-Hasan, Tawus, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the abrogation applies to the parents only, not to the relatives.

Then they differed regarding one who bequeaths a third of his wealth to a stranger (ajnabi). Some of them said: a third of what he bequeaths goes to the relatives, and two-thirds to the stranger.

Some of them said: two-thirds go to the relatives, and a third to the stranger.

Some of them said: the whole third goes to the relatives, and nothing to the stranger. The most sound view is that it has been abrogated with regard to all, and the recommendation (istihbab) remains regarding the relatives who do not inherit.

It was also said: at the beginning of Islam it was recommended (nadb), and what is recommended in bequest is less than a third.

It is related from some of the early predecessors (salaf) that he said: a fifth is reasonable, a quarter is a struggle, and a third is the limit that judges would enforce.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 181:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever alters it after he has heard it﴾. If someone asks: why did He say "fa-man baddalahu" (whoever altered it) with the marker of the masculine, when the thing mentioned is feminine, namely "al-wasiyya" (the bequest)? It is said: its meaning is "whoever alters the matter of the bequest."

It is also said: its meaning is "whoever alters the statement of the testator," because the bequest issues from the statement of the testator; so the reference returns to the meaning rather than the wording. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever has received an admonition (mawʿiza)﴾, meaning: an admonition (waʿz) has come to him, so the reference returns to the meaning. And he meant by the alteration: altering the witnesses, the executors and the guardians.

﴿Then its sin is only upon those who alter it﴾, not upon the testator. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of what the testator bequeathed ﴿Knowing﴾ of the alteration of those who alter it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 182:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then whoever fears injustice (janaf) or sin (ithm) from a testator﴾. Here "fear" (al-khawf) carries the meaning of "knowledge" (al-'ilm).

This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ (2:229), and His saying: ﴿And if you fear a breach between the two﴾ (4:35). That is: "if you know." He expressed "fear" for "knowledge" because fear is close to knowledge, for one only fears falling into a thing once he has knowledge of it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿min mawsin﴾ (from a testator) is read with light and with intensive pronunciation of the letter (wa); it is said that aw-sa (awsa) and wassa (wassa) have one meaning.

As for janaf, it is inclination (al-mayl), and ithm is wrongdoing (al-zulm). Sibawayh recited:

(My she-camel has swerved from the direction of al-Yamama, and my intention was not its people, nor your pasture.)

Al-Suddi said: janaf is error (al-khata'), and ithm is deliberate intent (al-'amd).

The meaning of the verse according to the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid: when a man attends the bequest of a testator and sees him inclining, either by negligence, or by extravagance, or by placing the bequest in other than its proper place, and he counsels him and returns him to the truth, this is permissible for him, and this is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then there is no sin upon him who makes settlement between them﴾ (2:182).

It was also said: this refers to the bequest to the nearest relatives at the time when it was obligatory. So when he sees him bequeathing to someone other than the nearest relatives, he returns him to the bequest to the nearest relatives.

It was also said: he intended by it the ruler (al-imam) who reconciles between the testator's beneficiaries and the heirs, returning them to the truth.

﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾, that is: there is no blame upon him. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 183:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾, meaning: fasting has been made obligatory upon you.

Al-sawm (fasting) linguistically means abstention (al-imsak). It is said: "The horses fasted" (samat al-khayl) when they refrained from fodder and travel. From this is the words of the poet:

(Horses fasting and other horses not fasting... beneath the dust cloud, and others chewing the bit)

From this also is said: "The day fasted" (sama al-nahar) when the sun rose high and the pace of travel slowed as if standing still; and that is at the time of midday heat. From this is the words of the poet:

(So leave her, and turn your soul away from yourself by means of a swift she-camel... [docile] when the day fasts and grows hot at noon)

From this is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾, meaning: silence (samtan), and in silence there is abstention from speech.

As for sawm in the Shari'ah, it is abstention from eating, drinking and sexual intercourse, together with intention, at a specific time.

﴿As it was prescribed for those before you﴾. The scholars differed regarding this comparison.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Fasting at the beginning of Islam was obligatory from the 'atamah (late night prayer time) until the following night, and likewise it was obligatory upon those before us.

It was said: He intended by this: the fast of Ramadan was prescribed for the Muslims as it was prescribed for those before them, meaning: the Christians.

Daghfal ibn Handhalah said: Fasting was obligatory upon the Christians for thirty days. Then a king of theirs fell ill, and said: "If God cures me, I will add ten days." God cured him, and he added ten. Then another king of theirs fell ill and said: "If God cures me, I will add seven days to it." God cured him, and he added seven. They said: "What is this deficiency?! Complete it with fifty." And they said: "We will fast it at a time that is neither hot nor cold." So they would fast the fifty in the season of spring. This is the origin of the fast of fifty days in regard to the Christians.

It was said: He intended by this: the fasting of three days of every month. It was obligatory at the beginning of Islam, as it was prescribed upon the Jews.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal narrated: "When the Prophet emigrated to Madinah, he saw the Jews fasting three days of every month and the day of 'Ashura', so God made it obligatory upon him in this manner."

He would fast it thirty-seven days, from spring to spring. Then that was abrogated (naskh) by the fast of ﴿In it was revealed the Qur'an as guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and criterion. So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, [namely] Ramadan.

It was said: He used to fast three days in the White Days (ayyam al-bid).

Ibn 'Abbas said: The first things abrogated after the Hijrah were: the direction of prayer (qiblah) and fasting.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿So that you may become righteous﴾, meaning: through fasting; because fasting is a means to taqwa (God-consciousness) through what it contains of subduing the self and breaking desires.

It was said: its meaning is: so that you may guard yourselves against desires, [such as] eating, drinking and sexual intercourse.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 184:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿A number of specified days﴾. If we say that the verse has been abrogated (mansukh), then it was a fast that was obligatory and then abrogated.

If we say that the verse is not abrogated, then by His saying ﴿a number of specified days﴾ is meant the days of Ramadan. In this there is an indication of ease (taysir), in that He did not make obligatory the fasting of the whole year, but made it obligatory for specified days only. ﴿So whoever among you is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days.﴾ Dawud and the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Zahir) said: the traveller must fast a number of other days even if he fasts Ramadan, holding to the apparent meaning of the verse.

The majority hold that there is an elision (idmar) in it, and its estimated sense is: "So he breaks his fast, then [fasts] a number of other days."

Then they differed concerning the limit of the illness that permits breaking the fast. Dawud and the people of the apparent meaning said: it is whatever is called illness. This is also the view of Ibn Sirin among the early generation (al-salaf). Al-Hasan said: it is the illness with which prayer while seated is permitted.

The school of al-Shafi'i: it is the illness in which one fears that fasting will increase the illness.

As for the limit of the journey that permits breaking the fast, they differed. Dawud and those who follow him said: it is whatever is called a journey. The school of al-Shafi'i holds that it is the distance of shortening the prayer, sixteen farsakh.

﴿And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days. God desires ease for you and does not desire hardship for you.﴾

The school of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him [Abu Hanifa], is that it is a distance of three days' travel, as he said regarding shortening the prayer.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for those who are able to do it, a ransom: feeding a poor person.﴾ There are readings of the verse. The well-known reading is this.

Ibn Abbas, Abbas, and Aisha recited, and it is sound, from Ibn Abbas: "and upon those who are able to do it (yutawwiqunahu)" [written with a different vowelling: "yatawwaqunahu"]. Mujahid recited: "and upon those who make it a burden (yutawwiqunahu)." These two are irregular (shadh) readings.

As for the reading "a ransom, feeding a poor person," there are two well-known readings: the first is this one;

and the second is the reading of the people of Medina and Syria: "a ransom, feeding poor people" with the alif (masakin).

As for the well-known reading ﴿And for those who are able to do it, a ransom﴾, it means: at the beginning of Islam they had the choice between fasting and the ransom, so He said: "And for those who are able to do it, a ransom"; if they chose the ransom.

It was also said its meaning is: "And for those who are able to do it during youth, but are unable to do it in old age, a ransom if they break the fast." This is related from Ali. According to this, the verse is not abrogated.

As for the reading of Ibn Abbas, its meaning is: "And for those who make it a burden, so they are not able to do it, a ransom."

As for the reading of Mujahid, "yutawwiqunahu" means: they make it a burden on themselves (yatatawwaqunahu) and impose it upon themselves, so they are not able to do it.

As for His saying ﴿a ransom: feeding poor people﴾, He only attributed the ransom to the food because the ransom is a measure of food, and "food" is a generic noun, as one says "a silver ring," "a silk garment," and the like.

As for the second reading ﴿ransom﴾ in the nominative, it is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿feeding a poor person﴾ is an explanation of it and a substitute for it. He said "a poor person" because each day one feeds one poor person.

And whoever reads "masakin" (poor people), it is because the total food for the days of fasting goes to the poor.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾. Ibn Abbas said: it means that whoever feeds two poor persons while his obligation is one poor person, or feeds a sa' while his obligation is a mudd, it is better for him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾. If we adopt the view of abrogation, its meaning is: "And that you fast is better for you than the ransom."

If we say the verse is not abrogated, then its meaning is: "And that you fast during youth is better for you than the ransom in old age and infirmity."

It was also said: this concerns the decrepit elder, that his undertaking the fast is better for him than that he pay a ransom. The sound view is one of the first two opinions. ﴿If you knew.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 185:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The month of Ramadan﴾. The month was named thus for its prominence (shuhra).

As for Ramadan, in the pre-Islamic era the month was called Shahr Ramadan "Natiq" (the month of Ramadan, with the epithet nātiq, "speaking" or "burning").

Abu 'Ali Qutrub said: It was only named Ramadan because they used to fast in the intense heat, and from it comes al-ramda', meaning sand that has been heated by the sun.

Mujahid said: It is one of the names of God, and for this reason it is not made plural as ramadanat. This is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) in a rare (gharib) report, but the correct view is that it is the name of the month.

Reports have come concerning the excellence of the month and of fasting. Among them is what is related with a raised (marfu') chain: "The lord of the months is the month of Ramadan."

It is authentically established from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "When the first night of Ramadan comes, the gates of mercy are opened, the gates of Hell are closed, and the devils are chained." Muslim related it in his Sahih.

He also said: God, may He be exalted, says: "Every deed of the son of Adam is for him except fasting, for it is for Me and I will reward it..." The report continues.

They differed concerning the singling out of fasting. Some said: because it is the most severe of the acts of worship in breaking desires and subduing the self. Others said: because it is a secret between the servant and his Lord.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾. If someone says: The Qur'an was only sent down over twenty-three years, so how does He say, "in which the Qur'an was sent down"? The answer: Ibn 'Abbas said: God, may He be exalted, sent down the Qur'an all at once in Ramadan to a house in the lowest heaven called Bayt al-'Izza (the House of Majesty), and then from it it was sent down to the earth in installments.

Wathila ibn al-Asqa' related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The scrolls of Abraham were sent down on the first night of Ramadan, the Torah was sent down on the sixth night of Ramadan, the Gospel was sent down on the thirteenth night of Ramadan, and the Qur'an was sent down on the twenty-fourth of Ramadan."

Concerning it there is a third view, meaning: the Qur'an was sent down with the obligation of fasting Ramadan in it.

The Qur'an was named Qur'an because it gathers together the surahs, the verses and the letters. The root meaning of Qur'an is "gathering," and from it comes the saying of the poet:

(The two forearms of a long-necked, white-skinned, virgin she-camel, of pure colour, which has not gathered (taqra') a foetus.)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿A guidance for mankind﴾ means guidance and clarification. His saying: ﴿And clear proofs of the guidance and the criterion﴾ means clear indications concerning the lawful and the unlawful, and al-Furqan (the criterion) is that which distinguishes between truth and falsehood.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾. Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad said: its meaning is: whoever of you is resident in the settled place (al-hadar) and reaches the month, let him fast it.

Then the Companions differed concerning one who reached the month while resident and then travelled, into two views. 'Ali (may God be pleased with him) said: it is not permissible for him to break the fast. Most of the Companions held that it is permissible to break the fast, and this is the more correct view, because of what is authentically established from the Messenger of God, through the report of Jabir, that he travelled in Ramadan, and when he reached Kura' al-Ghamim he broke his fast, and the people broke their fast.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿let him fast it﴾ means: to the extent of what he reached while resident. ﴿And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾. He repeated this only so that it be known that this ruling in the abrogating (nasikh) text is like what it was in the abrogated (mansukh) text.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ means: in permitting the breaking of the fast due to illness and travel, and postponing the fast to other days.

It is related from al-Sha'bi that he said: No man was given the choice between two matters and chose the easier of them except that it was the more beloved of them to God.

Muhajjan ibn Adra' related: that the Prophet was told of a man who used to prolong prayer in the mosque the whole day; he came to him, took hold of his shoulders and shook them vigorously, then said: "Indeed God, may He be exalted, is pleased for this community with ease, and dislikes hardship for them. And this man is content with hardship and dislikes ease."

It is well known from the Messenger of God: "God loves that His concessions be accepted, as He loves that His strict commands be carried out."

(﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the one who calls when he calls upon Me; so let them respond to Me﴾ and that you complete the period (al-'idda)) meaning: the period of the month, by making up what was broken during illness or travel. ﴿And that you glorify God for having guided you﴾ meaning: that you exalt Him for guiding you to what He is pleased with, the fasting of Ramadan. Ibn 'Abbas said: this refers to the takbirs of the night of the Festival of Breaking the Fast (Eid al-Fitr), and it is related from Ibn 'Umar and 'A'isha (may God be pleased with them both). He also said: It is incumbent upon every Muslim to say the takbir on the night of the Festival until he finishes the Festival prayer. ﴿And that you may be grateful﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 186:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾. Concerning the occasion of the revelation of this verse there are two accounts. The first: the Companions said, "O Messenger of Allah, is our Lord near so that we may confide in Him privately, or is He far so that we must call out to Him?" So this verse was revealed.

The second: when His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Call upon Me; I will respond to you﴾ was revealed, they said, "O Messenger of Allah, how should we call upon Him, and when should we call upon Him?" So this verse was revealed.

As for His saying ﴿indeed I am near﴾, it means that nothing is hidden from Him. He is nearer to the servants than their jugular vein, and nearer to the heart than the one who possesses it.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾, there is an ellipsis in it. Its implied meaning is: "I respond to the invocation of the supplicant if I will." This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾.

Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is, "I hear the invocation of the one who calls." The Arabs say, "So-and-so calls upon one who does not respond," meaning one who does not hear. This is because a person may be called upon and not respond, so it shows that by "response" is meant hearing.

It has also been said that it is in its literal sense of response, and its meaning is that He does not disappoint the one who calls upon Him. For if he calls upon Him for what has been decreed for him, he is given it; and if he calls upon Him for what has not been decreed for him, the reward is stored up for him in the Hereafter, so his supplication is not disappointed.

It has been transmitted from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no servant who says, [O Lord], except that Allah, may He be exalted, says: 'Here I am, My servant.' He hastens for him what He wills, and stores up for him what He wills."

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿So let them respond to Me and believe in Me﴾: it has been said that "istijabah" (responding) here has the meaning of "ijabah" (answering), and this is indicated by the saying of the poet:

(And one who calls to generosity calls out, but no one answers him at that time.)

That is, no one answered him. Abu 'Ubaydah said: its meaning is, "So let them seek from Me the response."

Its reality is: "So let them obey Me." ﴿And believe in Me, that they may be guided﴾: its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 187:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Permitted for you﴾, meaning: made lawful for you (laylat al-siyam, the night of the fast), ﴿the approach to your wives (al-rafath ila nisa'ikum)﴾.

It has been said: al-rafath is everything a man desires from his wife, and here it means intercourse (al-wat').

Ibn 'Abbas said: Indeed Allah is Modest and Generous; He uses the fair term to refer to the foul.

﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾. It has been said: the meaning is, they are a source of tranquility for you, and you are a source of tranquility for them. It has also been said: nothing finds rest in another as one spouse finds rest in the other. It has also been said: He meant by it the literal sense of garment, for each of them becomes a garment for the other during intimate contact. He said: ﴿Now, lie with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you, and eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread [of dawn]﴾. The poet said:

(When the bedfellow bends her neck, she bends and becomes a garment over him.)

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the meaning is, they are a bed (firash) for you, and you are a covering (lihaf) for them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾ is an ifti'al form from khiyana (betrayal), meaning: you were betraying yourselves by opposing the command and abandoning caution. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now, lie with them﴾. It has been said: He meant by it intercourse. It has also been said: He meant what is less than intercourse. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾. Anas ibn Malik said: He meant by it seeking offspring.

Abu al-Jawza' related from Ibn 'Abbas: He meant by it seeking the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr).

Qatada said, and it is the best of the sayings: meaning, seek what Allah has decreed for you of the concession by permitting eating, drinking and intercourse, in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz).

Ibn 'Abbas read, among the irregular readings (shawadh): "wa-ittaba'u ma kataba Allahu lakum wa-kulu wa-ashraba".

The occasion of the revelation of the verse: Allah, exalted is He, had originally made the fast obligatory from the 'atama (night prayer time) until the following night, and whoever slept or prayed the 'isha' prayer became forbidden to eat, drink and have intercourse. It is narrated that a man called Sirma, Abu Qays, worked all day, then returned to his home and asked his wife for food. She delayed, so sleep overcame him. When he awoke, eating and drinking had become forbidden to him. He woke up having suffered greatly, until he collapsed unconscious. This was reported to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the verse was revealed: ﴿The white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn. Then complete the fast until the night﴾, permitting eating and drinking at night.

The reason for the permission of intimate contact: it is narrated that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of Allah, I approached my wife after I had slept." He said: "You were not deserving of this, O 'Umar." It is also narrated that a man among the Companions informed the Prophet of a similar matter, and the verse was revealed permitting intimate contact. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿you were betraying yourselves﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn﴾, Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna said: by "thread" He meant color, and the meaning is the whiteness of day distinguished from the blackness of night.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of the dawn﴾. The occasion of its revelation: it is narrated that when this verse was revealed, 'Adi ibn Hatim took two cords (iqalayn), one white and one black, and placed them under his pillow. When it was morning he would look at them, and eat the pre-dawn meal until the white became distinct from the black. He informed the Prophet of this, and he said: "Indeed you have a broad pillow."

In another narration: "Indeed you have a broad nape; it is only the whiteness of day from the blackness of night." This is an expression they used to refer to lack of understanding. Then He revealed ﴿of the dawn﴾. The dawn is of two kinds: ﴿And do not approach them while you are secluding yourselves in the mosques. These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them. Thus does Allah make clear His verses to the people that they may become righteous﴾. One is a stretched dawn like the tail of a wolf (dhanab al-sirhan), which rises and then disappears, and darkness prevails; this is the false dawn.

The second, after it, is a spreading dawn, which quickly spreads across the horizon. It has been said: redness mingles with it. This is the true dawn, which makes eating forbidden and makes fasting obligatory.

The Arabs say: "the dawn is the herald (bashir) of the sun."

A remarkable divergent view is related from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, and it is well known from him, that he said: by "the dawn" He meant the rising of the sun, and he permitted the pre-dawn meal after the rising of the dawn.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾. This implies the prohibition of fasting at night, since He has made it a limit.

He has also said: "Whoever fasts at night has exhausted himself and has no reward."

And He also said: "When the night approaches from here and the day departs from here, the fasting person has broken his fast."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach them while you are secluding yourselves in the mosques﴾. Al-'Ukuf is staying in a place.

It has been said: the verse was revealed concerning people among the Muslims who would leave their seclusion (i'tikaf), have intercourse with their wives, and then return to the place of seclusion. So Allah, exalted is He, forbade intercourse during seclusion.

Seclusion is permitted in all mosques. Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman is reported to have held an isolated and anomalous view on this, saying: seclusion is not permitted except in three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, the Farthest Mosque, and the Mosque of Madina. He used to criticize 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud for secluding himself in other mosques, and 'Abd Allah would deny this and reject his view, and the community follows the view of 'Abd Allah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾, which are what Allah, exalted is He, has forbidden from sins.

The root of hadd is prohibition. From it comes hiddad for the doorkeeper, because he prevents people; and from it comes hadid (iron), because one is protected by it to defend against enemies.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not approach them﴾, meaning: so do not commit them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear His verses to mankind that they may become righteous﴾, whose meaning is apparent.

"The Most High said: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾, meaning: let none of you consume the wealth of another by falsehood. Consuming wealth by falsehood is of two kinds:

The first: by way of usurpation, plunder and wrongdoing.

The second: by way of frivolity, such as gambling, wagering, the fee of a singer, and the like.

And His saying, the Most High: ﴿and proffer it to the judges﴾. It has been said: its meaning is: "And do not proffer it to the judges", that is, do not bribe them and curry their favour so that they rule for you unjustly.

It has also been said: its meaning is: "And do not consume your wealth among yourselves by falsehood, attributing it to the rulings of the judges and taking their verdict as proof."

﴿while you know﴾ is an elliptical clause (khalafa). This is evidence for those who hold that a judge's ruling is binding outwardly and inwardly. Al-idla' (proffering) means casting: one says "adlā dalwahu" (he let down his bucket) when he sends it down, and "dallā" when he draws it up.

And His saying, the Most High: ﴿so that you may consume a portion (fariqan)﴾, that is, a group (ṭā'ifa) ﴿of the wealth of people with sin﴾, that is, with wrongdoing, ﴿while you know﴾."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 189:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the new moons.﴾ "Al-ahilla" is the plural of "hilal" (the new crescent), which is the name for the moon when it first appears thin. It is called hilal because people raise their voices (yastahillu) when they see it. It is said: "istahalla al-sabiyy" (the child cried out), when he shouted with crying. The Arabs give each group of three nights of the month a specific name. They say for the first three: "gharar"; then the one after it, "nafl"; then the one after it, "tis'", then the one after it, "ashr"; then the one after it, "bid"; then the one after it, "rab'", and the more correct is "ru'"; then the one after it, "zulam"; then the one after it, "hanawis"; then the one after it, "wadi"; then the one after it, "muhaq".

The occasion of revelation of the verse: it is narrated that Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'laba ibn Ghanma said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the matter with the state of the moon? It appears thin, then becomes full at once, then returns thin." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: they are signs of time for the people and for the Hajj.﴾

That is, "He made it so that they would be appointed times for your fasting, your breaking of the fast, your Hajj, and the due dates of your debts."

And the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs.﴾ Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "The verse was revealed concerning us, the group of the Ansar. When a man among us went out for Hajj and then returned, he would not enter his house through the door, but would make a breach in the back of the house and enter through it, and he considered entering through the door of the house to be wickedness." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs.﴾ That is, from their rear.

﴿But righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah.﴾ That is, the righteousness of one who fears Allah. ﴿And enter houses through their doors.﴾ He returned them to the doors. ﴿And fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 190:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾. It has been said: this was at the beginning of Islam, when Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet to refrain from fighting the polytheists. Then, when he migrated to Madinah, He commanded him to fight them if they fought him, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾. [Then] He commanded him to fight them, whether they had fought or not.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not transgress﴾, meaning: do not initiate fighting against them.

It has also been said: "and do not transgress" means: do not kill those among them who have covenants (mu'ahadun, those bound by a treaty). ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 191:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And kill them wherever you encounter them﴾. It was said: this verse abrogated the earlier verse (naskh, abrogation) by this, as we have explained. And it was said: rather, it was abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾.

And they said: about seventy verses were abrogated by it.

﴿Wherever you encounter them﴾ means: wherever you find them.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and expel them from where they expelled you﴾. That is because they had expelled the Muslims from Makkah, so He said: expel them from their homes as they expelled you from your homes.

﴿And fitnah (trial, persecution; here, disbelief) is worse than killing﴾. By fitnah He means disbelief. The reason for this: when Allah, exalted is He, made it unlawful for them to begin fighting in the sacred month, some Muslims hastened to fight them, so the disbelievers reproached them for it. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾, meaning: the shirk (polytheism) you are upon is worse than the fighting they began.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you therein﴾. Thus it was at the beginning that beginning the fighting in the sacred city was forbidden, and then it became abrogated (mansukh).

Ata' said: this did not become abrogated. The more sound view is that the verse is abrogated.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾.
﴿Then if they desist﴾ meaning: if they embrace Islam. ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ toward what has passed.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 193:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾, i.e., shirk, ﴿and the religion is for Allah﴾, i.e., fight them until they submit to Allah. It is also said: until there is no worship (sajdah) except to Allah.

The words of the Most High: ﴿But if they desist, then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., if they embrace Islam, then there is no plundering, no taking captive, and no killing, except against those who remain upon shirk.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 194:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and violations of sacred things are subject to retaliation.﴾ There are two opinions regarding the meaning of this verse.

The first: He intended by it the matter of the ʿUmrah (the lesser pilgrimage). This is what has been related: that the Prophet (ﷺ) set out performing ʿUmrah in Dhu al-Qaʿdah. When he reached al-Ḥudaybiyah, the polytheists barred him, so he made a treaty with them that he would return in the following year. Then he returned performing ʿUmrah in the following year, in Dhu al-Qaʿdah, and God compensated him for what had been missed in the first year by what he did in the second year. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾, meaning Dhu al-Qaʿdah. ﴿And violations of sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾, meaning: the sanctity of the sacred month, the sanctity of the sacred city, and the sanctity of the state of ihram.

The second opinion: that it refers to the matter of fighting. Its meaning is: if they initiate fighting with you in the sacred month and violate its sanctity, then fight them in it and do not concern yourselves with its sanctity, for it is retaliation for what they have done.

﴿So whoever transgresses against you, then transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you.﴾ The word iʿtidāʾ (transgression) means injustice. The recompense for injustice is called iʿtidāʾ only for the sake of verbal parallelism (izdiwāj al-kalām). A similar example is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The Arabs say: "Falān wronged me, so I wronged him," meaning: I repaid him for the injustice. It is also said: "Falān acted ignorantly toward me, so I acted ignorantly toward him." The poet said:

(Surely let none of them act ignorantly toward us, lest we act more ignorantly than the ignorant ones.)

And another said:

(I have a horse for forbearance, bridled with forbearance; and I have a horse for ignorance, saddled with ignorance.)

﴿And fear God, and know that God is with the God-fearing.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 195:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾. He meant by it: spending in jihad, and every good deed is "the way of Allah," but when "the way of Allah" is mentioned without qualification, it is understood to refer to jihad.

﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. It has been said: the bāʾ (the preposition "with") is superfluous, and the sense is: "and do not throw your hands into destruction," and "hands" is used to mean the selves, as Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾, meaning: for what you have earned. It has also been said: the bāʾ is in its proper place, and there is an ellipsis, and the sense is: "and do not throw yourselves, by your own hands, into destruction."

Al-tahlukah (destruction) and al-halak (perishing) are one and the same. It has been said that there is a difference between them: al-tahlukah is what can be guarded against, while al-halak is what cannot be guarded against. Regarding its meaning there are two opinions:

The first: "and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction" by abandoning spending in the way of Allah.

The second: al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir and al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib said that it refers to a man who commits a sin and then says, "There is no repentance for me," and so despairs of the mercy of Allah. We seek refuge in Allah.

The first is more sound, because of what has been related from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "This verse was revealed about us, the group of the Ansar. When Allah, may He be exalted, granted victory to His religion and exalted His Prophet, we said: 'If we remain with our wealth, tending to it, and abandon jihad, it will be lost.' So the verse was revealed: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾," meaning: by abandoning spending in jihad and remaining attached to wealth. Furthermore, it is related that when this verse was revealed, Abu Ayyub continued to campaign until his last campaign, which he undertook at Constantinople, in the army sent by Muʿawiyah, and he died there and was buried at the foot of the wall of Constantinople, and they would seek rain through him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do good﴾, meaning: by spending in the way of Allah.

ʿIkrimah said: its meaning is: think well of Allah.

It has also been said its meaning is: perform the obligations of Allah. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the good-doers﴾. Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said: whoever has a hen under his hand and does not treat it kindly is not among the good-doers.

**Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 196:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah (lesser pilgrimage) for Allah﴾. Ibn Mas'ud recited, as an irregular reading (shadhdh): "And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah to the House," without the words "for Allah." Al-Sha'bi recited: "And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah," beginning a new sentence.

They differed over the meaning of completion (al-Itmam). Umar said: its completion is that it is not abrogated (naskh), since it was permissible to abrogate it at the outset. Ali and Ibn Mas'ud said: its completion is that one enters into ihram for both from one's household dwelling (duwayrat al-ahl). It was said: its completion is that the provision and expenses be from what is lawful. Sufyan al-Thawri said: its completion is that one intends ﴿until the offering reaches its place. So whoever among you is ill, or has an ailment of the head, must make a compensation of fasting or⁠﴾ the Hajj, and does not intend trade.

It was said: its completion is that one does not disobey Allah in it, and performs it in the manner He commanded.

Know that the 'Umrah is obligatory. This is the view of Ibn Umar. According to Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, it is a sunnah, and this is also narrated from Jabir.

The evidence for its obligation is the apparent meaning of the verse, namely His saying: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾, and the apparent meaning of a command indicates obligation.

Reports have come concerning the virtue of the Hajj and the 'Umrah, among them what is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The two 'Umrahs expiate what lies between them, and for an accepted Hajj (al-Hajj al-mabrur) there is no reward but Paradise."

As for His saying: ﴿But if you are prevented (fa-in uhsirtum)﴾, Ibn Umar said: al-Ihsar (being prevented) is from an enemy. (Ibn Mas'ud also said: al-Ihsar is from an enemy.) Illness is also a valid cause. Two reports are narrated from Ibn Abbas on this. Al-Ihsar and al-Hasr have the same meaning.

Al-Farra' said: al-Ihsar is by confinement, while al-Hasr is the prevention by an enemy. The correct view is that it refers to an enemy and not to illness, because of His saying: ﴿But when you are secure (fa-idha amintum)﴾, and security is from an enemy. Whoever holds the first view says there is an ellipsis here, its meaning being: when you are secure from the enemy and recovered from illness.

As for His saying: ﴿then what is feasible of the offering (fa-ma istaysara min al-hadyi)﴾: the least that is obligatory of it is slaughtering a sheep; the best is sacrificing a camel (badanah); the middle is slaughtering a cow. Al-Hadyu and al-Tahdiyah and al-Hadyu have the same meaning, namely what is sent as a gift to a place or to a person. The poet said:

*"I swore by the Lord of Makkah and the place of prayer,*
*and by the necks of the offerings, adorned with garlands."*

As for His saying: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place (mahalluhu)﴾, that is: until ﴿...charity or a sacrifice. Then when you are secure, whoever performs Tamattu' (combining 'Umrah with Hajj) by the 'Umrah until the Hajj, then what is feasible of the offering. And whoever⁠﴾ slaughters it in its place. The place of slaughter, according to us, is where one is prevented and exits the state of ihram.

Abu Hanifah said: its place is Makkah. Our view is more sound, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he reached al-Hudaybiyah in the state of 'Umrah, was prevented by the polytheists, and he exited ihram and slaughtered there.

As for His saying: ﴿So whoever among you is ill, or has an ailment of the head﴾: this was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah. Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla narrated from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah that he said: "I was with the Messenger of Allah at al-Hudaybiyah, and I was blowing under the cooking pot while lice were falling onto my face. He (peace be upon him) said: 'What is this? Shave your head, slaughter a sheep, or fast three days, or feed six poor people.'" This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿then a compensation of fasting or charity or sacrifice﴾, meaning the slaughtering of a sheep.

This is the school of thought according to us: in the compensation for harm, one slaughters a sheep, or fasts three days, or gives charity of a faraq of food. The faraq is three sa's, each sa' being four mudd, so one gives two mudd to each poor person.

Ata' said: one feeds ten poor people.

As for His saying: ﴿So when you are secure, whoever performs Tamattu' by the 'Umrah until the Hajj﴾: Ibn al-Zubayr said: Tamattu' is restricted to the one who was prevented, because of His saying: ﴿when you are secure﴾. But the majority of the Companions held that it is permissible in general for everyone.
