Then the school of the people of Madinah and of Kufa holds that Tamattu' is: that one enters ihram for 'Umrah in the months of Hajj, ﴿then whoever cannot find (an offering) must fast three days during the Hajj and seven when you return; those are ten complete. That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque. And fear Allah and know that Allah is severe in punishment⁠﴾, and then remains in Makkah and performs Hajj in that same year.

It is called Tamattu' because one enjoys (yastamti'u) the prohibited things after exiting the state of ihram from the 'Umrah until one enters ihram for the Hajj.

Tawus said: Tamattu' is not restricted to the months of Hajj; rather, if one enters ihram for 'Umrah outside the months of Hajj, one is a Mutamatti'.

As for His saying: ﴿then what is feasible of the offering﴾, that is: slaughtering a sheep.

As for His saying: ﴿then whoever cannot find (an offering) must fast three days during the Hajj﴾, this means that one fasts one day before the Tarwiyah, the day of Tarwiyah, and the day of 'Arafah. It is permissible to fast the three days separately.

Ibn Umar and Aisha said: one fasts the three days of Mina, which are the days of Tashriq. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i in his earlier opinion (al-Qadim).

As for His saying: ﴿and seven when you return﴾, Ibn Umar said: its meaning is when you return to your families.

The sound view is that it is when one wishes to return from Hajj, so that if one fasts the seven on the road, it is permissible. It is also permissible to fast them separately.

As for His saying: ﴿those are ten complete﴾: if someone says: it is not unclear that three and seven are ten, so why did He say: "those are ten complete"? We say: it was said that He said it for emphasis. Similar to it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

*"Three and two, then they are five,*
*and a sixth inclining toward a dash of mixture."*

This is because the Arabs did not have the skill of arithmetic, and they needed additional explanation and further clarification.

(﴿196﴾) ﴿The Hajj is in known months, so whoever undertakes Hajj in them, there is no obscenity, no wickedness, and no disputing⁠﴾

It is authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The month is like this, and like this, and like this," and he folded his thumb at the third time. He pointed to them with his fingers so that they would know the count.

It was also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, meaning: the fasting of ten days, three days in the Hajj and seven when you return. It was said: He said that only to cut off the suspicion of addition, for His saying "three days in the Hajj and seven when you return" might suggest "and five when you do such-and-such," and the like. So He said: "those are ten," to cut off the suspicion of addition.

As for His saying: ﴿complete﴾, that means complete in reward. It was said: complete in what is intended by it, and the fasting takes the place of the offering.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾. Some of the Companions said: by "those present at the Sacred Mosque" He meant the people of Makkah. Ibn Abbas used to say: "O people of Makkah, there is no Tamattu' for you; Tamattu' is only for the strangers (ghuraba')."

It was also said: they are all the people of the Haram. Al-Shafi'i said: everyone who lives in Makkah at a distance less than the distance of shortening the prayer (masafat al-qasr) is among those present at the Sacred Mosque.

﴿And fear Allah﴾, that is: in performing the commands. ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ for committing the prohibitions.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 197:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months.﴾ Most scholars hold that what is meant by it is Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah.

Malik said: all of Dhu al-Hijjah. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever undertakes the Hajj in them﴾ — Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud said: He meant by it, "whoever undertakes the Hajj in them by pronouncing the talbiyah." That is: whoever recites the talbiyah.

﴿...there shall be no lewd speech, no wickedness, and no quarrelling during the Hajj. Whatever good you do, Allah knows it. And take provision, but the best provision is taqwa (God-consciousness). So fear Me, O people of understanding.﴾

According to us, entering into ihram for Hajj is restricted to the months of Hajj, whereas according to Abu Hanifah it is permissible throughout the entire year. There is a disagreement among the Companions on this, and it is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿there shall be no rafath﴾ — it was said: it is intercourse (al-wat'). It was also said: rafath is obscene speech.

It was also said: it is to allude to matters of intercourse with women, such as by saying, "When we come out of ihram, we will do such-and-such." It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that when he was in ihram he recited:

(They walk with us in gentle steps... If the bird gives good omen, we shall lie with them.)

He was asked: "Do you engage in rafath while you are in ihram?" He said: "Rafath is what is said to women in their presence," that is, what is mentioned in their company.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and no wickedness (fusuq)﴾ — fusuq is abuse. It was also said: it is every sin.

His saying: ﴿and no quarrelling (jidal) during the Hajj﴾ — Ibn Mas'ud said: jidal is when a man disputes with his companion until he angers him.

It was also said: He meant by it what the people of the Jahiliyyah had of disagreement regarding the matter of Hajj, to the point that some of them would stand at 'Arafah and others at Muzdalifah, and some would perform Hajj in Dhu al-Qa'dah and others in Dhu al-Hijjah, and each would say, "What I did is correct." So He said: ﴿there shall be no quarrelling during the Hajj﴾, meaning: the matter of Hajj has been settled upon what the Messenger did, so there is no disagreement about it after that. This is the meaning of his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed, time has returned to its original form..." — the hadith.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾ — that is, it is not hidden from Him, nor will He waste it, but rather He will reward for it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And take provision﴾ — it was revealed concerning a people from Yemen who used to set out for Hajj without provisions and would ask people for food, and sometimes their situation would lead them to plundering and robbery. So He said: ﴿And take provision﴾, that is: set out with provisions.

His saying: ﴿but the best provision is taqwa﴾ — meaning: (that which protects) from plundering and begging.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Take provisions of ka'k and sawiq (barley porridge)."

Someone else said: "Take provisions of khushknanaj and sawiq."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So fear Me, O people of understanding﴾ — its meaning is well known.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 198:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾. Concerning the occasion of revelation of this there are two accounts. The first: what is related from Abu Umamah al-Taymi, who said: I said to Ibn Umar: "We hire out (camels) on this route," meaning to Makkah, "and people say: 'You have no hajj.'" Ibn Umar said: "Do you not stand (at 'Arafat)? Do you not run (between al-Safa and al-Marwah)? Do you not circumambulate (the Ka'bah)?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then you have a hajj." And Ibn Umar related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about that, and he did not answer with anything until Jibril descended with this verse.

The second: Ibn Abbas said: "In the Jahiliyyah there were markets called 'Ukaz, al-Majannah, and Dhu'l-Majaz, and the people of the Jahiliyyah would trade in them. When Islam came, the Muslims would feel uneasy about trading in those markets, so there was revealed His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾," meaning: by trading in those markets.

Ibn al-Zubayr recited: "fadlan min rabbikum fi mawasim al-hajj" (seeking bounty from your Lord during the seasons of the hajj).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when you pour forth from 'Arafat﴾. As for 'Arafat, it was so named because Jibril, when he stood with Ibrahim, would say to him: "Have you recognized (ʿarafta)?" and he would say: "I have recognized (ʿarafta)."

And al-ifadah (pouring forth) is pushing off in large numbers. It is said: "fada al-ina'" (the vessel overflowed) when it becomes full until it flows from its sides. From this comes "rajul fayyad" (a generous man) when he is abundant in giving. The poet said:

(And a fair, overflowing one, whose hands are a cloud over those who seek him, whose gifts never cease.)

He said ﴿when you pour forth﴾ only because some of them push others in large numbers during the return.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram﴾. Al-Mash'ar al-Haram, al-Muzdalifah, and al-Jam' are names of one place. Al-mash'ar means the landmark, for al-Muzdalifah is a landmark for spending the night, standing, supplication, and the combining of the two prayers. It was named "al-Jam'" (the gathering) only because the two prayers, maghrib and 'isha', are combined there.

It was named "Muzdalifah" from al-izdilaf, which is gathering together. Muzdalifah is a place between two mountains, one of which is called Quzah, upon which the Imam stands. It is part of the sacred area (al-haram), and for this reason it is called al-Mash'ar al-Haram.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, that is: remember Him with monotheism and magnification, just as He has mentioned you with guidance.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, before it, you were among the astray﴾. It is said: the meaning is "you were not but among the astray before it." It is also said: the meaning is "you had indeed been among the astray before it."

The Exalted's words: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾ meaning: from 'Arafat.

If it is asked: how does He say "then" (thumma), a particle of sequence (ta'qib), when departing from 'Arafat occurs before arriving at Muzdalifah? We say: "then" here has the meaning of "and" (waw), meaning: "and depart." It is like His words: ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾, meaning: "and he was among those who believed," so that it combines the two rulings.

It is also said that its implied meaning is: "Then He commanded you to depart from 'Arafat." This is like the Exalted's words: ﴿then We gave Musa the Book﴾ (though He gave him the Book before Muhammad, but its meaning is: "then I inform you that We gave Musa the Book"). Likewise here, so the function of "then" applies to the command, not to the departure.

As for the meaning: it is said that Quraysh and their allies used to stand at Muzdalifah and say: "We are the people of God's sacred precinct (haram), so we will not leave God's sacred precinct." For 'Arafat was in the outer area (hill), whereas the rest of the Arabs used to stand at 'Arafat.

So His words ﴿then depart﴾ are addressed to Quraysh, meaning: stand at 'Arafat, and depart from it ﴿from where the people depart﴾, meaning: the rest of the Arabs.

It is also said that by "the people" in His words ﴿from where the people depart﴾ He meant Abraham, and a single person may be called "people" (nas), as the Exalted said: ﴿those to whom the people said﴾, and by it He meant Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i alone.

Al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited ﴿from where the people depart﴾, meaning: Adam, peace be upon him.

The Exalted's words: ﴿And seek forgiveness from God; indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 200:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾, meaning: when you have finished the rites (manasik), and that is at the stoning of the Jamrat al-'Aqabah and settling in Mina. And His saying: ﴿then remember God as you remember your fathers﴾, meaning: remember God with takbir (saying "Allahu akbar"), glorification (tamjid), and praise of Him.

Regarding His saying: ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾, there are two opinions. 'Ata' said: it is that a child, when he first begins to speak, only babbles with the mention of his father, saying "Ya abati" (O my father), and mentions no one else. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Remember God﴾, not other than Him, ﴿as you remember your fathers, or with greater remembrance﴾.

The second: it is that the Arabs, when they finished the Hajj, would mention the glorious deeds of their fathers. So He, exalted is He, said: {Remember God instead of your remembrance of your fathers, or with greater remembrance}.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾, He meant by it: the polytheists. They would not ask God during the Hajj except for worldly things, and a man among them would say: "O God, indeed my father was great in tent-pole, large in cooking-pot, abundant in wealth; O God, give me the like of what You gave him."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and he has no share in the Hereafter﴾, meaning: no portion (nasib).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 201:

The words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good."﴾ He meant by this the Muslims, and they differed regarding its meaning.

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: ﴿In this world good﴾ means knowledge and worship, and ﴿in the Hereafter good﴾ means Paradise.

It is related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: ﴿In this world good﴾ is the righteous wife, and ﴿in the Hereafter good﴾ is Paradise.

And it has been reported in a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever is given a grateful heart, a remembering tongue, and a righteous wife who helps him in matters of his religion, has been granted the good of this world and the Hereafter."

Qatadah said: ﴿In this world good﴾ means well-being (al-ʿafiyah), and ﴿in the Hereafter good﴾ means the outcome (al-ʿaqibah).

It is narrated from Anas, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he visited a sick man whom illness had worn down until he became like a young bird. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "What were you supplicating with?" The man said: "I said, 'O Allah, if You are going to punish me for something in the Hereafter, then hasten it for me in this world.'" He said: "Glory be to Allah! You cannot bear that. Why did you not say: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾?" It is said that this was the most frequent supplication of the Messenger of Allah.

As for the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, meaning: turn away from us the punishment of the Fire.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 202:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾, i.e., the response (to their supplication) ﴿from what they have earned﴾ from the supplication. ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning﴾. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: He reckons with the servants more swiftly than the blink of an eye.

The people of ma'ani (the science of meanings) said: He reckons with the servants without deliberation or seeing, because He is knowing of what belongs to the servants and what is upon them, so He has no need to see (them).

Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is that Allah brings the Resurrection soon, for what is certain to occur is near, so in it there is an indication of the nearness of the Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 203:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember God during the appointed days﴾, meaning: the days of Mina, which are the days of tashriq (the days of tashriq, the three days after the Day of Sacrifice). Ibn 'Umar said: "The known days (al-ayyam al-ma'lumat) and the counted days (al-ayyam al-ma'dudat) are four days: the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) and the two days after it are the known days, and the three days after the Day of Sacrifice are the counted days."

Al-ma'dudat means "those that are counted (al-muhsiyat)." He only said this because of their small number. The remembrance meant here is the takbirs after the prescribed prayers.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, he intended by it: departing on the second day of the days of tashriq, meaning: whoever hastens to depart by returning from Mina on it, there is no blame upon him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾, meaning: whoever delays the second departure to the third day of the days of tashriq, there is no blame upon him.

If it is said: the verse refers to the one who returns after completing the rites, so how is blame negated from him when he is in a position of deserving reward and not a position of blame? We say: Ibn Mas'ud said: what is intended by it is that whoever [is free] from blame has returned forgiven. This is supported by the hadith, and what is related with a raised chain: "Whoever performs this House's pilgrimage and does not engage in obscenity nor commit wrongdoing, returns as on the day his mother bore him."

Al-Nakha'i said its meaning is: whoever hastens, there is no sin upon him for the hastening, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him for the delay.

There is also a third view: he only said that because some of them would add to their stay at Mina beyond three days out of piety and seeking nearness (to God). So God, may He be exalted, said: whoever returns on the second or third day and does not add beyond three days, there is no blame upon him, meaning: in leaving off the addition.

There is also a fourth view, which is good: its meaning is: whoever takes the concession of hastening, there is no sin upon him for taking the concession, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him for forgoing the concession. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) had encouraged the concession by his saying: "Indeed God loves that His concessions be taken, just as He loves that His obligations be fulfilled."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For him who fears (God)﴾. Abu al-'Aliya said: its meaning is: for him who fears God after the Hajj throughout his whole life.

The others said: its meaning is: for him who avoids sins during the Hajj. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fear God, and know that you will be gathered unto Him﴾, its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 204:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the worldly life pleases you﴾. The verse was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, an ally of the Banu Zuhra. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "I love you, and I want to believe in you, and Allah knows what is in my heart." He was concealing his hatred, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was pleased by his speech and delighted in it. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the worldly life pleases you﴾, meaning, openly.

As for His words: ﴿and calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾, Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa-shahid Allah 'ala ma fi qalbihi" (and a witness is Allah concerning what is in his heart). Ibn Muhaysin read: "wa-yushhidu Allah 'ala ma fi qalbihi" (the same as the standard reading). These two are among the irregular readings (shadh), and the well-known reading is the first.

As for His words: ﴿And he is the most contentious of opponents﴾, meaning: intensely quarrelsome. The poet said:

(Indeed beneath the dust are resolve and generosity... and an opponent most contentious, one who is stubborn.)

Mujahid said: ﴿most contentious of opponents﴾ means: the unjust one in disputation.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 205:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein﴾. Concerning him, the verse was also revealed. For he went out from the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), saw a donkey and hamstrung it, and passed by a field of crops and burned it. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein, and destroys the crops and the offspring﴾. So al-ḥarth (the crops) means the sown produce, and al-nasl (the offspring) means the young of every animal.

﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾, i.e., He does not approve of corruption. It has also been said that among corruption is breaking a dirham and tearing a garment without any benefit.

Almost all of the passage is translatable as given. I'll render it now.

God Almighty says: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride in sin seizes him.﴾ This verse was also revealed concerning him. ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride seizes him﴾, meaning: the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance (ḥamiyyat al-jāhiliyyah). ﴿Pride in sin﴾, meaning: in injustice. And ʿizzah (pride) means arrogance and self-protection, and from this is God's words: ﴿in arrogance and opposition﴾.

It is related from Ibn Masʿud, who said: It is enough of a sin for a person that it be said to him, "Fear God," and he replies, "You are the one who commands me to piety."

It is also narrated that it was said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him: "Fear God." So he placed his cheek upon the ground, in humility before God.

In another narration, it was said to ʿUmar, "Fear God," and al-Mughirah ibn Shuʿbah denounced the one who said it. ʿUmar said: "You will not cease to be in good as long as they say that to us, and we accept it from them."

As for God's words: ﴿Then Hell is sufficient for him﴾, meaning: it is enough for him. Imru' al-Qays said:

(And you fill our house with curds and clarified butter... and sufficient for you of wealth is satiety and drink.)

As for God's words: ﴿And how evil is the resting place﴾: al-mihad means every bed upon which a person settles.

The words of His Exalted saying: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "The verse was revealed concerning Suhayb ibn Sinan. He left Makkah as a emigrant (muhajir) to Madinah, and the polytheists pursued him and caught up with him. He emptied his kinanah (quiver) and said: 'You know that I am among the best of you at archery. By Allah, you will not reach me until I have shot all that is in my quiver. Then I will take my sword and strike until I am unable, or until you turn back from me. My wealth is not with me there.' They said: 'Where is your wealth?' He showed them where it was, and they turned back from him. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of that, he said: 'The sale has profited, O Abu Yahya.'" This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾, that is, sells.

Al-shira' (the word for "purchase") means sale, and from it is the saying of the poet:

(And I sold Bardan, would that I had not... after Bard I became a skull [sarat hamah])

A man had a slave named Bardan, and he was infatuated with him. He sold him and then regretted it.

And His saying: ﴿And Allah is Compassionate toward the servants﴾, that is, Most intensely merciful toward them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 208:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, enter into Islam completely﴾. "Believed" means: they affirmed the truth.

"Enter into Islam completely" means: enter into Islam all together.

Al-Azhari said: al-silm means reconciliation (al-sulh), and al-silm also means submission (al-inqiyad), and what is meant by it here is Islam.

Al-Azhari also said: its meaning is: enter into Islam and its laws completely.

There is a third view regarding it, its meaning being: enter into Islam to the furthest extent of its laws, restraining yourselves from going beyond it to anything else, from al-kaff (restraint).

Ibn 'Abbas said: the verse was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Salam and a group of Jews who had embraced Islam, and they wanted to combine Islam and Judaism. They said: "We will keep the Sabbath, and we will not eat camel meat, and similar things," so the verse was revealed. That is: be devoted to Islam alone, do not combine it with Judaism, and restrain yourselves from going beyond it to anything else.

If someone asks: how did He address the believers with entering into Islam? It is said: its meaning may be steadfastness upon Islam, and it may be an address to those who professed faith with the tongue but had not believed in their hearts.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾. That is: the traces of Satan. The word khutuwat is the plural of khutwa (step), and the khutwa is the distance between the two feet. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 209:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then if you slip﴾. Zalla yazillu (زل يزل): when one goes astray and swerves from the path. And azalla yuzillu (أزل يزل): when one bestows a favour upon another. From this is his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever has been shown a favour, let him be thankful for it."

And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾: the manifest evidences.

﴿Then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾. Al-'Aziz (العزيز, the Mighty): the Overpowering, from whom nothing escapes. Al-Hakim (الحكيم, the Wise): the one who is correct in His command.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 210:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels?﴾ And the verse is among the mutashabihat (the ambiguous verses whose meaning is not clear from the apparent wording).

The people of hadith narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Mujahid that both of them said, in explaining the verse: Allah will come on the Day of Resurrection in canopies of clouds.

As for Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Naqqash, the exegete, he did not address the verse with anything. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse may be understood linguistically as: Allah will come with what He promised them of punishment.

The Shaykh, the Imam, said: The preferable course regarding this verse and what resembles it is that we affirm its apparent meaning, entrust its knowledge to Allah, the Exalted, and declare Allah, glorified and exalted be He, free from the attributes of createdness (hadath) and deficiency (naqs).

As for His saying ﴿in canopies﴾, it is the plural of ẓull (canopy), which is a covering of clouds. We have already mentioned the meaning of ghamam (clouds).

﴿And the angels﴾ has been recited with both the nominative (raf') and the genitive (khafd). When it is recited in the nominative, it is coordinated with Allah (i.e. the subject of the verb). When it is recited in the genitive, it is coordinated with ẓulal (canopies).

﴿And the matter is decided﴾ means: the affair is finished, and that is Allah's final judgment with truth among the creatures.

﴿And to Allah are all matters returned﴾ Qatrub said: It was specified for the Day of Resurrection only because the affair will be entirely Allah's on that day, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 211:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾ is an address to the Messenger, meaning: ask those among them who embraced Islam. ﴿How many clear signs have We given them?﴾ That is, how many clear proofs of the prophethood of Musa (Moses).

It has also been said that its meaning is: the proofs that were given to them in the Torah and the Injil (Gospel) concerning the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And whoever substitutes the favour of Allah after it has come to him, indeed Allah is severe in penalty.﴾ Regarding its meaning there are two opinions:

The first: whoever changes the covenant of Allah.

The second: its meaning is, whoever denies the proof that points to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

**Verse 2:212:** ﴿Adorned for those who disbelieve is the life of this world﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The one who adorns is Satan, for Allah the Exalted has made people disinterested in this world and has encouraged them toward the Hereafter. Most scholars said: The one who adorns is Allah the Exalted. The adornment from Allah is that He created good things and pleasing sights, so people looked at them far more than they deserved, which pleased them and led them into temptation; [therefore] the adornment is from Allah.

﴿And they mock those who believe﴾, meaning they ridicule them. These were the leaders of Quraysh, such as Abu Jahl and others, and they used to mock the poor.

Ibn 'Abbas said: By those who believe he meant 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ammar ibn Yasir, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, and Abu Dharr.

﴿But those who fear Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, because these poor believers are in the highest 'Illiyyin, while those others are in the lowest depths of the lowest.

﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾. There are several views on this. The first: He grants abundance to whom He wills without restriction or constraint.

The second view: its meaning is that He does not take anything from a fixed measure. It is like a servant who takes a thousand out of two thousand and is then given a portion of his due, fearing that his wealth will be diminished. But Allah provides for His servants from His treasuries, which never run out.

The third: its meaning is that He restricts whom He wills and expands for whom He wills, and He does not give each person according to his need. Rather, He gives much to one who does not need it, and gives little to one who does.

The fourth view: Ibn 'Abbas said: This refers to what Allah made easy for His Messenger from ﴿they differed concerning it, except those who were given it after clear proofs had come to them, out of envy among themselves; so Allah guided those who believed to the truth﴾ [2:213], namely the seizure of Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir in the easiest manner, without fighting or hardship.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 213:

And His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾. Now, "ummah" (community) in the language has several meanings. Among them: ummah in the sense of religion (dīn), and from this is the saying of al-Nābigha:

(I swore, and I did not leave for you any doubt... and does one who has a religion (dhū ummah) sin while he is obedient?)

That is, one who has a religion (dhū dīn).

Ummah also means a group of people and others. So the Turks are an ummah, the Romans are an ummah, the Persians are an ummah, and among birds are ummahs. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And there is no creature that moves on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you﴾.

Ummah also means a period of time, and God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And he remembered after a period (ummah)﴾, that is, after a time.

Ummah also means a leader who is followed, and from this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a community (ummah)﴾.

Ummah also means one who teaches goodness. Ummah also means stature, and from this is the saying of the poet:

(And indeed Mu'awiyah, the most noble... fair of faces, tall of statures)

Ummah with a kasra on the alif (ʾimmah) means blessing (niʿmah), and the intended meaning of ummah here is religion.

That is: mankind was upon one religion, then they differed concerning its meaning.

Some of them said, and this is the view of Mujāhid, that it refers to Adam, who was one community.

It was said, and this is the view of Qatādah and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, that it refers to twenty generations of the children of Adam, and Noah and they were upon Islam.

It was said: it refers to the people in the time of Abraham, who were upon the religion of disbelief.

﴿So God sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book with truth, that it might judge between people concerning that about which they differed﴾.

If someone says: how can the Book judge? It is said: ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī recited "li-yaḥkuma bayn al-nās" with a ḍammah on the yā', so that the judging is by the prophets.

As for His saying ﴿li-yaḥkuma bayn al-nās﴾, it means: that those who were given the Book, from among the prophets, might judge.

And His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And none differed concerning it except those who were given it﴾, meaning: those who were given the Book. ﴿After clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves﴾, that is, out of envy and injustice. ﴿So God guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed, by His permission﴾. Zayd ibn Aslam said: they differed concerning the qiblah, and God guided us to the Kaʿbah; they differed concerning the days, so the Jews chose Saturday and the Christians Sunday, and God guided us to Friday; they differed concerning ʿĪsā, so some of them said he was a liar, and some of them said he was the son of God, and God guided us to his being a prophet and a servant; they differed concerning Abraham, and every sect claimed him, and God guided us to his being a ḥanīf and a Muslim.

And it is narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "We are the last (in order) and the first (in standing) on the Day of Resurrection, and the first of people to enter Paradise, although they were given the Book before us and we were given it after them. People are followers of us: today is ours, that is, Friday; tomorrow is for the Jews, and the day after tomorrow for the Christians."

﴿And God guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 214:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise﴾.

It was revealed concerning the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) to Medina, when a fierce heat and great poverty afflicted them, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse, to console their hearts and to comfort them.

As for His saying, "Am" (أم, "or"), it is a word used to move from one speech to another, and it carries the meaning of "bal" (بل, "rather"). Allah the Exalted says to them: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the like of those who passed away before you?﴾, meaning: and there has not befallen you what befell them. His saying, ﴿the like of those who passed away﴾, means: the description of those who passed away. ﴿Before you, misfortune and hardship touched them﴾: al-ba's' (البأساء, "misfortune") is poverty, and ﴿ad-darra'* (الضراء, "hardship") is sickness. ﴿And they were shaken﴾: they were moved violently and frightened. ﴿Until the Messenger and those who believed with him said: "When will the help of Allah come?"﴾: to the point that they grew impatient for the help of Allah. ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾

They ask you what they should spend. Say: whatever good you spend is for parents and close relatives.

It was said: what is meant is the bequest that was obligatory at the beginning, for parents and close relatives.

It was also said: what is meant is voluntary acts of charity, which are to be given to parents, close relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil).

And it was said: this was at the beginning, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by the verse on zakat.

﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾ That is: He counts it and will reward it. This is like His saying, ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾, meaning he will see the reward for the deed, because the deed is gone and so he does not see it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 216:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Fighting is prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you﴾, meaning: it is burdensome for you.

Know that most of the scholars hold that jihad is a collective obligation (fard kifayah). ʿAtaʾ said, and it is the view of al-Thawri, that it is a voluntary act (taṭawwuʿ). They said: the verse concerns those among the Companions who were ordered to fight.

﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing﴾, meaning: fighting, ﴿and it is good for you﴾, through attaining martyrdom, acquiring booty, and victory over the enemy.

(And it may be that you love a thing), meaning: sitting back from fighting, ﴿and it is bad for you﴾, through the loss of ranks (al-manazil). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "I was riding behind the Messenger of Allah, and he said to me: 'O boy, be content with what Allah has decreed for you; for it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you,' and he recited this verse: ﴿And Allah knows while you do not know﴾."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 217:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it.﴾ That is: "about fighting in it," (the phrase) being in the genitive by way of substitution (badal). ﴿Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin)﴾, meaning grave. Then he began (a new clause) and said: ﴿and barring from the way of Allah﴾, meaning: your barring of the Muslims from Islam.

﴿and disbelief in Him﴾, that is: your disbelief in Allah. ﴿and (barring from) al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, that is: and your barring of the Muslims from al-Masjid al-Haram.

﴿and expelling its people from it﴾, that is: expelling the people of Makkah from Makkah. ﴿are greater in the sight of Allah, and persecution is worse than killing﴾, that is: the disbelief in which you are, and those deeds of yours, are greater in the sight of Allah and more severe than fighting the Muslims in the sacred month.

ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: The occasion of revelation of the verse is what has been related: that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent ʿAbdullah ibn Jahsh with eight men toward Makkah, and gave them a letter and said: "Do not open it except after two days." When two days had passed, they opened the letter, and in it was: "Proceed to Batn al-Nakhl, which is a place between Makkah and al-Ta'if, and there gather information about the Quraysh." They halted there, and they were gathering information secretly. A caravan from al-Ta'if passed by them, carrying raisins and leather, and ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami was among them. One of the Muslims shot him and killed him, and they led the caravan to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). That occurred on the last day of Jumada al-Akhirah, or on the first day of Rajab, and they were uncertain about it. The polytheists reproached them for killing Ibn al-Hadrami in the sacred month, and then the verse was revealed.

That is: the deeds you have committed are greater and more severe than their killing in the sacred month.

And in a report: the Prophet (ﷺ) did not put his hand to anything of that caravan until the verse was revealed, and then he divided it among the Muslims.

﴿They will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able.﴾ That is: the polytheists were fighting the Muslims and reproaching them for Islam.

﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire, therein they will abide forever.﴾

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the way of Allah﴾. This verse is connected in meaning to the previous one, and the reason is that when Abdullah ibn Jahsh passed by the expedition (al-sariyya) and the one who killed Ibn al-Hadrami was among those who killed him, the polytheists said: "If they have not incurred sin, then they will not attain good." So this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾, meaning Abdullah ibn Jahsh and his companions, ﴿and those who emigrated﴾ from their homelands, ﴿and strove﴾, meaning through raiding, ﴿in the way of Allah﴾. ﴿Those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾. He informed that they are in hope of mercy. They did not decide for themselves that they would receive mercy, because a person knows from himself that he cannot fulfil the right of Allah the Exalted in the proper manner, so he is not safe from shortcoming; therefore he cannot be certain for himself of mercy.

(﴿218﴾) ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.﴾

And because he may, in the future, commit something that deserves punishment.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Al-Ghafur: the Concealer (al-sattar). Al-Rahim: the Compassionate (al-'atuf).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 219:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling.﴾ As for khamr (wine), it is every intoxicating drink, and intoxicants are called khamr because they cover (yukhamir) the intellect and conceal it.

The root meaning of khamr is covering and concealment. From it comes khimar (head-covering), because it covers the head. It is also said: "So-and-so entered among the people's khimar," meaning he hid himself among them.

ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Khamr is that which covers the intellect." This is the proof of the people of hadith that every intoxicant is khamr. From this it is said of a drunkard, whatever the drink, that he is makhmur (intoxicated).

As for maysir (gambling), it is qimar (games of chance). Ibn Masʿud said: "Leave the knucklebones (kiʿab), for they are part of maysir."

Ibn Sirin said: "Whatever is played with is maysir, even the walnut with which children play." Then the scholars differed over which verse prohibited khamr.

Some said: it is by this verse, for He said: ﴿Say: In them is great sin﴾, and the word "sin" (ithm) indicates prohibition. For He prohibited khamr with the word "sin" in another verse, where He said: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin (ithm)﴾, and by it He meant khamr. From this is the saying of the poet:

(I drank sin until my intellect went astray… thus does sin take away the intellects.)

Ibn ʿAbbas and most of the commentators said: the prohibition of khamr is by the verse in Surat al-Ma'idah. When this verse was revealed, ﴿Say: In them is great sin﴾, some refrained and some did not. Then He revealed: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾, so they would wait for times to drink, until a man would drink after the final evening prayer and wake in the morning with the intoxication gone, and drink again after the dawn prayer and become sober by the time of noon. Then the verse of al-Ma'idah was revealed. Ibn ʿUmar said: "Khamr was prohibited by the verse of the hundred" (i.e., the verse of al-Ma'idah, 5:90–91), and he narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "The prohibition of khamr is by the verse of al-Ma'idah."

It is also reported from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that when he heard His words: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾, he said: "We have desisted, our Lord."

﴿Say: In them is great sin.﴾ Ḥamzah and al-Kisa'i read kathir with the thaʾ (ثير), and the rest read kabir with the bāʾ. So kabir means "great," and kathir means "abundant," because of the abundance of sins in khamr mentioned in the verse of al-Ma'idah: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you﴾, and the rest of the verse.

As for His words: ﴿and benefits for people﴾, the sin in khamr is what occurs in it of enmity, hatred, and turning people away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer.

As for the benefits in khamr: pleasure, joy, enjoyment of food (istimra' al-ta'am), and profit in trading it.

Ḥassan ibn Thabit said, about khamr and its benefit:

(We drink it, and it leaves us lions and lionesses, and battle does not weaken us.)

Another said:

(When I am drunk, I am lord of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadir; and when I am sober, I am lord of the sheep and the camel.)

As for the benefit for people in gambling: it is the acquisition of wealth in it without toil or exertion.

Its sin: when a man's wealth is lost in it without any return he receives, it grieves him, so he becomes hostile to his companion and intends harm toward him.

As for His words: ﴿and their sin is greater than their benefit﴾, it is said: its meaning is: their sin after the prohibition is greater than their benefit before the prohibition.

It is also said: their sin is greater than their benefit before the prohibition, meaning: the sin that khamr becomes the cause of, of enmity and disorderly conduct, is greater than their benefit.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus.﴾ Abu ʿAmr alone read al-ʿafw with a ḍammah on the waw, and the rest read it with a fatḥah. Whoever reads with ḍammah, his construction is: "What is it that they spend?" and he answered: "Say: that which they spend is the surplus." Whoever reads with fatḥah, his construction is: "What should they spend?" and he answered: "Say: they spend the surplus." They differed over the meaning of al-ʿafw. Ṭawus said: it is the little of every thing. Most of the commentators said: al-ʿafw is the excess, because charity is only obligatory on what is in excess of need. The Companions used to earn wealth, keep what was needed for expenses, and give away the excess, by the ruling of this verse; then that was abrogated by the verse of zakat.

It is also said its meaning is: charity from a position of independence (ʿan ẓahr al-ghina), that one gives while he is wealthy, and does not give while he is poor, so that he remains a burden on people. This is the meaning of His words: "The best charity is that given from a position of independence."

The essential meaning of al-ʿafw is what is easy (al-maysur). From it is His words: ﴿Take what is easy﴾, meaning: what is easy of the characters of men.

﴿Thus does Allah make the signs clear to you, that you may reflect.﴾

(In) this world and the Hereafter. There is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, and its implied meaning is: Allah makes the signs clear to you concerning this world and the Hereafter, so that you may reflect upon this world and the Hereafter; thus you will recognize the superiority of the Hereafter over this world, and you will renounce this world and spend out of desire for the Hereafter.

And His Exalted saying: ﴿And they ask you about the orphans.﴾ It is related that when the saying of the Exalted was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies﴾, the Muslims became extremely scrupulous regarding the property of orphans, to the extent that they separated the orphans' property from their own in terms of pasture, food, and condiments. So this verse was revealed permitting mixing with them in all of that; but on condition that if one employs the orphan's servant, he should have him serve, and if he eats from the orphan's food, he should replace it.

Mujahid said: He may be generous with his own food, but he should not be generous with the orphan's food.

And His Exalted saying: ﴿Say: Reforming them is good.﴾ Al-Dahhak read: "Qul islah ilayhim khayr" (Say: Reforming toward them is good), while the recited reading is: "Qul islah lahum" (Say: Reforming for them). Its meaning: reforming them is good for you in religion. ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ — this is the permission of mixing.

﴿And Allah knows the corrupter﴾, meaning: one who mixes and betrays, ﴿from the reformer﴾, who is one who mixes without intending betrayal. ﴿And if Allah willed, He would have put you in difficulty﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: He would have destroyed you. Ibn 'Abbas said: He would make what you have taken from the orphans' property a ruin for you. It was also said: its meaning is: And if Allah willed, He would not have permitted you to mix with them.

The people of linguistics said: al-'anat (difficulty) is hardship. Its meaning: ﴿And if Allah willed, He would have put you in difficulty﴾, i.e., He would have obligated you in everything with what is hard upon you.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ As for al-'Aziz: He is the One who commands with might; He makes it easy for the servants or does not make it easy. As for al-Hakim, we have already mentioned its meaning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 221:

Allah's words: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: marrying disbelieving women is never permissible, until the Day of Resurrection, by the ruling of this verse.

All the other exegetes and the scholars among the Companions and others hold that the verse is abrogated (mansukh, superseded) with regard to the women of the People of the Book, by His words: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Book﴾.

It is narrated from ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, that he married Nailah bint al-Farafisah, who was a Christian, and she embraced Islam while married to him. It is also narrated from Talhah ibn ʿUbaydullah that he married a Christian woman, and from Huthaifah that he married a Jewish woman. Qatadah and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: by "polytheistic women" He meant idolatresses (wathaniyyat).

If someone says: "You consider all disbelievers to be polytheists. How, then, is one who denies only the prophethood of Muhammad a polytheist with respect to Allah?"

We say: Abu al-Husayn ibn Faris, the author of al-Mujmal, said: he is a polytheist, because he says that the Qur'an which Muhammad brought is speech other than Allah's, whereas this Qur'an is miraculous and none could say it except one who is a god; so it is the speech of other than Allah. Thus they have associated with Allah something other than Allah.

As for the occasion of revelation of the verse: it is narrated that Abu Murthad al-Ghanawi had a beloved woman in Makkah, whom he used to have illicit relations with, and she was called ʿAnaq. When he emigrated to Madinah and embraced Islam, she desired a certain need from him, so he returned to Makkah. She adorned herself for him, and Abu Murthad said: "I have entered the religion of Islam, and fornication is forbidden in my religion. But I will return and ask the Messenger of Allah for permission to marry you." He returned and asked permission, and then the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾.

As for His words: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist woman, even if she pleases you﴾, this was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Rawahah. He had a black slave-woman whom he slapped. Then he informed the Messenger of Allah of that, and the Prophet asked him about her. He said: "She is a believer; she believes in Allah and the messengers, and she performs wudu' well and prays." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "What you did was wrong." He said: "By Allah, I will certainly marry her," so he freed her and married her. A free polytheist woman had been proposed to him, but the polytheists reproached him for marrying the black slave-woman, so the revelation came: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist woman, even if she pleases you﴾.

﴿And do not marry polytheistic men until they believe﴾: in this there is consensus that a Muslim woman may not be married to any polytheist at all. ﴿And a believing slave is better than a polytheist, even if he pleases you﴾. If someone says: "How does He say ﴿better than a polytheist﴾ when there is no good in a polytheist?" It is said: such usage is permissible, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾ And it is said: returning to the truth is better than persisting in falsehood.

﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾, i.e., to the causes of the Fire. ﴿But Allah invites to the Garden and forgiveness by His leave﴾, i.e., by His decree and His will. ﴿And He makes His signs clear to the people, that they may remember﴾.

**The Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 2, Verse 222**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about menstruation.﴾ As for the questioner about it, he was Usayd ibn Hudayr and Abbad ibn Bishr. As for al-mahid (menstruation), it is a noun of place from *al-hayd* (the menstrual flow), and what is meant by it is the menstruation itself.

Al-Azhari said: It is said, "The woman menstruated (*haydan* and *mahidan*) when blood came down to her from the womb at a known time."

And it is said: "The woman was afflicted with *istihadah* (irregular bleeding) when blood came down to her from a vein, not from the womb, and not at a known time."

﴿Say: It is a harm (*adha*)﴾, meaning: filth (*qadhar*). Al-Kalbi said: *Al-adha* is the blood.

﴿So keep away from women during menstruation (*al-mahid*)﴾. The occasion of revelation of this verse is what was related from Anas: The Jews used to separate themselves from the woman during her menstruation with the utmost separation. They would not eat with her, nor drink with her, and they would expel her from the house. So they asked the Messenger of Allah about that, and the verse was revealed.

But by this separation, what they used to do was not intended. Rather, it was intended as separation by abstaining from intercourse, until lying together and all other kinds of physical contact become permissible.

It has been related from the Prophet that he said: "Do everything except intercourse."

There is another opinion on this: that one may do everything but avoid what is beneath the waist-wrapper (*izar*), which is the area between the navel and the knee. This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

﴿And do not approach them﴾: by this approaching is meant intercourse, for approaching them without intercourse is permissible. ﴿Until they are purified (*yathurna*)﴾ is read with a light (*takhfif*) pronunciation, and what is meant by it is: until they are purified from menstruation. The people of Kufa other than Hafs read *hatta yatthahharna* with a doubled letter (*tashdid*).

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, read *hatta yatatahharna* as an irregular reading (*shadh*).

The phrase ﴿yathurna﴾ means *yatatahharna*, except that the *ta'* has been assimilated into the *ta'* (*idgham*). Its meaning is: until they perform ghusl (wash the whole body).

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: The word ﴿yathurna﴾, read with the light pronunciation, may mean ghusl, from the act of purification.

All of these are evidence for al-Shafi'i regarding the obligation of ghusl, since [permitting intercourse] extends the prohibition to it.

The words ﴿So when they have purified themselves﴾ mean: when they have performed ghusl. ﴿Then come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. The first: its meaning is, from where Allah has commanded you to avoid during menstruation. The second, which is the view of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, means: from where Allah has permitted, and that is by way of marriage.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves.﴾ It has been said: Its meaning is: those who repent from sins, and those who purify themselves from defects.

The second opinion: the meaning of "those who are constantly repentant" is those who return to Allah in repentance and seeking forgiveness, and the meaning of "those who purify themselves" is those who disavow their own power and strength.

There is a third opinion: that "those who are constantly repentant" means those who turn in repentance, and "those who purify themselves" means those who cleanse themselves with water (*istinja'*) after using stones.

This is like the words of the Exalted: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾, meaning: those who purify themselves by cleansing with water after using stones.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 223:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾, meaning: a place of tilling for you and a field of sowing. The poet has said:

"When the locusts eat the crops of a people, my tilth is the sustenance of the locusts."

He called dependents "tilth" (ḥarth). Recited by al-Mubarrad.

﴿So go to your tilth however you wish﴾. The occasion of revelation of this: what Jabir narrated, that the Jews said: whoever comes to his wife from behind, the child will be born cross-eyed. So this verse was revealed.

﴿So go to your tilth however you wish﴾, meaning: facing or from behind, standing or sitting, and however you wish.

It is also said: its meaning is: whenever you wish.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of His words ﴿however you wish﴾ is: if you wish, practise withdrawal ('azl), and if you wish, do not practise withdrawal.

The Shaykh said: Know that the verse does not indicate the permissibility of approaching women in other than the place of approach, because He said: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth﴾, thereby restricting the approach to the place of tilling, which is the front.

Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he used to permit approaching a woman from behind. They denied this against Nafi', and said: the slave lied against his master, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, for he never permitted it at all. This is also related from Malik, and his companions denied it.

It has been reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "Indeed Allah is not shy of the truth; do not approach women in their rear passages."

From Ibn 'Abbas that he said: it is the greater sodomy (al-lūṭiyya al-kubrā). And he said regarding withdrawal: it is the lesser burying alive (al-mawʾūdah al-ṣughrā).

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And send forward for yourselves﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is saying the Name (tasmiya) at intercourse. It is also said: it is seeking offspring. It is also said: all acts of goodness.

﴿And fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him﴾, i.e., you will return to Him. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, O Muhammad.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 224:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle (ʿurḍah) for your oaths﴾. The verse was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Rawahah. He had a son-in-law (khatan) through his daughter, and he swore that he would not do him any kindness. When it was said to him, "Will you not visit your son-in-law?" he said, "I have sworn." He was one of his relatives, so the verse was revealed. ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths that you would be righteous﴾.

Al-ʿurḍah: everything that stands in the way and prevents something. Its meaning: do not make swearing by Allah a cause that prevents you from righteousness (al-birr) and piety (al-taqwa).

It was said: its meaning is: do not multiply oaths, for whoever multiplies his oaths has made the name of Allah an object of disrespect (lil-hatk).

There is another opinion concerning it: its meaning is: "And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths that you would not be righteous," with "not" (lā) being elided. This is like the words of the poet:

(So the oath of Allah said, "I will not leave off sitting," even if my head and my joints are cut off before you.)

That is: "I will not leave off sitting."

﴿And that you would be mindful of Allah, and make peace among the people. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 225:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths﴾. Al-laghw (that which is cast off, useless) is every discarded element of speech. There are five opinions regarding its meaning here:

The first is the saying of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The oath of laghw is a man's saying: 'No, by Allah,' 'Yes, by Allah,' and 'Yes indeed, by Allah.'" This is the view of al-Shafiʿi.

The second is the saying of Abu Hurayra and Ibn ʿAbbas: it is that a man swears about something that he did, claiming he did it when he did not, or the reverse. This is the view of Abu Hanifa. Al-Shaʿbi said: it is the oath made in a state of anger. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: it is swearing by the prohibition of what is lawful.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is that a man says: "May Allah blind my sight, or destroy my wealth, if I do not do such-and-such." This is the oath of laghw, and Allah does not hold one accountable for it; and if people were held accountable for it, He would have hastened their punishment.

The most correct view is that of ʿĀʾisha, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿But He holds you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾. The earning of the heart is the intention of the heart toward the oath. Thus it is shown that the oath of laghw is that which the heart does not intend.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving﴾, that is, Concealing, ﴿Forbearing﴾, who is the One who does not hasten punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 226:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months﴾. The alya (al-ala', "oath") is the oath. Likewise, the iyla' (ila', "vow of abstinence") is the same, as the poet said:

(Few are his oaths, and he guards his oath... and even if an oath slips from him, he fulfils it.)

So His saying, ﴿those who swear off [yu'lun]﴾, means: those who take oaths. Ibn 'Abbas said: The iyla' is only valid when one swears to abstain from intercourse permanently and without restriction. The position of Abu Hanifa is that the iyla' is valid by swearing to abstain for four months. The position of al-Shafi'i is that one becomes a mu'li (one who has made an iyla') only by swearing to abstain for four months, and this is ﴿a waiting period of four months﴾, meaning: a waiting of four months.

﴿And if they return [fa'u]﴾, meaning: if they go back on the oath by resuming intercourse, with regard to one who is able to have intercourse, or by speech, with regard to one who is not able to have intercourse, ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "fa-in fa'u fihinna" (if they return within them), meaning within the period. This agrees with the view of Abu Hanifa.

﴿And if they resolve on divorce﴾, meaning: by pronouncing it, ﴿then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, hearing the husband's words and knowing what he conceals.

The school of al-Shafi'i (Shafi'i school) holds that return (al-fay'a) is permissible after the period has elapsed, by delaying until he returns, meaning: he divorces, and this is ﴿the divorce, then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing (227) and divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods, and not﴾. This is narrated from 'Umar, 'Ali, and Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with them all.

Abu Hanifa held that she is divorced with one irrevocable divorce (talaqa ba'ina) upon the expiry of the period. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Ibn Mas'ud, and 'Ali, in a weak narration. The matter is discussed in the book of disputed questions (al-khilafiyyat).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 228:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the divorced women﴾, meaning: the women who have been released (al-mukhallayat). It is said: "aṭlaqa al-asīr" and "aṭlaqa al-baʿīr" when he released them (khallāhu).

﴿shall wait by themselves for three quru'﴾ (qurū'): "yatarabbaṣna" means they wait. The qur' (qurū') is the purity (ṭuhr), and this is the view of the people of the Ḥijāz.

Al-Zuhrī said: No one from the people of the Ḥijāz said that al-aqrā' are menstruation (ḥiyaḍ) except Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab.

The position of Abū Ḥanīfa is that al-aqrā' are menstruation, and this is narrated from ʿUmar, ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, and it is the view of the people of Kufa.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: al-qurʾ is a term that applies to menstruation, and applies to purity, and is also used with their meanings.

The root of al-qurʾ is "al-jamʿ" (gathering). It is said: it is derived from al-qurʾ in the sense of "the time," as in: "aqrat al-riyāḥ" when the winds blew at their time; and "qaraʾat al-nujūm" when they set; and it can mean "ṭalaʿat" (rose) at a known time.

They recited, for al-qurū' in the sense of the periods of purity, the verse of al-Aʿshā:

"Do you every year undertake a raid, whose final destination is pressed by your resolute hardships?
Bequeathing wealth, while in the tribe there is rank, for what was lost in it of your women's qurū'."

What is lost during travel is the time of purity, not the time of menstruation, because those are a loss (of time).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs﴾, meaning: of menstruation and pregnancy.

Qatādah said: Allah knew that among women there would be liars: a woman says "I have menstruated" when she has not menstruated, "I have become pure" when she has not become pure, and "I am pregnant" when she is not pregnant.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿if they believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying "if they believe in Allah," when the ruling for the disbelieving woman is the same as for the believing woman? It is answered: its meaning is that this is an act of believing women, as one says: "If you are a believer, then pay my right," meaning: it is an act of believers to fulfill rights. And His saying ﴿and their husbands﴾, meaning: their spouses, ﴿have more right to take them back﴾, meaning: to reconciliation (raj'ah) ﴿in that﴾, meaning: in that period. ﴿if they desire reconciliation﴾: its meaning is: if they intend by the reconciliation goodness and good companionship, and their intention is not harm, as they used to do in the Jāhiliyyah. A man among them would divorce his wife, then take her back when her waiting period was about to end, then divorce her, then take her back again in this manner, intending to prolong the waiting period over her.

﴿And they have rights similar to those upon them according to what is reasonable﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said regarding its meaning: "I love to adorn myself for my wife just as my wife loves to adorn herself for me, because Allah Exalted says: ﴿And they have rights similar to those upon them according to what is reasonable﴾." There is another view regarding it, meaning: the man must guard her rights just as the woman must guard his rights, meaning: from what is forbidden.

﴿And the men have a degree over them﴾. Mujāhid said: by jihad and inheritance. It is said: it means in divorce, because divorce is in the hands of men. Ḥumayd said: by the beard.

﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾, meaning: Unassailable.

(﴿Either retain them in kindness or release them with good treatment. And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them, except when both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah. But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon either of them concerning that by which she ransoms herself﴾, Wise.)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 229:

Allah's statement: ﴿Divorce is twice; then either keep (them) in honour or release (them) with kindness﴾. ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr said: "In the beginning, people would divorce without limit or number. A man would divorce his wife, and when her waiting period (ʿiddah) was nearly over, he would take her back. Then he would divorce her again in the same way, and take her back again, and he would say: 'I will never let you remarry.' So this verse was revealed: ﴿Divorce is twice﴾." He means: the divorce after which the husband may take her back is twice.

﴿Then either keep (them) in honour﴾ is taking her back (al-rajʿah). It was also said: it is keeping her after taking her back for companionship. His words ﴿in honour﴾ mean everything recognized in the Sharia as the fulfilment of the rights of marriage and good companionship. ﴿Or release (them) with kindness﴾ means that he leaves her after the divorce until her waiting period ends.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: "Where is the third divorce?" He said: "Or release (them) with kindness."

The words "release" (tasrih) and "separation" (firaq) are explicit (sarih) terms, like "divorce" (talaq), according to al-Shafiʿi.

Abu Hanifa said: the explicit term is one word only, which is "divorce" (talaq).

Allah's statement: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them﴾ means: by seizure and injustice. This is like His statement in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿And if you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take from it anything. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾

Allah's statement: ﴿Unless they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ means: taking is only permissible when the wish for khulʿ (divorce by compensation) arises and the fear is present.

His words ﴿unless they both fear﴾ are read with a fatha on the yāʾ, which is the well-known reading. Al-Aʿmash and Hamzah read "unless they both fear" with a ḍammah on the yāʾ. Ibn Masʿud read "unless you (plural) fear."

As for the first reading, it refers to the spouses. As for Ibn Masʿud's reading, it is addressed to the rulers and judges.

As for Hamzah's reading, it was said: he intended to take into account the meaning of Ibn Masʿud's reading, and its meaning is: unless the spouses fear, [and the rulers and judges know]. They said: he was not correct.

They differed about the meaning of this fear. Abu ʿUbaydah, the imam of language, said: "fear" here means knowledge.

Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: it is in its true sense of fear, meaning: unless the suspicion of fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah prevails.

There is a third view: that fear here means suspicion (ẓann). The poet said:

(A speech came to me from Nusayb, which he says,
And I did not fear, O Salam, that you would blame me.)

That is: I did not suppose.

Allah's statement: ﴿And if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon them for what she gives up to be released﴾, meaning: for what she ransoms herself with. They differed about khulʿ.

Tawus and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: the permissibility of khulʿ is restricted to a situation of fear of disobedience (nushuz), holding to the apparent meaning of the verse.

Al-Zuhri said: the permissibility of khulʿ is restricted to the amount of dowry she gave him, so that it is not permitted to exceed it. Al-Hasan said: khulʿ is only permissible for the rulers and judges, holding to the apparent meaning of the verse.

Most scholars hold that khulʿ is permissible in every situation and for any amount agreed upon by the spouses and others.

The verse came in accordance with the custom that khulʿ usually takes place in a situation of fear of disobedience, and it is better that khulʿ be carried out in a situation of disobedience and for an amount equal to the dowry.

Allah's statement: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾, meaning: do not go beyond them. The limits of Allah are everything the Sharia has forbidden to exceed.

Allah's statement: ﴿And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, then it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾. The apparent meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 230:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that﴾ refers to the third divorce. Its ruling is the prohibition of the marriage contract until a second husband is found. Then, the making lawful (tahlil) for the first husband is achieved only by the marriage contract and the consummation together, according to the view of most of the scholars.

It is related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and it is said: from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that it is achieved by the mere marriage contract, in accordance with the apparent wording of the verse. This has been counted among the anomalous (shawadh) views of disagreement.

The evidence for the correctness of the first view is what is related: that the wife of Rifa'ah al-Qurazi came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Rifa'ah divorced me, and after him I married 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr, but with him is only like the fringe of a garment." He (ﷺ) said: "Do you wish to return to Rifa'ah? No, not until you taste his honey and he tastes yours." The Sunnah thus indicates the condition of consummation, and this report is sound.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until she marries another husband﴾, here "nikah" carries the meaning of consummation, and it may also carry the meaning of the contract. ﴿So if he divorces her﴾ means the second husband. ﴿There is no blame on either of them if they return to each other﴾, and by "return" here he intended the renewal of the marriage contract with the first husband.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿if they think they can keep within the limits of Allah﴾ means: if they both know that there will be goodness between them and good companionship.

His saying: ﴿And these are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear to a people who know﴾, meaning: who know what Allah has commanded.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 231:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term﴾, meaning: they approach the end of the term, as it is said: "I reached the dwelling" when one has come close to it.

And His saying: ﴿then retain them in kindness﴾, meaning: take them back in a reasonable manner.

﴿Or release them in kindness﴾, or leave them until the waiting period (iddah) ends.

﴿And do not retain them to harm them so that you transgress﴾, meaning: do not intend by taking them back to harm the woman, as they used to do. ﴿And whoever does that has wronged himself﴾, meaning: he harms himself, not anyone else.

(And do not take the signs of God in jest.) ʿĀʾisha said, and this is the more correct view: it is the prohibition against intending harm by taking back (the wife). For whoever opposes the command of the Shariʿa has taken the signs of God in jest. Abu al-Darda', and this is also the view of al-Hasan, said: it refers to a man among them who would divorce [his wife], then say: "I was not serious," and free [a slave], then say: "I was not serious, I was joking."

There is a third view: that it forbids exceeding the number of the three divorces.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember the favour of God upon you﴾. ʿAṭāʾ said: He meant by it the favour of Islam.

﴿And what He has sent down to you of the Book﴾, meaning: the Qur'an, ﴿and the wisdom﴾, meaning: the Sunnah.

﴿He instructs you thereby﴾, meaning: guides you with it. ﴿And fear God and know that God is Knowledgeable of all things.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 232:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term﴾. By reaching the term in this verse he meant the complete expiry of the waiting period ('iddah).

The Almighty's saying: ﴿then do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾. Al-'adl (prevention) means restraint.

Al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) said: It is said, "a hen (dajaj) is mu'dal (obstructed)" when an egg becomes lodged inside her and she is unable to come out, because of the narrowness of the exit. From this comes "al-da' al-'udal" (the incurable disease), which is one whose treatment cannot be borne.

It is related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The people of Kufa have 'a'dal me (overwhelmed me)", meaning: they constrained me and placed me in a severe matter.

Most scholars and exegetes hold that this is addressed to the guardians (awliya'), forbidding them from refusing to marry.

Al-Shafi'i said: "This is clear, that it is evidence that a woman does not conclude a marriage contract herself."

The verse was revealed concerning Ma'qil ibn Yasar al-Muzani, for he had married his sister to a man, who divorced her and left her until her waiting period expired. Then he came to propose to her along with the other suitors, and the woman was inclined toward him. Ma'qil said: "I married my sister to you rather than anyone else, and the noblemen of my people proposed to her and I chose you! I divorced her; I will never marry her to you again." So the verse was revealed.

There is another opinion: that it is addressed to the husbands, because the beginning of the verse is addressed to them.

The prevention by the husbands is what we mentioned, that they should divorce, then take her back, then divorce again. The first (view) is more correct.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿when they agree among themselves in a reasonable manner﴾. ﴿This is an admonition for whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾. He specified them only because admonition has effect only on believers.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿That is more virtuous for you and purer﴾. "More virtuous for you" means better for you, and "purer" means more wholesome. ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 233:

His saying, exalted is He: (And mothers shall breastfeed their children) — this is a report with the meaning of a command.

﴿for two full years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing.⁠﴾

So "the two years" is the period of nursing. If someone says: why did He say "full"?

It is said: because "the two years" may be applied to a year and part of a second year, as in His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾, where "months" is applied to two months and part of a third. So He said "full" to make clear that He meant the complete two years. It is also said that He said it for emphasis.

It is related that a woman bore a child after six months from the time of her marriage, and her husband came to ʿUthman about this. ʿUthman intended to stone her, but ʿAli said: "You have no authority over her, for God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning is thirty months﴾, and He says: ﴿And mothers shall breastfeed their children for two full years﴾. So when the weaning is two years, six months remain for the pregnancy." So ʿUthman left her alone and averted the hadd punishment.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon the one to whom the child is born⁠﴾ means: the husband, the father of the child. ﴿their provision and their clothing according to what is customary⁠﴾, and that is the maintenance for the period of nursing. ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity⁠﴾, that is, except according to its ability. ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity. No mother shall be harmed through her child, nor a father through his child. And upon the heir is the like of that. And if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them. And if you wish to have your children nursed by a wet nurse...⁠﴾ — meaning: upon the wealthy according to his means, and upon the poor according to his capacity.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No mother shall be harmed through her child⁠﴾ is read with a fatha on the rā'. Abu ʿAmr and others read it with a ḍamma on the rā'. Aban [ʿan] ʿAsim read: "lā tuḍārir" (with doubled rā'), and it is among the irregular readings. As for the one who reads with a fatha on the rā', its meaning is: the woman should not be harmed through her child — that is, the father should not snatch her child from her and hand it over to someone else while she is willing to nurse.

It is possible that its meaning is: the mother should not harm her child by leaving it to someone else and refusing to nurse. The one who reads with a ḍamma (raf') also has this meaning, and this is the meaning of the third reading.
