His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor a father through his child⁠﴾ means the father should not harm his child by handing it over to someone other than the mother.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that⁠﴾. ʿUmar said: he meant by it that upon those other than the parents is the like of that maintenance. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, for he obliges maintenance of relatives upon brothers and paternal uncles.

The second view: he meant by "the like of that" the abstention from harm. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, who did not hold maintenance to be due from anyone other than the parents. This is the position of Malik and al-Shafiʿi.

There is also a third view: by "the heir" he meant the child, and upon him is his maintenance from his own property, if he has property.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they both desire weaning⁠﴾, that is, before the two years. ﴿by mutual consent from both of them⁠﴾, meaning from both parents, ﴿and consultation⁠﴾, that is, they consult people of knowledge about it until they report that weaning at that time does not harm the child. Mushawara (consultation) means extracting an opinion.

It is said: ʿUmar rode a horse to test it (yushawiruhu), that is, to extract its pace, and it stumbled under him. So he brought the matter before Shurayh, who ruled against him, making him liable for compensation. He said: "I rode it only to test it." So he appointed him as judge, and he judged for seventy years afterward.

His saying: ﴿then there is no blame upon them⁠﴾, that is, there is no fault in weaning before the completion of the two years.

His saying: ﴿And if you wish to have your children nursed⁠﴾, that is, to hire a wet nurse for your children, with the preposition omitted. Its meaning is: to have nursing done for your children.

His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon you when you hand over what you gave, according to what is customary⁠﴾.

It is read: "ātaytum" with a long alif, and it is read: "ataytum" without it. The meaning of the first is: when you hand over to the mother, and "what you gave" means what you stipulated for her as the wage of nursing, in proportion to what she nursed. It is also possible that it means handing over to the hired nurse her wage for nursing.

As for the one who reads "ataytum", its meaning is: when you hand over what you brought, according to what is customary, that is, when you submit to His command and comply with His ruling in the good you have done. ﴿And fear God, and know that God is seeing of what you do.⁠﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 234:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And those of you who are taken in death﴾. He recited to me: "yatawaffawna" with a fatha on the yā', and its meaning is: they complete their lifespans. The well-known reading has a ḍamma on the yā', and its meaning is: those who die, and their terms are completed. ﴿and leave behind wives﴾, that is: and leave behind wives. What is meant by "azwāj" (spouses) here is wives.

﴿They shall wait﴾, meaning they shall refrain, ﴿with themselves for four months and ten [days]﴾. The verse concerns the waiting period (ʿiddah) for death, and it is fixed at four months and ten days by the consensus of the community, based on the explicit text of the Book.

It has been said: that period was fixed for a wisdom, namely that the child moves in the womb of the pregnant woman for half the duration of pregnancy, and four months and ten days is close to half the duration of pregnancy.

Irtikāḍ (movement of the child in the womb) means motion. It is said: "a woman is murkaḍah" when something moves in her belly. The poet said:

(And a woman who moves, her father is a noble, / the boy and the girl are humbled for her sake.)

As for His statement, ﴿ten﴾, it refers to nights; it is said "ten days and ten nights," and nights are specified because every term begins at night.

Al-Mubarrad said: he meant by it ten periods, each period being a day and a night.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then when they have reached their term﴾, that is: their ʿiddah has ended.

﴿there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in an honourable manner﴾, meaning: for what they do of choosing husbands without a marriage contract, since the contract belongs to the guardian (walī).

It has been said: its meaning is regarding what they adorn themselves with for the husbands, an adornment that the Sharīʿah does not reject. ﴿And fear Allah, and know that Allah is well-Aware of what you do.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 235:

God the Exalted says: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you hint at in proposing to women﴾. Allusion (ta'ridh) to a proposal of marriage during the waiting period ('idda) is permissible. The word khutba here means the proposal of marriage (khutbat al-'aqd). It is said: khataba yakhtubu khutba, when he proposed the contract. And khataba yakhtubu khutba, when he addressed the people with a speech of known beginning and end.

The form of allusion to a proposal is that he says to the woman: "Indeed you are beautiful, and indeed you are noble to me, and indeed I am desirous of women," or "What God decrees will come to pass," and similar words. This is not objectionable with regard to the woman in the waiting period. But an explicit proposal is not permitted.

Mujahid said: It is that he says: "Do not outrun me with marriage," or he says: "Do not let yourself slip away from yourself," or "I will propose to you when you are free, then I will marry you," and similar words.

﴿But do not make promises to them in secret, except that you say a fair saying. And do not resolve on the tie of marriage until the prescribed term reaches its end. And know that God knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him. And know that God is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾.

It is said: this is permitted with the guardian (wali), by his saying to him: "Do not outrun me with marriage," and similar words.

What is not permitted is explicit proposal to the woman herself. The evidence for the permissibility of allusion to a proposal is what is related: that Sakina bint Handhala was widowed from her husband, and Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir entered upon her and said: "You know my kinship to the Messenger of God, my kinship to 'Ali, my right in Islam, and my honour among the Arabs." Sakina said: "Do you propose to me while I am in the waiting period, and you are who you are?" meaning: "From you is knowledge taken?!" He said: "I did not propose to you, but I mentioned my standing."

Then it is related that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered upon Umm Salama while she was in the waiting period for her husband Abu Salama, and he (peace be upon him) mentioned his honour with God and his station with God, and he would mention that and lean upon his hands until the mat left its mark on his hands." All of this is allusion to a proposal, and the hadith indicates its permissibility.

God the Exalted's words: ﴿Or you conceal it within yourselves﴾, meaning: you hide within yourselves the matter of marriage. ﴿God knows that you will remember them﴾, meaning: in your souls. ﴿But do not make promises to them in secret, except that you say a fair saying﴾. Regarding the meaning of this "secret" there are several views, the soundest of which is that it is taking a pledge of marriage from them, which the Law forbids during the waiting period.

It is also said: the "secret" is fornication (zina). It is said: it is intercourse (wat'). Imru' al-Qays said:

(Has it not been claimed to Basbasa today that I have grown old, and that one like me does not do well at secret [intercourse]?)

meaning: copulation. Al-Shafi'i said: God's words "do not make promises to them in secret" mean that he describes himself with abundance of intercourse, in order to make her desire his marriage.

God the Exalted's words: ﴿except that you say a fair saying﴾ refer to what we have mentioned of permitted allusion.

His words: ﴿And do not resolve on the tie of marriage﴾, meaning: do not firmly resolve upon concluding the marriage contract during the waiting period. ﴿until the prescribed term reaches its end﴾, meaning: the prescription of the Book, because the waiting period is an obligation of the Book.

﴿And know that God knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him﴾: this is a warning against what He has forbidden them. ﴿And know that God is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 236:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them an obligatory payment (farida)﴾. Its implied meaning is: "and you have not touched them, and you have not specified for them an obligatory payment."

This verse concerns the divorced woman before the specifying of a dower (fard) and before consummation (masis). The verse is evidence for the permissibility of concluding a marriage without naming the dower (mahr). It is also evidence for the obligation of a consolatory gift (mut'a) in general, since He says: ﴿and provide for them﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said concerning the mut'a: "The highest of it is a servant, the middle of it is silver (warq), and the lowest of it is a garment for clothing." Al-Shafi'i said: "It is preferred that the mut'a be from twenty to thirty dirhams. In general, it is left to the discretion of the rulers, so that each person is required to determine what he sees fit: ﴿upon the wealthy according to his means and upon the poor according to his means, a provision according to what is reasonable, a duty upon the doers of good﴾."

Al-Sharh said: This is guidance and a recommendation toward giving provision, and he (al-Shafi'i) did not consider the mut'a obligatory. The rest of the scholars held that the mut'a is obligatory. The position of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, is that every divorced woman has a mut'a.

Ibn 'Umar said: Every divorced woman has a mut'a, except the one for whom her husband specified a dower and divorced her before consummation; for her, half of the specified amount suffices. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

There is also a third opinion: that it is obligatory only for the one for whom no dower was specified and who was divorced before consummation.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 237:

And His Exalted saying: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already specified for them a bridal gift, then half of what you have specified﴾. This verse concerns the divorced woman after the specifying of the dower and before consummation; she is owed half of the named dower at the time of divorce before intercourse.

﴿Unless they forgo﴾. This refers to the wives. It is said: taʿfū (they forgo, feminine singular), taʿfuwān (feminine dual), yaʿfuna (feminine plural). The meaning of the woman's forgoing (ʿafw) is the bounty of waiving the half that is owed to her.

﴿Or he in whose hand is the marriage tie (ʿuqdat al-nikah) forgoes﴾. ʿAli said, and this is the view of Shurayh and al-Shaʿbi, that what is meant by it is the husband, and his forgoing is the bounty of giving the full dower.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: He intended by it the guardian (al-wali), and this is more fitting to the composition of the verse, and he held it permissible for the guardian to release the woman from her dower.

There is a third view: that it refers specifically to the father of a virgin, and that he has the right to forgo the dower of his daughter as long as she is a virgin.

The fatwa is that the guardian has no share at all in forgoing, and the verse concerns the husband, as ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said.

﴿And that you forgo is nearer to piety﴾. The address is to everyone. ﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾, i.e., the bounties of some of you upon others. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 238:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾. It is a command to guard all the times (of prayer).

As for the middle prayer, there are seven opinions concerning it. The first: ʿUmar, ʿAli, Abu Hurayra, Abu Ayyub and ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with them all, said it is the ʿAsr prayer, because it is the middle of the two prayers of the night and the two prayers of the day.

It is related from Hafsa that she said to the scribe of her codex: "When you reach His saying, ﴿Guard strictly the prayers﴾, inform me." When he reached it, he informed her, and she said: "Write: ﴿and the middle prayer, the ʿAsr prayer﴾."

The report is authentically transmitted from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said on the day of the Trench: "They kept us busy from the middle prayer, the ʿAsr prayer. May Allah fill their bellies and their graves with fire."

The second opinion, which is the saying of Zayd ibn Thabit, is that it is the Dhuhr prayer, because it is the middle of the day.

The third opinion, which is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar and Jabir, is that it is the Subh (dawn) prayer. This is the choice of al-Shafiʿi, because it is the middle of the two prayers of the night and the two prayers of the day.

Beyond this there are four rare opinions. The first, said by Qabisa ibn Dhuʾayb, is that it is the Maghrib prayer, because it is the middle in the number of rakʿas.

The second, the saying of Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib and al-Rabiʿ ibn Khuthaym, is that it is every one of the five prayers, because each of the five prayers is a middle between four. Its being singled out after the mention of the prayers is for emphasis and encouragement to guard all the prayers.

The third opinion: it is Friday prayer.

The fourth opinion: it is congregational prayer.

Scholars differ on whether the Subh prayer belongs to the night prayers or the day prayers.

The majority of scholars hold that it belongs to the day prayers.

Some said that it belongs to the night prayers. This disagreement goes back to whether the day begins at dawn (fajr) or at sunrise (tuluʿ al-shams).

Whoever says the day begins at dawn makes the Subh prayer one of the day prayers.

Whoever says the day begins at sunrise makes it one of the night prayers. The proponent of this view cited the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

(And the sun rises every final night... red, its color dawning and reddening.)

Ibn al-Anbari said: there is pure night, pure day, and what is shared between night and day. So the Maghrib and ʿIsha prayers are in pure night, the Dhuhr and ʿAsr prayers are in pure day, and the Subh prayer is shared between night and day.

There is another opinion, which is the preferred one: it is night linguistically and day in the sacred law (shar').

His saying: ﴿And stand before Allah in devotion﴾ means: obedient and silent.

This is because speech was permitted in prayer at the beginning; when this verse was revealed, they fell silent.

The reciter in prayer is silent from speech. The school of al-Shafiʿi holds that if someone swears not to speak and then recites the Qur'an, he does not break his oath, because it is the speech of Allah, not his own speech.

In contrast to Abu Hanifa, who said: he breaks it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 239:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if you fear, then on foot or riding﴾. This refers to the prayer of fear: they pray on foot or mounted.

And His saying: ﴿So when you are secure, remember Allah as He taught you what you did not know﴾. That is: as He taught you of the essence of the prayer in a state of security.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 240:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind—a bequest for their wives﴾. It is read with a fatha (wasiyyatan, in the accusative), and its implied sense is: "Let them make a bequest (awsaw wasiyyatan)." It is also read with a damma (wasiyyatun, in the nominative), and its implied sense is: "There is incumbent upon you a bequest (alaykum wasiyyatun)." This [ruling] appeared at the beginning of Islam, when the waiting period for death (al-'idda li'l-wafat) was a full year, and the maintenance of the wife for the entire year was obligatory upon the husband. It was therefore incumbent upon him to bequeath maintenance for them if he died. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿a bequest for their wives: provision for a year without eviction﴾, that is, maintenance for a year.

As for His words ﴿without eviction (ghayra ikhraj)﴾: it was forbidden for the heir to expel the woman observing the waiting period from the house before the year was complete. However, if she left of her own accord, her maintenance lapsed. This was abrogated (nusikha dhalika) by the verse of the waiting period for death, as has already been mentioned. That verse, although it comes earlier in the recitation, is later in meaning, and it abrogates this verse.

It was said to Uthman: "Why do you not place that verse in the position of this verse, and this one in the position of that?" He said: "I dislike altering the Qur'an from its place."

As for His words, may He be exalted: ﴿If they leave, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves of what is reasonable﴾, it refers to what we have mentioned, after the completion of the waiting period.

As for His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾, its meaning is evident.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 241:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for divorced women is a provision in accordance with what is acceptable﴾. He repeated the mention of provision (mut'ah) for emphasis.

The occasion of revelation of the verse: it is narrated that when they heard His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿a provision in accordance with what is acceptable, a duty upon the doers of good﴾, they said: "If we wish, we will give provision, and if we wish, we will not give provision." So this verse was revealed.

﴿And for divorced women is a provision in accordance with what is acceptable﴾, that is: the provision belongs to them as a possession; He made it theirs by the lam of ownership (lam al-tamlik). And His saying, ﴿a duty upon the righteous﴾, means: obligatory upon the believers.

Allah's saying: ﴿Thus does Allah make His verses clear to you﴾ — because He had mentioned before many verses and rulings, so He meant by it that (the preceding ones). And His saying: ﴿so that you may reason﴾ means: that you may understand and comprehend.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 243:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: They were four thousand. Another said: They were eight thousand. Al-Suddi said: They were [some] thirty thousand. In a narration from Ibn Jurayj: forty thousand. Ibn Duraid said: "Uluf" means "mu'talifah," that is, their hearts were united. The sound view is that what is meant by it is the number, as we have explained.

His saying: ﴿Then Allah said to them, "Die," and then He brought them to life.﴾ That is, Allah caused them to die, and then He brought them to life. This (concerns) a people from the Children of Israel who fled from the plague and said: "We will go to a land where there is no plague." So they went, and Allah the Exalted caused them to die there, and they remained dead for seven days in that state. Then a prophet called Ezekiel (Hizqil) passed by them, and he supplicated to Allah the Exalted, and He brought them back to life. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: Allah the Exalted caused them to die before their appointed terms as a punishment for them, then He brought them to life so that they might complete their appointed terms.

In the narratives (al-qasas) it is related that after He brought them back to life, the scent of death would be found on them, and likewise on their descendants. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ it has been said: this is general regarding all people in the world. And it has been said: it is specific regarding the believers. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿but most of mankind are not grateful﴾ as for the disbelievers, they are not grateful.

As for [the believers], they have not attained the utmost degree of gratitude.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 244:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾. It is said that the address is to the Companions. The meaning in it is that those people, when they fled from death, fleeing did not benefit them until death overtook them. So do not sit back from fighting out of fear of death; rather, strive and fight in the way of Allah.

It is also said: the address is to those people from the Children of Israel, for they only sat back from fighting; so Allah caused them to die, then brought them back to life, and commanded them to fight.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 245:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a good loan?﴾ Al-qard (qarḍ) is cutting. From it comes al-miqrad (miqrāḍ, scissors), and the loan is called qarḍ because the lender cuts off a portion of his wealth in order to be repaid for it, or to have its like returned to him.

Labid said:

(And when you are repaid a loan, then repay it; for it is only the young man who repays, not the camels.)

If it is said: How can lending be from Allah, exalted is He? It is said: its meaning is that one lends to the prophets of Allah. Al-Dahhak said: its meaning is that one gives charity for the sake of Allah, and it is called a loan because Allah, exalted is He, has promised reward for it.

His words: ﴿a good loan﴾ mean: lawful (ḥalāl). It is also said: "good" means that his soul is content with it.

His words: ﴿so He will multiply it for him many times over﴾ are recited in several readings: "fayuḍā'ifahu" with a ḍammah on the fa', following His words ﴿yuqriḍu﴾.

It was also read: "fayuḍā'afahu" with a fatḥah on the fa', in the accusative as an answer to the interrogative (the question).  It is also read "fayuḍ'ifahu" with the yā', and read with the nūn: "fanuḍ'ifahu."

Taḍ'īf (doubling) and muḍā'afah (multiplying) have one meaning. Ḍi'f (multiple) is everything that exceeds the like.

His words: ﴿manifold increases﴾ — al-Suddi said: "many, whose number none knows except Allah."

Others said: seven hundredfold.

His words: ﴿And Allah straitens and expands﴾ — concerning this there are four views. [First]: al-Hasan said: He straitens by restriction and expands by widening.

al-Zajjaj said: He straitens by accepting the charity and expands by giving reward for it.

The third view: He straitens by shortening lifespans and expands by lengthening lifespans.

The fourth view: He straitens by prohibition and expands by permission.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ — its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 246:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs (al-Mala') of the Children of Israel after Moses?﴾ Al-Mala': the nobles (ashraf) of every people. In a report: "When the heads of the polytheists, such as Abu Jahl, 'Utbah and others, were killed on the day of Badr, a man from the Ansar said: 'We have only killed bald old women,' meaning: the young men of the people were old men (shuyukh). The Messenger of Allah disliked that and said: 'Those are the chiefs (al-Mala') of Quraysh. Had you seen them, you would have been in awe of them, and if they had commanded you, you would have obeyed them, and you would have belittled your deed alongside theirs.'"

And His words: ﴿When they said to a prophet of theirs: Raise up for us a king that we may fight in the way of Allah﴾. It was said: that prophet was Samuel (Ishmawil); it was also said he was Joshua son of Nun; and it was said he was Shim'un, and he was named so because Allah called him and he heard (sami'a). The story concerning this is that the enemy overcame the Children of Israel and took captive four hundred and forty men from among the sons of their kings, and they had refrained from fighting for four years. So they came to their prophet and said to him: Raise up for us a king upon whom our affair may be united, so that we may fight in the way of Allah.

And His words, the Exalted: ﴿He said: Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, not fight?﴾ The well-known recitation is with a fatha on the sin (ʿasaytum, pronounced with fatha). It was also recited with a kasra on the sin (ʿasiytum), and both are the same in meaning. The fatha is more correct.

And His words: ﴿If fighting is prescribed for you, you will not fight.﴾ The meaning of the verse: perhaps you will be cowardly about fighting, so you will not fight.

And His words: ﴿They said: What is [the matter] with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah?﴾ That is: what prevents us from fighting in the way of Allah? ﴿And we have been expelled from our homes﴾ because they had been expelled from Bayt al-Maqdis.

﴿And our sons﴾ meaning: we were expelled from our sons through captivity (al-sabi). The word "captivity" here has an implied element, and similar to it is the saying of the poet: "And I saw your wife in the battle, girded with a sword and a spear." That is: and carrying a spear.

And His words, the Exalted: ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a few of them. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾ By "the few" He meant those who were content with the handful (al-ghurfah) and crossed over with Talut, and it will come.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 247:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And their Prophet said to them, "Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut (Saul) as a king."﴾ It is said: he was a water-carrier who used to draw water and carry it on a donkey.

Talut was so named because of his tallness, for he was taller than everyone else by his head and shoulders.

It is also said: when a man among them raised his hands, they would reach his head, meaning the head of Talut.

As for His words: ﴿They said, "How can he have kingship over us, when we are more deserving of kingship than him?"﴾ That is, how can he have kingship over us when he is not from the tribe of prophethood or of kingship?

This is because the tribe of prophethood was the tribe of Levi ibn Ya'qub, which is the tribe of Musa ibn Imran, while the tribe of kingship was the tribe of Judah. Talut was from the tribe of Benjamin, and he belonged to neither the tribe of kingship nor of prophethood. That was because they had committed a great disobedience against Allah, so Allah removed from them prophethood and kingship, and they were called the tribe of sin.

As for His words: ﴿And he has not been given abundance of wealth﴾, that is because he was a water-carrier, as we have explained.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you."﴾ That is, He selected him over you.

As for His words: ﴿And has increased him broadly in knowledge and physique﴾: as for the increase in physique, it is well known.

As for knowledge: it is said that it refers to knowledge of warfare, and Talut was the most knowledgeable of them regarding matters of war. It is also said that it refers to knowledge of religion, but the first view is more sound.

As for His words: ﴿And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing﴾: "Al-Wasi'" is the One possessing abundance, who gives out of richness.

As for "Al-'Alim": it is said that al-'Alim and al-'Alim have the same meaning. Others distinguish between al-'Alim and al-'Alim, saying: al-'Alim refers to what has happened, and al-'Alim refers to what will happen.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 248:

Allah's words: ﴿And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the Ark will come to you."﴾ They asked him for a sign of the kingship, so their prophet informed them of the sign of his kingship, which is the coming of the Ark.

It is said: it is the Ark that was with Musa and Harun. The Children of Israel used to take it out to the battles and seek victory through it.

﴿In it is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind, carried by the angels.﴾

It is also said: it was made of shamshad wood, and it was three cubits by two cubits.

There is another view: it is the Ark that Allah sent down to Adam along with the Black Stone (al-Rukn), and in it were images of the prophets.

As for His words, ﴿in it is tranquility from your Lord﴾, 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The tranquility (al-sakinah) has a face like a human face, and it is a light wind that blows gently."

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a basin of gold in which the hearts of the prophets were washed. It is also said: it is a thing resembling a cat, with two eyes that have rays of light, and it has two wings of emerald and chrysolite. When they heard its voice, they were certain of victory. When they went out to war with the Ark, they would place it before them; if it moved forward they advanced, and if it stopped they halted.

Mujahid said: the tranquility is a sign by which they found calm.

As for His words, ﴿and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind﴾, this refers to the staff of Musa, his sandals, the turban of Harun, the fragments of the tablets that were broken, and a qafiz (measure) of the manna that was sent down upon the Children of Israel.

It is also said: by it He means the Torah, which was in the Ark. ﴿What the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind﴾ means Musa and Harun themselves. A similar usage is the words of the poet:

(So do not weep for a dead man after a dead man whom they buried... 'Ali and 'Abbas and the family of Abu Bakr)

That is, he buried him, meaning: and Abu Bakr.

As for His words, ﴿carried by the angels﴾, al-Hasan said: the Ark was with the angels in the heaven, and when Talut assumed the kingship, the angels carried the Ark and placed it among them.

It is also said: the 'Amalaqah (Amalekites) overcame the Ark and buried it, so Allah commanded the angels until they extracted it and carried it to them.

Ibn 'Abbas said: when the 'Amalaqah overcame the Ark, they were afflicted with the bubonic plague (al-basur), and they knew that this was a punishment upon them on account of the Ark. So they tied it to a cart, carried it on two bulls, and drove them to the desert and left it there. Then the angels came and drove it to the Children of Israel.

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾, its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 249:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿So when Talut set out with the troops﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: The number of the troops was eighty thousand.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: Indeed, Allah is going to test you with a river﴾. That was a river that lay between Jordan (Urdunn) and Palestine. Its meaning: Allah is going to try you by that river, in order to make manifest the one who has an intention and purpose in fighting, from the one who has no intention.

His statement: ﴿So whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾. Talut said it, meaning: he is not of the people of my allegiance and my companionship.

﴿And whoever does not taste it, indeed he is of me﴾. That is, whoever does not taste it. The poet said:

(If you wish, I will forbid women to all but you, and if you wish, I will not taste sweet water or cold drink.)

That is: I will not taste water or sleep. It is said: "al-bard" (cold) prevented "al-bard," meaning: the cold prevented sleep.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Except one who takes a handful with his hand﴾. It is read in two ways, with a fatha and with a damma on the ghayn (of ghurfa).

Al-ghurfa with a fatha on the ghayn means: one scoop. Al-ghurfa with a damma on the ghayn means: the full measure of the palm.

His statement: ﴿So they drank from it, except a few of them﴾. 'Ikrimah said: The number of the few who limited themselves to a handful was four thousand.

Most of the exegetes, and this is the more correct view, hold that they were three hundred and thirteen men.

Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: We used to say that the number of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the Battle of Badr, may Allah be pleased with them, was equal to the number of those who crossed with Talut, and they were three hundred and thirteen men. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: None crossed except a believer.

In the narratives: when they reached the river, Allah had cast thirst upon them, so all drank except this small number. Everyone among them who drank had his lips blackened and was not quenched, and remained on the bank; and everyone who limited himself to a handful was quenched and crossed over.

It is also said: all of them crossed, but some of them took part in the fighting and some did not.

His statement: ﴿So when he and those who believed with him had crossed it, they said: We have no power today against Jalut and his troops﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: It was said only by those who fell back and did not cross. It is also said: it was said by those among those who crossed whose insight in religion was weak, as opposed to those whose insight was strong.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who were certain that they would meet Allah said﴾. That is, those whose insight was strong.

﴿Who were certain﴾: they were certain that they would meet Allah. We have mentioned that "zann" (supposition) can mean certainty. It is also said: it is in its literal sense of supposition, meaning: those who expected to attain martyrdom in the encounter.

His statement: ﴿How many a small company has overcome a large company by the permission of Allah﴾: by His decree and management.

﴿And Allah is with the patient﴾: with victory and aid.

And His words: ﴿And when they went out against Jalut and his soldiers﴾: Jalut was the commander (ra'is) of those Amalekites.

And His words: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾: its meaning is "pour upon us."

And His words: ﴿and make our feet firm﴾, i.e., in the fighting, ﴿and help us against the disbelieving people.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 251:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: they broke them. It is said: a waterskin is "mihzam" and "munhazim", meaning: broken, with some of it folded over other parts.

His words ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: by His decree and His will.

His words: ﴿and David killed Goliath﴾. In the narrative it is related that David's father attended the battle together with thirteen of his sons, the youngest in age of whom was David. He had with him a sling and a catapult. Goliath came forward and demanded single combat, and David went out to him. He struck him with a stone from the sling between his eyes, and it came out from the back of his neck, and it also struck other people and killed them.

His words: ﴿and Allah gave him the kingdom and the wisdom﴾. He combined for David kingship and wisdom, meaning prophethood. It is said this was seven years after him (Goliath's death). Previously they had not been combined; rather kingship was in one tribe and prophethood in another tribe. It is also said: kingship and wisdom is knowledge together with action.

His words: ﴿and taught him of what He willed﴾. It is said: the craft of making coats of mail, the voices of birds, and the Psalms (al-Zabur).

His words: ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted﴾. Nafi' recited: "Wa-law-la difa' Allah" (and had it not been for the defense of Allah), and the meaning is one.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: its meaning is: had Allah not repelled the disbelievers by means of the believers, disbelief would have multiplied, wrath would have descended, and the earth would have been uprooted.

'Ali and the general body of exegetes said: Allah repels through the pious against the non-pious, through the righteous against the wicked, through the reformer against the non-reformer, and through the believer against the disbeliever. This is the meaning of the Prophet's saying: "Were it not for the elders who bow, the beasts that graze, and the infants who nurse, the punishment would have been poured upon you in a torrent."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah repels calamity through a righteous man from a hundred households of his family and neighbours."

His words: ﴿but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds﴾. Its meaning is clear.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿These are the verses of Allah; We recite them to you in truth, and indeed you are among the messengers﴾. "These" refers to the verses that were mentioned.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 253:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others.﴾ This verse explains that some messengers were given preference over others, although they are equal in the essential matter of prophethood.

His saying: ﴿Among them are those whom Allah spoke to.﴾ This refers to Musa (Moses).

His saying: ﴿And He raised some of them in rank.﴾ This refers to Muhammad. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) said: No prophet was given a sign except that our Prophet was given something like that sign. He was given the splitting of the moon, the moaning of the trunk (of the palm tree), the speech of the trees, water gushing from between the fingers, and the Great Qur'an. He was sent to the red and the black (all of mankind), whereas other prophets were sent to specific peoples.

His saying: ﴿And We gave Isa (Jesus), son of Maryam, the clear proofs and supported him with the Holy Spirit.﴾ This has already been mentioned.

His saying: ﴿And if Allah had willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them.﴾ This is evidence against the Qadariyya (Qadariyya, a theological school that affirmed human free will in a way that denied the universality of divine decree), since they attributed the fighting to the will (of humans) and not to the will of Allah.

His saying: ﴿But they differed: some of them believed and some of them disbelieved.﴾ Some of them were favored by Allah and so believed, and some of them were forsaken by Allah and so disbelieved.

His saying: ﴿And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought,⁠﴾ He repeated it a second time for emphasis. His saying: ﴿But Allah does what He intends.﴾ Its meaning is clear.

O you who have believed, spend from what We have provided for you before there comes a Day in which there is no exchange, nor friendship, nor intercession. And the disbelievers — they are the wrongdoers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 254:

Allah's words: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from what We have provided for you﴾. Al-Suddi said: He meant by it the obligatory zakat. Others said: He meant by it spending in the way of Allah. His words: ﴿before there comes a Day﴾ mean: the Day of Resurrection.

His words: ﴿in which there is no exchange (bay')﴾ mean: in it there is no ransom (fidyah). He called it "exchange" (bay') because in ransom there is a purchase of one's own self.

His words: ﴿nor friendship (khullah)﴾. If someone says: He has negated friendship here on the Day of Resurrection, yet He said in another verse: ﴿The friends on that Day will be enemies to one another﴾, and so He affirmed friendship.

It has been said: Its meaning is: the friends in the world will be enemies to one another on the Day of Resurrection. He only said ﴿nor friendship nor intercession﴾ because the disbelievers used to say: The angels are our friends and the idols are our intercessors. So He said: Their friendship will not benefit them, nor will their intercession.

His words: ﴿And the disbelievers — they are the wrongdoers﴾: the meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 255:

His saying, Most High: ﴿Allah, there is no god but He﴾ is mentioned as an intensification in praise, and it is like the saying of people: "No one is generous except so-and-so," which is more emphatic than their saying: "So-and-so is generous."

And His saying: ﴿the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. ʿUmar recited "al-Qiyam," and ʿAlqama recited "al-Qayyim," while the well-known reading is ﴿al-Qayyum﴾. So al-Hayy is the One who remains, enduring forever, and it is derived from life (ḥayāh).

Life is an attribute of God, Most High. As for al-Qayyum, it has been said: he is the One who stands over every person by His management in this world.

It has also been said: he is the One who stands over every soul with what it has earned, for recompense in the Hereafter.

And it has been said: he is the One who stands by (sustains) affairs.

And His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾. Al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī said: drowsiness (sinah) is in the head, and sleep (nawm) is in the heart, so sinah is the beginning of sleep, and it is nuʿās (light drowsiness).

Among them are those who distinguished between sinah and nuʿās, saying: sinah is in the head, nuʿās is in the eye, and nawm is in the heart.

Sleep is a heavy veil that falls upon the heart, preventing knowledge of things.

It is reported in the traditions that Moses, peace be upon him, said: "O Lord, do You sleep?" So God revealed to him: "O Moses, consider what you are saying. Take two flasks." He took them in his hands, and God cast sleep upon him, so one of them fell upon the other and both broke. God, Most High, said: "If I had sleep, neither the heavens nor the earth would have stood."

And His saying: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ ﴿...the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills. His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾

Because they claimed that the angels and idols would intercede for them, He said: ﴿Who is it that﴾ can intercede except with His approval.

And His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them﴾ means: the Hereafter, ﴿and what is behind them﴾ means: this world. It has also been said: ﴿what is before them﴾ is what they have sent forward, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ is what they have left behind.

And His saying: ﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills﴾.

Iḥāṭah (encompassing) is knowledge of a thing in all its aspects and kinds. Its meaning is: they do not encompass anything of the knowledge of the Unseen except what He wills, that is, except what the Messengers have been informed of. It is like His saying in Surat al-Jinn: ﴿He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾.

And His saying: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾. Yaʿqub al-Ḥaḍramī recited: "wasiʿa kursiyyuhu al-samawāti wa'l-arḍa," while the well-known reading is the first.

Scholars differed concerning the Kursi. Al-Ḥasan said: it is the Throne itself. Abū Hurayrah said: the Kursi is placed in front of the Throne.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾ is: its vastness is like the vastness of the heavens and the earth, and wider than them. This is evident in the reading of al-Ḥaḍramī. And in the traditions: "The heavens and the earth in comparison with the Kursi are like a ring in a desert, and the Kursi in comparison with the Throne is like a ring in a desert."

In the narration of ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās: the heavens and the earth in comparison with the Kursi are like seven dirhams on a shield.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he meant by the Kursi His knowledge. Similar to this is the saying of the poet: "My affair with You is no Kursi I conceal, nor is the Kursi of Allah's knowledge His creation."

Its meaning is: knowledge. It has also been said: it is His dominion and authority. Al-Zajjaj said: in general, it is a great matter indicating the completeness of His power.

And His saying: ﴿And their preservation does not weary Him﴾. It has been said: it refers to God, Most High, meaning: the preservation of the heavens and the earth does not weigh upon Him.

It has also been said: it refers to the Kursi. It has been said, on this view, that the Kursi is beneath the earth as the Throne is above the heavens, and the heavens and the earth are upon the Kursi. It has been said: they are suspended from the Kursi.

﴿And it does not weary him﴾, that is: the preservation of the heavens and the earth does not burden the Kursi.

﴿And He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾. By "the Most High" is meant: exalted above things and rivals.

It has also been said: "the Most High" in dominion and sovereignty. And "the Great": the Grand.

Reports have been transmitted concerning the excellence of Ayat al-Kursi, among them:

What was related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "Which is the greatest verse in the Qur'an?" He said: "Ayat al-Kursi." He (ﷺ) said: "May knowledge be pleasant for you, Abu'l-Mundhir."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 256:

His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ It is said: the occasion of the revelation of the verse was that a woman from the people of Madina, whose children would not survive, used to make a vow and say, "If a child of mine survives, I will make him a Jew." When a child of hers survived, she would place him among the Jews. Then, when Islam came and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) expelled the Banu al-Nadir to al-Sham, a number of the sons of the Ansar who had become Jews remained among them, and they asked the Messenger of Allah for permission to retrieve them. So the verse was revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ Whoever among them wishes to enter Islam, let him enter, and whoever does not wish, there is no compulsion in religion.

Al-Sha'bi said: this refers to the People of the Book, who are not compelled to accept Islam when they offer the jizya (poll tax).

There is a third view: that it was at the beginning, and then it was abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of fighting.

His saying: ﴿The right course has become distinct from the error.﴾ That is, the truth from falsehood, and faith from disbelief.

His saying: ﴿So whoever disbelieves in the Taghut and believes in Allah...﴾ The Taghut (the object of worship other than Allah, or a transgressor) is the Shaytan, and the term applies to the singular and the plural. It is also said: everything that is worshipped besides Allah is a taghut.

As for the taghut in His saying: ﴿They wish to take their disputes to the Taghut﴾, it refers specifically to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf.

His saying: ﴿Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which has no breaking.﴾ The 'urwa (handhold): the handle of a pitcher and of a bucket. What is meant here by the "trustworthy handhold" is a firm, sound bond in the religion.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the statement "There is no god but Allah." Mujahid said: it means Islam. It is also said: it is the Qur'an, and its meaning is: he has held fast to a firm holding.

﴿It has no breaking﴾, that is, it has no severance. ﴿And Allah is Hearing﴾ of your calling them to Islam, ﴿Knowing﴾ of your eagerness for their acceptance of Islam.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 257:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah is the Guardian (walī) of those who believe﴾, meaning: the One who watches over them with victory, help and reward.

And His saying: ﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾, meaning: from disbelief (kufr) into Islam. He called disbelief "darknesses" because the path of disbelief is confused and ambiguous. He called Islam "light" because its path is clear and evident.

And His saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their guardians are the taghut; they bring them out of the light into the darknesses﴾, that is: from Islam into disbelief.

If someone says: How can they bring them out of Islam when they never entered it? It is said: this refers specifically to a group of apostates (murtaddīn).

It is also said: it is general. That is because when they deviated and turned away from Islam, it was as if they had been expelled from it. A man says to another: "You have expelled me from your kindness (ṣila)," meaning: you did not give me, and you did not show me kindness.

And His saying: ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever﴾, its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 258:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ Its meaning: Has the report of the one who argued with Abraham reached you? He was Nimrod. This was said by Qatadah.

He was the first to act tyrannically on earth and to claim lordship. Al-muhajjah (argument) means al-mujadalah (disputation). Then he explains the argument within the context of the verse.

His saying: ﴿that Allah had given him the kingdom﴾ means: that argument about lordship was from the authority of the kingship and its tyranny.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When Abraham said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death."﴾ In the narratives it is related that the people suffered a famine in the time of Nimrod, and they used to seek food from him. Whenever a man came to him seeking food, he would ask him, "Who is your lord?" If he said, "You," he would sell him food. Abraham came to him among those who came seeking food, and Nimrod said to him, "Who is your lord?" He said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." Nimrod was occupied with the argument and did not give him anything, so Abraham turned away from him and passed by a heap of sand, and he filled the sacks with it to comfort the hearts of his family. When he reached his home, there was flour in them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "I give life and cause death."﴾ This is the saying of Nimrod when Abraham said to him, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death."

Sufyan said: He summoned two men, one of whom deserved execution, so he killed one of them and did not kill the other. This was his giving life and causing death.

His saying: ﴿Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west."﴾ If someone says: Why did Abraham move from one argument to another, and does this not amount to incapacity? It is said: The first argument was binding, and Nimrod's counter-argument to it was invalid, because he meant by life and death the creating of them, whereas he did not oppose him with the like of that. But Abraham feared that it might be confused for the listeners, so he brought an argument clearer than the first, as an exaggeration in imposing the proof and a cutting off of confusion.

His saying: ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded.﴾ That is: he was bewildered by the overwhelming of the argument against him. From this is the saying of the poet:

(And it was nothing but that I saw her suddenly, so I was bewildered until I could hardly answer.)

If someone says: How was he confounded, when he could have opposed Abraham by saying to him, "Ask your Lord to bring it from the west"? We say: He did not say it only because he feared that if he asked him that, He would supplicate and bring it from the west, and that would have been an increase in his disgrace and defeat.

The correct view is that Allah turned him away from that counter-argument as a manifestation of the proof against him, and so that it would be a miracle for Abraham.

His saying: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ Its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 259:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾. Its implied meaning: "Have you not seen the one who argued with Ibrahim, and the one who passed by a town?"

It was also said: its implied meaning is: "Have you not seen someone like the one who argued with Ibrahim, and like the one who passed by a town?"

﴿Its roofs fallen in. He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him up. He said, "How long did you remain?"﴾

The scholars differed concerning the one who passed by the town. Qatadah said: he was the Prophet Uzair. Wahb said: he was the Prophet Irmiya. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: he was al-Khidr, peace be upon them.

The sound view is that he was the Prophet Uzair, who passed by a town, meaning Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

As for His saying: ﴿and it was desolate upon its roofs﴾, it was said: the ceilings had fallen onto the ground, and the walls had collapsed onto the ceilings, so it was "desolate upon its roofs" (ʿurush, the roofs or frameworks). Its meaning is that it was empty, and that Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar), the Babylonian king, had ruined it.

As for His saying: ﴿He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?"﴾ In the story: Uzair passed by it while he was on a donkey, and with him were figs and grape juice. He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?!"

If someone says: how could he say "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?", when this would be caused by doubt about His power? It is answered: he was not in doubt about it; he only said that out of astonishment at what is customary among people, meaning: Allah will not bring this to life after its ruin.

ʿAta said: what enters people's hearts entered his heart.

As for His saying: ﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him up﴾, meaning: He brought him back to life. The revival is called "raising" (baʿth) because when one is brought back to life, he is roused to affairs.

In the story: when he uttered that statement, sleep overcame him, and Allah took his soul for a hundred years, and sent an angel who restored Bayt al-Maqdis during those years. Then, when He revived him, He sent to him an angel who asked him: "How long did you remain?"

This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿He said, "How long did you remain?"﴾ And His saying: ﴿He said, "I remained a day or part of a day."﴾ Because Allah had caused him to die at the beginning of the day and raised him at the end of the day, before sunset, so he said: ﴿"I remained a day or part of a day."﴾ He said, ﴿"Rather, you remained a hundred years. But look at your food and your drink; they have not changed with time. And look at your donkey—and that We may make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them up﴾ — he remained a day. Then he looked at the sun, and it had not yet set, so he said: "or part of a day." ﴿He said﴾, meaning the angel: ﴿"Rather, you remained a hundred years. But look at your food and your drink; they have not changed"﴾, meaning they had not altered. The figs he had with him had not changed; it was as if they had been picked that very hour, and likewise the juice was as if it had been pressed that very hour.

Al-Kisa'i said: "lam yatasanna" means that it was as though the years had not passed over it, and it had been picked that very hour.

Mujahid said: its meaning is "it did not become foul-smelling," and from it is His saying: ﴿from black mud, moulded﴾ (ḥamaʾ masnun).

It was also said: its original form was "lam yatasannan," and one of the two nuns was changed into a hāʾ, and similar examples are numerous in the speech of the Arabs, such as "yatamaṭṭa," which originally was "yatamaṭṭaṭ," and one of the two ṭāʾs was changed into a yāʾ. The poet said: "yaqḍī al-bāzī idhā al-bāzī inkasar..." and originally it was "yaqaḍḍḍ al-bāzī."

As for His saying: ﴿And look at your donkey﴾, it was said: he looked, and behold, white bones were shining and decayed. Allah assembled the bones, some upon others, and made a donkey of bones; then He put flesh into it, then covered it with skin, then breathed the spirit into it, and the donkey stood up and brayed while he was looking at it. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and that We may make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them up﴾. It is read with two readings: with the letter rāʾ, "nuḥyīhā" (We bring them to life); and with the letter zāy, "yarkabu baʿḍuhā ʿalā baʿḍ" (some are mounted upon others), from al-nashz, which means elevation.

As for His saying: ﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾, in the verse there is inversion and rearrangement, and its sequence is: "And look at your donkey, and look at the bones, how We raise them up, then We clothe them with flesh, so that We may bring them to life."

As for His saying: ﴿and that We may make you a sign for the people﴾, the explanation of the sign in it is that he was raised as a young man while his son was an old man.

ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Allah caused him to die at the age of fifty, while his wife was pregnant; then he was raised after a hundred years, at the age of fifty, while his son was a hundred years old.

As for His saying: ﴿So when it became clear to him, he said, "I know"﴾, meaning: when the power of Allah to restore Bayt al-Maqdis and to revive the dead became manifest to him, ﴿he said, "I know"﴾. It is read with two readings: as a statement, and as a command. As a statement, its meaning is: "I know that Allah is over all things capable." As a command, he said to himself: ﴿"Know that Allah is over all things capable."﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 260:

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."﴾ It has been said: the reason for his request was that Abraham passed by an animal on the shore of the sea that had been torn apart by beasts of prey and wild animals, and fish of the sea were eating from it. So he said: "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."

There is another view: when Nimrod disputed with him about the giving of life to the dead, he wanted to know by direct observation what he had believed through report and reasoning.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Have you not believed?"﴾ meaning: "Have you not already believed, so that you do not ask?" This is like the saying of the poet:

(Are you not the best of those who have ridden the mounts...)

meaning: you are like that.

His statement: ﴿He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest."⁠﴾ If someone says: Was Abraham doubting it, ﴿so that my heart may be at rest⁠﴾? ﴿He said, "Take four birds and make them incline toward you. Then place on every mountain a portion of them"⁠﴾, until he needed to ask? And what is the meaning of his, peace be upon him, saying: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham"? The answer: he was not doubting it, but he had believed through report and reasoning, so he wanted to know it by direct observation.

ʿIkrimah said: so that he might increase in certainty upon certainty, because direct observation is higher than report in the elevation of knowledge. The Prophet, peace be upon him, also said: "Report is not like witnessing."

As for his statement: ﴿but so that my heart may be at rest⁠﴾: when he asked for that, his heart became attached to it, so he said: "but so that my heart may be at rest" from that attachment.

It has also been said: he said that because when Allah Exalted took him as a close friend (khalil), the Angel of Death said: "O Lord, permit me to give him good news." So he gave him the good news that Allah had taken him as a close friend. Abraham wanted Allah to show him the giving of life to the dead, singling him out with that honour, so that his heart might be at rest through the friendship.

It has also been said that its meaning is: "but so that my heart may be at rest, so that I may know that when I ask You, You give me, and when I call upon You, You answer me." As for his saying, "We have more right to doubt than Abraham," he said it by way of humility, meaning: we are lesser than him, and more deserving of doubt than him. So if we do not doubt, how would Abraham doubt?

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Take four birds"⁠﴾. It has been said: they are the peacock, the rooster, the dove, and the crow.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Then make them incline toward you⁠﴾, that is: gather them to yourself. Hamzah read it with a kasra on the ṣād (ṣurhunna).

There is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, and its sense is: "Take four birds to yourself, then cut them up (faṣurhunna)," that is: cut them into pieces.

His statement: ﴿Then place on every mountain a portion of them⁠﴾. It has been said: he placed them on four mountains.

Al-Suddi said: on seven mountains. Ibn ʿAbbas said: on four quarters of the world, a portion on a mountain beside the east, a portion on a mountain beside the west, a portion to the north, and a portion to the south.

There is another view: by his saying, ﴿place on every mountain a portion of them⁠﴾, he meant a tenth, and it was on ten mountains; some scholars went so far as to derive from this that if a person bequeaths a portion of his property, it is taken to mean a tenth.

His statement: ﴿Then call them; they will come to you in haste⁠﴾. In the narrative: he dismembered those four birds, mixed the flesh with the flesh, the feathers with the feathers, and the bone with the bone, and placed them on the mountains.

It has also been said: he pounded them in a mortar and took their heads between his fingers, and it is said: their beaks. Then he called them, and the feathers would fly to the feathers, the flesh to the flesh, the blood to the blood, and some would be joined upon others, and they came hastening to their heads.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And know that Allah is Mighty, Wise⁠﴾, its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 261:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾. It was said: "The way of Allah" is jihad (struggle in the cause of God).

It was also said: all the doors of goodness are the way of Allah.

And His saying: ﴿is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains﴾. He struck this as a parable for the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) and for what He promised of reward for spending.

If someone says: How is this given as a parable, and is it conceivable that each ear has a hundred grains?

It is said: since that was conceivable in general, it is valid to strike the parable with it, even if it is not known in detail. Similar to this is what Imru' al-Qays said:

(And a sharpened, blue-black [blade] like the fangs of ghouls...)

The fang of the ghoul is not known, but since its existence was conceivable in general, it was used as a comparison. It was also said: it is conceivable in the ear of millet (al-dukhn) and the like.

His saying: ﴿And Allah multiplies [it] for whom He wills﴾. It was said: its meaning is: He multiplies this multiplication for whom He wills. It was also said: its meaning is that He multiplies upon this and increases for whom He wills.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, meaning: encompassing in bounty, mercy and power, giving out of abundance.

His saying: ﴿All-Knowing﴾, meaning: knowing the intention of the one who gives.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 262:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders (of their generosity) or injury﴾. As for al-Mann (reminding of favour): it is that one says to the poor man, "I gave you such-and-such, and I did such-and-such for you," enumerating his favours upon him. As for al-Adha (injury): it is that one reproaches the poor man, saying to him, "How long will you keep asking, and how much will you keep hurting me? You will never cease being poor," and the like.

It has also been said: among injury is that one mentions his spending upon him in the presence of those who do not wish to know of it.

And His words: ﴿For them is their reward with their Lord﴾, that is, their recompense. His words: ﴿and no fear shall be upon them﴾, meaning they do not fear the loss of the reward. His words: ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾, that is, over what they spent, when they see the reward.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 263:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a kind word﴾. Al-Hasan said: it is the beautiful speech.

It has also been said: it is that he gives to him and blesses him for it, so he says, "May Allah bless you in it," or he withholds and prays for him.

As for His saying, ﴿and forgiveness﴾, it means: that you conceal his need and do not expose his concealment.

It has also been said: it is that you pardon the poor person if some offense or harm comes from him.

As for His saying, ﴿better than charity followed by injury﴾, He says: that kind word, and that forgiveness, are better than charity followed by injury.

As for His saying, ﴿and Allah is Free of need﴾, meaning: He is independent of your charities. As for His saying, ﴿Forbearing﴾, meaning: He does not hasten to punishment when you withhold charity.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 264:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders [of your generosity] or injury﴾ — we have already mentioned their meanings.

It has also been said: reminding [of one's charity] (al-mann) in charity is like a minor ritual impurity (hadath) in prayer, which nullifies it and renders it void.

His saying: ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by the people﴾ means: like the invalidation of the one who spends his wealth to be seen by the people, because showing off (riya') nullifies and voids charity.

His saying: ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ means: spending together with showing off is not the act of believers.

In general, whoever brings charity seeking nearness to a created being is not a believer.

His saying: ﴿So his example is like a smooth stone with dust on it﴾ — al-safwan: the hard, smooth stone.

His saying: ﴿and a heavy rain strikes it﴾ — al-wabil: the intense rain with large drops.

His saying: ﴿and leaves it bare⁠﴾ — i.e., smooth, ﴿not having power over anything of what they have earned.﴾ The meaning of this parable is that the one who shows off in spending scatters his expenditure and gains nothing of the reward, like the dust that is on the stone, so the heavy rain strikes it and the dust is lost, and the stone remains smooth, such that one cannot take anything from it.

His saying: ﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ — its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 265:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the approval of Allah﴾ meaning: sincerely for the sake of Allah's countenance.

And His saying: ﴿and as a strengthening from themselves﴾. Qatada said: it means that he spends seeking reward (ihtisab) from his giving.

Al-Hasan said: it means that he strengthens himself, so that if his intention is to give charity for Allah's sake, he acts, and if his intention is otherwise, he withholds. Al-Kalbi and al-Sha'bi said: it means that he gives charity with certainty of the reward and belief in Allah's promise concerning it.

And His saying: ﴿like a garden on a elevated ground﴾. The janna (garden): the orchard. The rabwa (elevated ground): the high place.

And His saying: ﴿a heavy rain strikes it﴾, as we have mentioned. And His saying: ﴿and it produces its yield twofold﴾, meaning: its fruit is double what other gardens yield. His saying: ﴿but if heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain (tall)﴾. The tall: the light rain of small drops, and it is continuous.

The meaning of this parable is that the one who spends sincerely for the sake of Allah, exalted is He, his spending does not go to waste, but grows and increases in every condition, just as the garden on the elevated ground does not fail, but grows and flourishes in every condition, whether it is struck by a heavy rain or by a light rain; for light rain, when it persists, produces the effect of a strong heavy rain.

His saying: ﴿and Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 266:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, beneath which rivers flow, with all kinds of fruits for him therein, and old age has overtaken him while he has weak offspring?﴾ That is, young children.

﴿Then it was struck by a whirlwind containing fire, and it was burned.﴾ The i'sar (whirlwind): a wind that rises up like a pillar toward the sky. The Arabs call it that, while all other people call it zawba'ah (dust devil). From it is the saying of the poet:

(If you were a wind, then you have met a whirlwind...)

As for the meaning of the verse: it is narrated that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, asked the Companions about the meaning of this verse. They said: "Allah knows best." ʿUmar became angry and said: "Say: 'We know,' or 'We do not know,' for we know that Allah knows." So they fell silent. Ibn ʿAbbas was among them and said: "There is something in my heart." ʿUmar said to him: "Speak, and do not belittle yourself; you have been given an example of an action." He related the complete explanation of it. Then they differed: some said the complete explanation came from ʿUmar, and some said it came from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Its completion is: Allah, exalted is He, struck this as an example for one who labors his whole life at an action, then nullifies it through showing off or through something at the end of his life, so that he loses it and it does not benefit him at the time he is most in need of it. It is like one who has a garden with trees, fruits and rivers, and old age overtakes him while he has a large dependent family and his children are young. When its maturity approaches and he needs it, a fire strikes it and burns it, so he loses it, and he cannot spend from it at the time he is most in need of it.

His saying: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs, that you may reflect.﴾ The meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 267:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned﴾, meaning: from the lawful (ḥalāl) of what you have earned. In this there is an indication that earning is of two kinds: good (ṭayyib) and bad (khabīth).

And His saying: ﴿and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾. It has been said: this is the command to pay the ʿushr (tithe on produce).

It has also been said: it is a command to pay the rights that were obligatory on the produce of the earth at the beginning, and which were then abrogated (mansūkh) by the verses of zakāt.

It has also been said: it refers to voluntary charity (ṣadaqāt al-taṭawwuʿ).

And His saying: ﴿and do not aim at the bad of it, to spend from it﴾. Tayammum (aiming, intending) means to intend something. By "the bad" (al-khabīth) he means here the inferior (radīʾ), that is: do not intend to spend the inferior part of it.

The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl) of the verse: it has been related that the owners of palm trees in the time of the Messenger of Allah used to bring a cluster (qinw) and hang it in the mosque so that the poor could eat it. A man brought a cluster of dry, worthless dates (ḥashf), wanting the worst kind, and hung it up, and the Messenger of Allah did not approve of it, and the verse was revealed: ﴿and do not aim at the bad of it, to spend from it﴾.

And His saying: ﴿while you would not take it except with closing your eyes to it﴾, meaning: except that you be lenient and tolerant in accepting it. Its meaning is: if a right were yours upon another, and he came with it inferior, you would not take it except by overlooking its defect, and you would consider that you had left part of your right and overlooked it.

And His saying: ﴿and know that Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾. He gives out of sufficiency (ghanā), praised in His sufficiency. In this is evidence that sufficiency belonging to other than Allah is blameworthy.

It has been said: al-Ḥamīd is the one deserving of praise.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 268:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾, i.e., he frightens you with poverty, and the preposition bi (with) is omitted.

And His saying: ﴿and commands you to indecency﴾, i.e., to the effect that you do not give charity and become stingy. From this is the saying of Tarafa:

(The noble wife of the wealth of the immoderate, the rigid one...)

i.e., the stingy, the rigid one.

Stinginess is a great disease; he (ﷺ) said, "There is no disease more harmful than stinginess."

And His saying: ﴿But Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾, forgiveness, i.e., the pardon of Allah, and bounty, i.e., with reward.

And His saying: ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾. We have already mentioned their meanings.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 269:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: This is the wisdom of the Qur'an, which is that one knows its abrogating (nasikh) and abrogated (mansukh) verses, its preceding and succeeding passages, its decisive (muhkam) and ambiguous (mutashabih) verses, its lawful (haram) and permitted (halal) matters, and its parables (amthal).

It was also said: It is the understanding of the religion (al-fiqh fi al-din).

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: It is knowing the meanings of things and understanding them.

And there is a fourth opinion concerning it: It is correctness (al-isabah) in both action and speech.

And His saying: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good. But none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾.

Ya'qub recited: "wa man yu'ti" with a kasra on the ta', meaning: and whoever God gives wisdom to.

It was said: This wisdom is writing and knowledge of penmanship.

It was also said: It is reason ('aql). And it was said: It is trustworthiness (amanah).

﴿But none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾, meaning: none will reflect except those possessing intellects.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 270:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whatever expenditure you spend or vow you vow﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions. One: that what is meant by "expenditure" is the obligatory zakat, and as for "vow," it is that one intends to do good and voluntary charity.

The second opinion: that "expenditure" is voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu'), and as for "vow," it is what is known as the vow of the tongue (nadhr al-lisan), which is that one makes it obligatory upon oneself to give charity.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah knows it﴾ — that is, He will recompense it. Mujahid said: He will count it.

His saying: ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ — that is, those who give charity from usurped and plundered property. ﴿Helpers﴾ is the plural of nasir, that is, they have no one who will support them or protect them from the punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 271:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾, its meaning: if you make them apparent. ﴿Then how excellent they are﴾ is read in the recitations with a fatḥa on the nūn and a kasra on the ʿayn, and it is read with kasra on both. Abū ʿAmr read it with a kasra on the nūn and a jazm (sukūn) on the ʿayn, and the grammarians of Basra (naḥwiyyūn, the grammarians) did not approve of this from him. They said that in it there is iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn (the meeting of two consecutive unvocalised letters). Abū ʿAmr cited in support his saying to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs: "Excellent is the good wealth for the righteous man." All of these are the same in meaning. Its meaning is: excellent is the act of giving, or excellent is the thing it is.

His saying: ﴿But if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾. It was said: this refers to voluntary charities (taṭawwuʿ), and concealment in them is better. It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The charity given in secret surpasses the charity given openly by seventy times."

As for the obligatory zakat: making it apparent in it is better. He (ﷺ) said: "The charity given openly surpasses the charity given in secret by twenty-five," and this is regarding zakat, while the first is regarding voluntary charities.

It was said: the verse refers to obligatory zakat, and concealment was better in all cases during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). But in our time, making it apparent is better in zakat because of the corruption of the times, lest suspicion fall upon him.

His saying: ﴿And will expiate from you﴾ is read with the nūn and with the yāʾ, and it is read with raf (ḍamma) and with jazm. ﴿From your misdeeds﴾: it was said that "min" is extra (ṣila) in it, and its implied sense is: "and will expiate your misdeeds from you." On this view, it includes minor and major sins.

There is another view: that "min" is partitive, and that expiation through charities applies to minor sins, whereas major sins are expiated only by repentance (tawba).

The first view is closer to the Ahl al-Sunna, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Secret charity extinguishes the anger of the Lord."

His saying: ﴿And Allah is All-Aware of what you do﴾: this is the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 272:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾. What is meant by it is not the guidance of invitation (hidayat al-da'wah), for that is obligatory upon him (the Prophet). What is meant by it is the guidance of success (hidayat al-tawfiq).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The occasion of revelation of the verse is what is related: that the Prophet forbade giving charity to the polytheists, and he forbade it only so that need would compel them to enter Islam. So the verse was revealed, and the Prophet commanded giving charity to the people of all religions."

Its meaning: It is not upon you to guide them, by compelling them and forcing them to enter Islam. ﴿But God guides whom He wills﴾, that is, He grants success to whom He wills and forsakes whom He wills.

His saying: ﴿And whatever good you spend is for yourselves﴾, that is, you do it for your own selves.

His saying: ﴿And you do not spend except seeking the Face of God﴾. This is a statement in the sense of a command, that is: spend for the sake of God's Face. Its meaning: seeking the pleasure of God.

It was also said: this is hyperbole (al-mubalaghah), for the saying of a man, "I did it for the sake of so-and-so's face," is more emphatic and more noble than his saying, "I did it for so-and-so." So we have mentioned the nobility of the two expressions.

His saying: ﴿And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full﴾, that is, its reward will be fully credited to you.

﴿And you will not be wronged﴾: clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 2, verse 273:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For the poor who are restricted in the way of Allah﴾ means: those charities previously mentioned are for the poor.

Mujahid said: He meant by it the poor among the Emigrants from Makkah.
